title: API Design
heading: Overview
text: Contracts, HTTP semantics, security, reliability, and three complete API design cases.

title: API Design
heading: 1. Start with the contract
text: 1. Start with the contract Before choosing REST, gRPC, a database, or a cloud service, write what a caller can ask for and what the service promises in return. A contract includes syntax and behavior: status codes, side effects, retries, consistency, and failure states. Follow one caller creating an order. The caller knows what it wants, but cannot see the server’s database transaction. It must learn the outcome through the documented response or a later status lookup. That is why a contract needs more than a JSON schema: the same valid body can mean “accepted for processing,” “committed,” or “rejected” depending on the agreed semantics. Before selecting a status code, write what a caller may safely do next. After success, may it display a confirmed order? After a timeout, may it retry with the same identity? After a validation error, which input must change? Those next actions turn an interface description into a usable agreement between independently changing systems. Syntax Methods, paths, headers, media types, schemas, required fields, and examples. OpenAPI can describe much of this mechanically. Semantics What the operation means, when it commits, whether it is safe to repeat, and how a caller discovers the final state. Compatibility Which additions are safe, which changes break clients, and how deprecated behavior will be retired. Operational promise Latency, availability, limits, freshness, consistency, and observability expectations that clients rely on. Client intent → API contract → Implementation → Observable outcome Design the observable outcome first. Internal classes and tables are implementation details. Example: payment creation contract POST /v1/payments Idempotency-Key: checkout-8f2a Content-Type: application/json { "amount": 49900, "currency": "INR", "orderId": "ord_123" } 201 Created { "id": "pay_7", "status": "AUTHORIZED" } 202 Accepted { "id": "pay_7", "status": "PROCESSING", "statusUrl": "/v1/payments/pay_7" } 409 Conflict { "code": "IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED", "message": "Payload differs" } The contract documents the identity key, replay behavior, conflict behavior, and asynchronous possibility. Those details matter more than whether the handler is written in Spring or Node.

title: API Design
heading: Before the mechanisms: follow one order
text: Before the mechanisms: follow one order An API contract describes what a caller may ask, what the service promises, and how the caller interprets success or failure. Begin with a customer submitting an order. The service must validate the request, decide whether the operation is allowed, commit the relevant facts and return a result. Those are separate responsibilities; a JSON schema alone cannot describe all of them. Now change one detail at a time. Two buyers request the last item: we need an atomic inventory decision. The customer sends the request again: we need operation identity and repeat-safe effects. The database commits but the response disappears: the caller has uncertainty, not proof of failure. Fulfillment takes minutes: acceptance must be distinguished from completion. Each later section supplies a mechanism for one of these problems. Read the lesson in that order of reasoning. Define the business invariant first, then the contract, then the authority that enforces it. Only afterward select an HTTP header, Spring library or AWS service. For each example, ask which facts are durable, which copies may be stale and which remote outcomes remain unknown. Check your understanding: Why does a 202 response not prove an order shipped? It promises acceptance according to the documented contract; completion needs a durable status path and separate recovery. Why does a timeout not prove creation failed? The response can disappear after the commit. After this lesson, use decision guides , failure investigations and the revision toolkit to apply the concepts.

title: API Design
heading: 2. Separate functional and non-functional requirements
text: 2. Separate functional and non-functional requirements Functional requirements describe what the API does. Non-functional requirements describe the conditions under which it must continue doing it. Add invariants: statements that must remain true even during retries, crashes, and concurrent requests. Use the order journey to separate three kinds of statements. “Create an order and retrieve its status” is functional behavior. “Most eligible status reads finish within 200 ms” is a measurable target. “Never allocate the same final unit twice” is an invariant. A latency target can have an error budget; an invariant defines an outcome the design must prevent. Then add constraints: current database, client capabilities, provider behavior and team operating skills. Two designs can satisfy the same happy path but differ under concurrency or a lost response. Write the expected failure behavior now so it participates in solution selection instead of becoming an undocumented surprise later. Functional Create, retrieve, update, cancel, or delete a resource. Validate fields and enforce business transitions. Return a stable error shape and status. Notify downstream systems or expose job status. Non-functional p95 read latency under 200 ms; p99 write latency under 800 ms. 99.95% monthly availability and bounded blast radius. Never charge one order twice; isolate tenants. Trace every request and recover from dependency timeouts. Requirement worksheet Question Example answer Design consequence Who calls it? Mobile clients and an internal checkout service Versioned REST; tolerant response parsing; OAuth scopes What is the peak? 8,000 writes/s during a sale Rate limits, queueing, partitioned ledger, load testing What must never happen? Two shipments for one order Unique order invariant, idempotent command, transactional state change What can be delayed? Receipt email and search indexing Outbox/event flow; return accepted status when needed What happens after timeout? Caller may retry without knowing commit state Idempotency key and status lookup are part of the contract

title: API Design
heading: 3. Model resources, actions, and state
text: 3. Model resources, actions, and state Use resources for durable nouns and actions for business commands that cannot be expressed safely as a generic update. A payment is a resource; “capture payment” is a command with a distinct invariant and side effect. Start with the facts the caller needs to identify over time. An order has stable identity and a lifecycle, so it is a resource. A capture changes a payment’s business state and may cause an external effect, so it deserves explicit command semantics. Neither choice should expose the names of your Java classes or database tables. Now ask what a generic update would permit. If clients can set status to SHIPPED, they may bypass payment or inventory rules. A named command or constrained transition expresses the business intent and lets the service check prerequisites. Naming alone provides no safety: enforce the transition atomically where competing updates are coordinated. Need Good shape Reason Read a resource GET /orders/{id} Safe and cacheable when authorized. Create with client intent POST /orders + idempotency key Server assigns identity; retries do not duplicate. Replace a known representation PUT /profiles/{id} Repeatable replacement semantics. Partial change PATCH /orders/{id} with explicit rules Avoid accidental field resets. Business command POST /payments/{id}/capture Names a state transition and its authorization. State machines beat boolean flags Define legal transitions before writing update code. For an order, CREATED → PAID → FULFILLING → SHIPPED is clearer than independently toggling paid , cancelled , and shipped . Reject impossible transitions with a conflict response and record who or what attempted them. Common modeling trap. POST /orders/{id}/status with an arbitrary string moves validation into every client. Prefer a named command or a constrained transition endpoint with a documented state graph.

title: API Design
heading: 4. Reliability is part of the API
text: 4. Reliability is part of the API Most production API bugs appear between the request and the response: a client times out after the server commits, a proxy retries a body, or a dependency returns slowly. Design the uncertain path explicitly. Keep the order identity fixed and remove the response from the timeline. The database may already contain the order while the caller sees only a timeout. A repeat request is now an attempt to learn or complete the same intention, rather than necessarily a new purchase. A fresh random request ID for each HTTP attempt cannot by itself connect those intentions. An idempotency policy therefore needs an operation identity, its scope, rules for payload mismatch, concurrent duplicates, retention and recovery of a committed outcome. The local effect and its duplicate guard must share a sound atomic boundary. If payment is remote, describe its boundary separately; a local transaction cannot roll back a provider that already acted. Can the operation be repeated safely? Use naturally idempotent methods where possible. For a non-idempotent command, define an idempotency key or a domain identity such as orderId . Where is the effect committed? Put request identity and the local effect in one transaction. A cache lock alone cannot prove that a charge or shipment happened. Can the dependency be queried? Persist a durable intent and reconcile an IN_DOUBT state when the provider result is unknown. How should a caller retry? Publish timeout, retryable status, backoff, jitter, and key-retention behavior. Never tell callers to blindly retry every 500. Can work be asynchronous? Return 202 plus a status resource when completion exceeds the request budget. Make terminal states and expiry clear. Failure timeline Client sends POST → Server commits → Response lost → Retry returns same result The retry must look up the original outcome. A new database insert or a second provider call is the failure. Practical REST + Spring pattern Use a unique key in the database, a transaction around the ledger and local effect, and an explicit replay response. The key is scoped to the principal and operation, and the request fingerprint detects accidental reuse with a different payload. Illustrative Spring JDBC fragment @Transactional public PaymentResult create(String accountId, String key, CreatePayment cmd) { String hash = fingerprint(cmd); int inserted = jdbc.update(""" INSERT INTO api_idempotency(account_id, idem_key, request_hash, status) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 'IN_PROGRESS') ON CONFLICT (account_id, idem_key) DO NOTHING """, accountId, key, hash); if (inserted == 0) return replayOrConflict(accountId, key, hash); Payment payment = paymentRepository.insert(cmd); // same transaction jdbc.update("UPDATE api_idempotency SET status='SUCCEEDED', response=? WHERE ...", serialize(payment)); return PaymentResult.created(payment); } This fragment assumes one relational database and no remote charge inside the transaction. If a provider call is involved, use an outbox or durable intent plus reconciliation; do not pretend a database transaction spans the provider. Practical AWS mapping API Gateway can enforce auth, throttling, and request shape; Lambda or ECS runs the handler; DynamoDB conditional writes reserve a key; SQS buffers work; Step Functions models long-running recovery; CloudWatch and X-Ray expose outcomes. The managed service does not remove the need to define ownership, deduplication scope, retention, and replay semantics.

title: API Design
heading: 5. Security, abuse, and data boundaries
text: 5. Security, abuse, and data boundaries Authentication answers “who is calling?” Authorization answers “may this caller perform this operation on this resource?” Enforce both at the service boundary and again at sensitive data access points. Assume Alice and Bob can both sign in. Alice requests Bob’s order ID. The request can have a valid token and still be forbidden. First establish the principal under the expected issuer/audience policy, then decide whether that principal may perform this action on this specific resource. Carry the same rule into repository access, exports, queue handlers and support operations. A tenantId in JSON is input, not proof of membership. Return only permitted fields, and ensure denied requests cannot cause an observable side effect before the check. The Security lesson expands the credential and policy stages in detail. Concern Implementation example Pitfall Tenant isolation Derive tenant from a verified token; include it in every query predicate. Accepting tenantId from the body as authority. Replay protection Short-lived signed webhook timestamp + event ID ledger. Validating signature but accepting an old valid message. Abuse control Per-principal rate limit, body limit, query complexity limit. One global limit allowing a noisy tenant to starve others. Data exposure Separate write DTO and read DTO; redact secrets in logs. Serializing an entity and leaking internal fields.

title: API Design
heading: 6. Implementation choices in context
text: 6. Implementation choices in context We now have a contract and guarantees to enforce. Assign each guarantee to an owner before choosing a tool: HTTP handles transport semantics, an application service owns domain transitions, the database enforces local constraints, and a durable workflow handles progress beyond one commit boundary. A library supplies a mechanism inside that allocation of responsibilities. For example, Bean Validation can reject a negative quantity but cannot decide whether two buyers may both reserve the last item. Spring Security can validate a credential but still needs resource policy. A queue can preserve pending work but cannot prove a payment completed. Read each implementation tab by asking which requirement it enforces and which boundary remains outside it. Spring Boot HTTP / REST AWS Spring Boot building blocks @RestController for transport; DTOs for input/output; Bean Validation for shape checks. @ControllerAdvice for a stable error envelope and correlation ID. @Transactional for local atomicity, with awareness of proxy/self-invocation boundaries. Spring Security method/resource authorization; WebClient/RestClient timeouts and bounded retries. JdbcTemplate or JPA plus a database uniqueness constraint for idempotency and concurrency. @PostMapping("/v1/orders") ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> create( @RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String key, @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest request) { return ResponseEntity.status(CREATED).body(service.create(key, request)); } HTTP / REST building blocks Use method semantics, status codes, conditional requests, cache controls, content negotiation, and a documented error format. ETags with If-Match protect against lost updates; Location points to a new resource; Retry-After communicates throttling or delayed retry. 412 Precondition Failed // If-Match version is stale 429 Too Many Requests // include Retry-After 409 Conflict // valid request conflicts with current state 202 Accepted // work is queued; provide status URL AWS building blocks API Gateway or ALB terminates traffic; Cognito or an external issuer supplies identity; WAF filters abuse; Lambda/ECS/EKS executes business logic; RDS supplies relational constraints; DynamoDB supplies conditional writes; SQS/EventBridge decouple work; CloudWatch metrics and X-Ray traces show the path. Selection rule: choose a service because it supplies a required guarantee—conditional write, durable queue, isolation, or operational scale—not because its name appears in an architecture diagram. Choosing a solution deliberately Constraint Likely choice Why Strong multi-row invariant Relational transaction Constraints and atomic commit are first-class. Single-key conditional state at high scale DynamoDB conditional write Atomic decision on one item without a join. Slow or bursty downstream work SQS + worker + status resource Buffers load and makes retry ownership explicit. Concurrent update of a representation ETag + If-Match Rejects stale writes without a global lock.

title: API Design
heading: 7. Tricky use cases to reason through
text: 7. Tricky use cases to reason through Case A — “The client did not send an idempotency key” tricky A mobile client retries a payment after a timeout, but the original request had no key. Reasoning: Do not hash the whole payload and assume equal payload means equal intent: two legitimate ₹499 payments can look identical. Prefer a server-issued checkout/order ID, a prior create-intent, or require a key for operations with irreversible side effects. If no identity exists, expose an inquiry/reconciliation path and make the ambiguity visible. Case B — “The queue says exactly once” tricky An SQS FIFO queue deduplicates repeated sends within its deduplication window, but a worker can still crash after shipping and before acknowledging. Reasoning: Delivery deduplication is not effect deduplication. Keep an inbox keyed by event ID or business command ID, commit the shipment state and inbox record atomically, then acknowledge. Make redelivery safe beyond the queue’s five-minute content-dedup window. Case C — “The PATCH succeeded but the response was stale” tricky A client updates an address while another device updates the same profile. Reasoning: Require If-Match: "v17" . The server applies the change only when the version matches and returns a new ETag. A 412 tells the client to refetch and merge. Last-write-wins is acceptable only when the product explicitly accepts lost updates. Case D — “The provider is IN_DOUBT” tricky Your timeout budget expires while a remote payment provider may have captured the card. Reasoning: Persist intent before calling the provider, use the provider’s idempotency key, record the provider request ID, and reconcile by lookup or webhook. Return 202 or a documented pending state. Never turn uncertainty into an automatic second charge.

title: API Design
heading: 8. Interview ladder: questions and answers
text: 8. Interview ladder: questions and answers Answer in layers: define the concept, state the invariant, choose a mechanism, explain failure behavior, then name a trade-off. Easy What makes an HTTP method idempotent? Repeating the same request has the same intended server-side effect as sending it once. It does not require the same response bytes. GET , PUT , and DELETE are defined as idempotent by HTTP semantics; a POST can be made safely repeatable with an application-level key. Easy When would you return 201, 202, 204, 409, and 422? 201 means a resource was created; 202 means accepted for later processing; 204 means success with no body; 409 means a state conflict such as a duplicate identity or stale workflow; 422 is useful for semantically invalid input when your API convention distinguishes it from malformed syntax. Easy Why use DTOs instead of returning JPA entities? DTOs keep persistence shape, security, and API compatibility separate. They prevent accidental lazy-loading or secret exposure and let the API evolve without making database refactoring a breaking change. Intermediate Offset pagination or cursor pagination? Offset is simple and useful for small, stable datasets. Cursor pagination scales better and avoids skipping or repeating rows when data changes, provided the cursor encodes a stable ordering and is treated as opaque. Always cap page size and define ordering. Intermediate How do you prevent lost updates? Use optimistic concurrency: return a version or ETag, require If-Match , and update only when the version still matches. Return 412 or a documented conflict. A lock may be appropriate for short local transactions, but it is not a safe cross-request or cross-service coordination mechanism by itself. Intermediate Where should retry logic live? Retry transient, bounded failures at the caller that understands the operation and can preserve identity. Use deadlines, exponential backoff, jitter, and a retry budget. Do not stack independent retries in gateway, client, service, and SDK until one request becomes dozens. Advanced How do you design a payment API across a remote provider? Create a durable local intent keyed by the business operation, validate the request fingerprint, call the provider with a stable provider key, persist the provider reference and result, and reconcile unknown outcomes through lookup/webhook. The local database transaction cannot atomically include the provider; model IN_DOUBT and recovery explicitly. Advanced Why is an outbox useful, and what does it not solve? An outbox commits a domain change and an event record in one local transaction, then publishes the event asynchronously. It closes the database-to-broker dual-write gap. It does not automatically provide global ordering, exactly-once effects, consumer idempotency, or a transaction across a remote API. Advanced How would you evolve an enum without breaking clients? Treat unknown values as possible, document forward compatibility, and avoid clients switching on an exhaustive set unless the contract supports it. Add values only when consumers tolerate them; use capability negotiation or a new version when semantics change, not merely because an implementation changed. Advanced What would you measure for an API? Traffic, error rate by route and cause, p50/p95/p99 latency, saturation, throttles, dependency latency, queue age, retry count, idempotency replays/conflicts, and business outcomes such as duplicate prevention. Correlate logs and traces with a request ID while redacting sensitive values.

title: API Design
heading: 9. HATEOAS: make the next action discoverable
text: 9. HATEOAS: make the next action discoverable Definition Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State means a client follows links and action metadata supplied by a resource representation to discover the next permitted interaction. The client still needs to understand link relations and media-type semantics. In the earlier state model, an order moves from awaiting payment to paid and then fulfillment. A client with hard-coded paths and status rules must be updated whenever the workflow changes. A representation can instead advertise a pay or cancel relation when that interaction is currently available. The client learns the next action from a documented relation rather than constructing every URL from assumptions. This is still a contract, not a self-explanatory universal UI. The client must understand the relation and the media type; links can become stale between reading and acting. The server must recheck authorization and state at mutation time. Choose hypermedia when discoverable workflows and independently evolving clients justify its representation/tooling cost, rather than adding links as decoration. Why it arises: a checkout workflow changes as an order moves from awaiting payment to shipped. Clients that construct every action URL and duplicate every transition rule become coupled to server internals. Hypermedia can expose the actions currently available. GET /orders/ord_123 Content-Type: application/hal+json { "id": "ord_123", "status": "AWAITING_PAYMENT", "_links": { "self": { "href": "/orders/ord_123" }, "payment": { "href": "/orders/ord_123/payment" }, "cancel": { "href": "/orders/ord_123/cancellation" } } } A HAL link identifies a related target; it does not by itself define the HTTP method or request schema. Document the relation, or use an action-capable format such as HAL-FORMS. After shipment the cancellation action may disappear, but the server must still enforce authorization and legal transitions when a stale client submits a command. Spring HATEOAS · representation assembly fragment EntityModel<OrderView> model = EntityModel.of(view); model.add(Link.of("/orders/" + view.id()).withSelfRel()); if (policy.mayCancel(principal, order)) { model.add(Link.of("/orders/" + view.id() + "/cancellation") .withRel("cancel")); } return model; Choose it when Cost / pitfall Several clients navigate changing business workflows; relations have durable meaning. Clients must actually follow relations. Adding unused links gives little benefit. Discovery and evolving resource relationships are valuable. More payload and media-type tooling; it does not eliminate semantic versioning. Personalized action links affect caching. A shared cached representation must not expose another user's available actions. Generate external links using a configured public base URL or trusted proxy information, never arbitrary forwarded headers.

title: API Design
heading: 10. Pagination, filtering, and stable ordering
text: 10. Pagination, filtering, and stable ordering Definition Pagination bounds a collection response. Offset pagination addresses a position; cursor pagination carries continuation state. Keyset pagination implements continuation using ordered field values. Begin with GET /orders returning every order. As the collection grows, response size, database work and client memory grow with it. A limit bounds one response. Offset adds a numeric position, which is easy to expose as page numbers. But if a new order appears before that position between requests, the position no longer identifies the same boundary. Follow a concrete descending list: 105, 104, 103, 102. Page one returns 105 and 104. Insert 106; offset 2 now starts at 104, repeating an item. A cursor based on the last ordered key asks for items after the earlier boundary instead of skipping the current first two. It also needs a unique tie-breaker when timestamps match. This avoids that positional shift, but does not freeze updates/deletes or create a consistent financial snapshot. Offset works well for small administrative tables with page-number navigation. Deep offsets become expensive and concurrent inserts can shift page boundaries. Keyset pagination is a better fit for feeds and large tables, but arbitrary page jumps and snapshot consistency require additional design. GET /orders?status=PAID&limit=25&cursor=opaque-token SELECT id, created_at, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND status = :status AND (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT :limit_plus_one; Use a supporting index such as (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC, id DESC) after validating the actual query plan. Fetch one extra row to determine whether another page exists. The unique ID breaks timestamp ties; timestamp alone can skip records. { "items": [{ "id": "ord_123" }], "nextCursor": "opaque-token", "hasMore": true } Link: </orders?status=PAID&limit=25&cursor=opaque-token>; rel="next" Bind the token to tenant, filters, sort order, and token version; reject incompatible or expired tokens. Base64 encoding provides neither integrity nor confidentiality. Sign the token or keep server-side state when appropriate. Allowlist filter operators and sort fields. Cap page size and query complexity. Parameterize values and never concatenate raw user sort expressions into SQL. Keyset traversal is not a frozen snapshot. Updating the sort field can still cause repeats or omissions. For exports, use immutable ordering plus a snapshot strategy, materialized result set, or explicit consistency contract. Exact totals can be more expensive than the page itself. Make them optional, approximate, or omit them with a clear contract. Spring mapping: Spring Data Page commonly entails a count query; Slice exposes whether another slice exists without requiring a total. Verify repository behavior and use a custom keyset query or supported scrolling API when that is the required contract.

title: API Design
heading: 11. Caching: freshness, validation, and isolation
text: 11. Caching: freshness, validation, and isolation Definition HTTP caching reuses stored responses according to freshness and validation rules. A fresh response can be reused directly; a stale response may be revalidated against the origin using a validator. Returning fewer orders bounded one response. Now consider repeating the same GET while the underlying representation has not changed. A cache can reuse a stored answer while it is fresh. When revalidation is required, a validator such as an entity tag (ETag), an opaque identifier for a representation version, lets the client ask whether the stored representation is still usable without always transferring the full body. Two questions must be answered before setting max-age: may this response be stored by a shared cache, and how long may this caller use it without checking? An authenticated order representation may contain private fields or user-specific links. A cache key that ignores the relevant identity or representation dimensions can return another caller’s data. Freshness optimization must preserve authorization and representation isolation. Directive / header Meaning and use Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 A public catalog may be reused for 60 seconds, subject to other cache rules. private, max-age=30 Permit private client caching; shared caches must not store the response. no-cache Storage is allowed, but reuse requires successful validation. no-store Instruct caches not to store this response. It does not erase previously stored copies. ETag + If-None-Match Validate a representation; an unchanged conditional GET can return 304 without a body. Vary: Accept-Language Separate representations selected using this request header. Configure the actual CDN cache policy too. GET /catalog/products/p7 → 200 OK Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 ETag: "product-p7-v8" GET /catalog/products/p7 If-None-Match: "product-p7-v8" → 304 Not Modified // no representation body For writes, a strong ETag with If-Match can protect against stale updates. A weak ETag ( W/ ) is unsuitable for strong If-Match comparison. The check and database update must be atomic; checking a version in Java and then issuing an unconditional update leaves a race. Implementation choices: Spring ResponseEntity supports cache-control and ETag headers. Service-level @Cacheable caches method results and is a separate layer from HTTP caching. CloudFront can cache public reads, but TTLs, cache keys, authorization handling, and invalidation must match the contract. Tricky case: a product price changes while cached pages remain fresh. Decide whether bounded staleness is acceptable. Always revalidate authoritative price and inventory at checkout; a cache TTL is not a business invariant.

title: API Design
heading: 12. Headers are part of the contract
text: 12. Headers are part of the contract Headers carry representation metadata, control information, credentials, and request context. Prefer standard fields where their semantics fit. Document custom fields, their limits, and whether intermediaries must preserve them. The URL and body do not carry the entire HTTP agreement. Content-Type tells the receiver how the actual representation is encoded; Accept expresses which response formats the caller can handle. Authorization presents credentials, while conditional fields such as If-Match change whether a mutation is allowed. These are different roles, so do not treat headers as an interchangeable bag of strings. Write a request and response together when documenting an endpoint. Show which fields are required, which are optional, and what happens when they conflict or are absent. Proxies may add metadata such as forwarding information, but the service should trust it only through its controlled proxy boundary. Keep credentials and sensitive identifiers out of diagnostic dumps. Field Purpose Nuance Content-Type / Accept Actual body format / acceptable response formats. Unsupported request media type: 415 ; no acceptable response representation: 406 when negotiation is enforced. Authorization Credentials such as a bearer token. Redact from logs; never use an unverified token claim as authority. Location New resource URI after creation; also used for redirects. For 202 , document how the status resource is exposed; it is not automatically standardized by choosing that status. Retry-After Suggested wait expressed as seconds or an HTTP date. Useful with throttling/unavailability; respect an overall client deadline. ETag , If-Match , If-None-Match Representation validation and preconditions. Distinct read validation and write concurrency behavior. Idempotency-Key Application retry identity. Publish scope, required operations, retention, payload mismatch, and replay policy. traceparent / tracestate Distributed trace propagation. Tracing context is untrusted metadata, never proof of identity. Access-Control-Expose-Headers Allows browser scripts to read selected non-safelisted response headers. Expose ETag or Location when needed. CORS is a browser policy, not authorization. Proxy boundary: strip or validate incoming forwarding headers at the trusted edge. Otherwise generated links, redirect URLs, client IP controls, and audit records can be spoofed. Header names are case-insensitive; header values follow their own field-specific rules.

title: API Design
heading: 13. Traceability from HTTP to background work
text: 13. Traceability from HTTP to background work Definition Distributed tracing connects spans across service boundaries. A correlation/request ID helps search related records; a trace also records parent-child relationships, timings, and propagation context. An audit record captures a business or security action and has different retention and integrity needs. The caller retries an order request three times. Operators may want one trace per attempt, an order ID for the durable business entity and an operation key linking the repeated intention. Those identifiers answer different questions. A trace explains an execution path where recorded; a durable operation record establishes whether the effect already committed. Pass supported trace context through HTTP and message carriers so the evidence can be connected across boundaries. Keep business identity in controlled logs/ledgers for recovery when traces are sampled out or expired. Avoid labeling a metric with every order ID; aggregate detection and individual diagnosis need different cardinality policies. traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01 Structured log: { "route": "/orders/{id}", "method": "GET", "status": 200, "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736", "durationMs": 42 } Use OpenTelemetry instrumentation or Spring Boot's Micrometer Tracing integration to extract inbound context and inject outbound context. Configured framework HTTP client builders usually preserve instrumentation; manually constructed clients and thread/executor boundaries need verification. Propagate context through SQS message attributes using an agreed carrier rather than assuming HTTP headers travel with a message. Validate incoming context; generate new context when invalid. A public caller must not control sampling cost or impersonate an internal actor through metadata. Use route templates in metrics. Raw URLs, user IDs, request IDs, and trace IDs create unbounded metric cardinality. Sampling means some requests have no retained trace. Keep essential outcome metrics and appropriate error/audit records independently. Exclude tokens, card details, and personal data from headers, baggage, and log fields. Baggage can propagate far beyond the original service. AWS mapping: an OpenTelemetry collector/ADOT pipeline can export to AWS observability services. Verify propagation and identifier conversion across API Gateway, application instrumentation, and workers; do not assume every service uses one native trace format.

title: API Design
heading: 14. Versioning and compatibility beyond URLs
text: 14. Versioning and compatibility beyond URLs A version identifies a contract boundary. Breaking changes include removing fields, changing types, tightening validation, changing defaults, or changing behavioral guarantees. Even adding an enum value can break a client that assumes an exhaustive set. A client can continue compiling and still break after a server change. Suppose a new enum value is added and an old client assumes its switch covers every possibility. The schema addition looks small, but the old behavior may crash or choose an unsafe default. Compatibility is a property of real consumers and semantics, not only whether an existing field remains present. Use explicit versions for the changes that need them, but also define additive-change policy, tolerant parsing, deprecation evidence and the mixed-version rollout. A /v2 path does not make database writes backward-compatible. Track which clients still depend on the old behavior before retiring it, and validate both old and new readers against data written during overlap. Strategy When useful Trade-off Path: /v1/orders Public APIs needing visible routing and documentation. Parallel surfaces and lifecycle ownership. Header or media type Clients explicitly negotiate a representation/contract. Less visible in URLs; gateways, docs, and caches need correct handling. Compatible evolution Add optional data while preserving semantics. Requires tolerant clients and automated compatibility checks. Choose one primary mechanism and document what “v1” guarantees. Avoid a new major version for every additive release. For a breaking migration, publish both contracts, track usage by client/version, provide examples and a sunset plan, and retire the old contract only after the agreed migration process. Tricky migration: integer money becomes decimal Changing amount: 49900 from minor units to 499.00 silently changes meaning even if JSON parsers accept both. Introduce an explicitly named field or new contract, keep old semantics during migration, and test old clients against new server releases. Implementation: OpenAPI diff checks identify many structural breaks; consumer/provider contract tests (for example Pact) exercise agreed interactions. Neither detects every semantic change. Include replay, authorization, pagination, and default-behavior examples in regression review.

title: API Design
heading: 15. Response mechanisms and error contracts
text: 15. Response mechanisms and error contracts Choose response behavior from completion time, payload size, and interaction needs. Specify when work is committed, how the caller learns the final outcome, and what disconnecting means. A short status read can return its result on the original connection. An export lasting minutes needs a different agreement: accept the work durably, return an operation identity, and expose progress and terminal states later. Returning 202 changes the completion contract; it does not remove the obligation to recover accepted work. Choose the mechanism from interaction and recovery needs. Polling is simple but adds repeat traffic; webhooks require authenticated durable delivery; streaming carries incremental data but a disconnect may leave partial results. In every case, document the commit point, retry identity, partial-output policy and how the caller learns the authoritative final state. Mechanism Suitable use Failure contract Synchronous JSON Bounded reads and short writes. Timeout can leave write outcome unknown; use identity/status lookup. 202 + job resource Exports and long-running commands. Persist acceptance before returning; expose queued/running/succeeded/failed states, expiry, and cancellation semantics. Webhook Server-to-server completion. Sign events, retry with limits, deduplicate by event ID; tolerate reordering and provide recovery/replay. SSE / WebSocket Server event streams / bidirectional interaction. Define reconnect, resume, heartbeat, buffering, and backpressure. Connection persistence is not durable delivery. Bulk / batch Many related actions. Declare all-or-nothing or per-item outcomes. Define per-item identities and retry only failed items. Problem Details instead of ad hoc error strings HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict Content-Type: application/problem+json { "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/order-state-conflict", "title": "Order cannot be cancelled", "status": 409, "detail": "The order has already shipped.", "instance": "/problem-occurrences/err_91", "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_SHIPPED", "requestId": "req_82" } RFC 9457 defines the standard members; code and requestId above are application extensions. Clients should use stable type/code values rather than parsing human detail. Do not expose stack traces or database messages. Spring ProblemDetail and @ControllerAdvice can centralize this mapping; keep the actual HTTP status consistent with the body. Job response example POST /exports → 202 Accepted Location: /exports/exp_7 { "id": "exp_7", "status": "QUEUED", "statusUrl": "/exports/exp_7" } GET /exports/exp_7 → 200 OK { "id": "exp_7", "status": "SUCCEEDED", "downloadUrl": "...", "expiresAt": "2026-10-30T12:00:00Z" } Once streaming response headers are sent, a later server failure generally cannot become a new HTTP status response. Define stream-level error framing and termination behavior. A 204 or 304 response must not carry a JSON body.

title: API Design
heading: 16. Documentation is an executable contract
text: 16. Documentation is an executable contract OpenAPI describes operations, schemas, security schemes, and responses. Readers also need the behavioral rules it cannot fully enforce: consistency, idempotency retention, ordering, pagination stability, and recovery from uncertainty. Documentation should let a developer implement the client’s next action without guessing. A successful curl example is useful, but a production client also needs to handle validation, permission denial, concurrency conflicts, throttling and an unknown write outcome. Describe these as sequences, including the headers and identities carried across attempts. OpenAPI makes much of the structure machine-readable. It cannot by itself prove that a retry after a timeout will not charge twice or that a cursor represents a snapshot. Put those behavioral guarantees beside examples and test them against the implementation. A generated contract is an artifact to review, not evidence that all semantics are correct. Start: a working authenticated request, required scopes, environment URLs, and sample credentials acquisition. Define: field units, null versus absent, time zones, defaults, limits, enum extensibility, and money precision. Demonstrate: success, validation failure, authorization denial, conflict, rate limiting, duplicate replay, and async completion. Explain recovery: timeout behavior, retryable errors, status lookup, support request ID, and webhook replay. Maintain: changelog, compatibility policy, deprecation schedule, and SDK version support. Practical toolchain: springdoc-openapi can generate a Spring API description; Swagger UI/Redoc renders it; OpenAPI Generator builds clients; Spectral lints conventions; Pact checks selected consumer interactions; Karate/REST Assured exercise runtime behavior. Use framework-compatible library versions and review generated schemas—generation does not prove the running API matches the document. paths: /orders: post: summary: Create an order parameters: - in: header name: Idempotency-Key required: true schema: { type: string, maxLength: 128 } responses: '201': { description: Created; Location identifies the order } '409': { description: Key reused with a different request } # Teaching excerpt: add requestBody, response schemas, security and errors. Completion gate: validate the specification, compare contract changes, run real database/API integration tests, verify auth and error examples, and exercise a generated client. For AWS API Gateway, distinguish importing an OpenAPI definition from proving that backend behavior and gateway policies agree. Additional interview questions Easy Is no-cache the same as no-store? No-cache permits storage but requires validation before reuse. No-store instructs caches not to store the response. Use an explicit policy appropriate for the data and verify browser and shared-cache behavior. Intermediate Does HATEOAS replace documentation and authorization? No. Links expose relationships and potentially available transitions; clients still need relation and payload semantics. The server checks authorization and current state on every command because links can be cached or become stale. Intermediate How can pagination still duplicate records with a cursor? A cursor with mutable sort fields can cross changed ordering boundaries. A timestamp without a unique tie-breaker is also ambiguous. Use a deterministic tuple and specify whether traversal is live or snapshot-based. Advanced A CDN leaks one user's action links to another. What failed? A personalized representation was reused across security contexts. Stop shared storage of those responses, correct the cache policy/key and invalidate affected cached objects as needed. Verify authorization at the command endpoint; hidden links never enforce access. Advanced How do you trace a retried command through SQS without double-counting business outcomes? Propagate tracing context through message metadata and record attempt-level spans. Separately use a stable business command/event ID for deduplication and outcome accounting. Trace IDs identify observations; they are not durable idempotency keys. Count the committed business transition once and retries separately.

title: API Design
heading: 17. REST, gRPC, or GraphQL?
text: 17. REST, gRPC, or GraphQL? An API style determines how clients express intent and how contracts evolve. Select it from the interaction and consumer constraints; one system can expose public REST while using gRPC internally. We have used REST/HTTP to make resources and failure behavior concrete. Now compare alternatives against the same user journey. A typed internal operation can fit gRPC; a client selecting a graph of related data can fit GraphQL; a resource-oriented public interface can fit REST. The important change is the interaction model and operating contract, not whether one format looks newer. Keep the invariant and failure questions constant while comparing. What limits query work? How are deadlines and credentials propagated? Can the client retry the operation safely? How does schema evolution affect consumers? A different API style can improve tooling or payload selection without removing storage concurrency, authorization or remote uncertainty. Style Choose when Costs and traps REST / HTTP Public integrations, resource operations, HTTP caching, broad client support. Over/under-fetching and many round trips may require a tailored read model or BFF. gRPC / Protobuf Controlled service clients, typed code generation, streaming, explicit deadlines. Browser use needs appropriate tooling such as gRPC-Web; proxies must support the protocol. Never reuse removed Protobuf field numbers. GraphQL Several UIs need different projections of related data. Resolver N+1 queries, query cost, field-level authorization, and less straightforward shared HTTP caching. Implementation choices: Spring MVC for REST, grpc-java for typed RPC, Spring for GraphQL with GraphQL Java for schema/resolvers. DataLoader can batch resolver reads, but its cache should normally be scoped to a request/security context. Bound depth, complexity, execution time, and list sizes; one GraphQL HTTP request can still create thousands of backend reads. Decision exercise: a mobile screen needs ten downstream calls. First consider an aggregated endpoint/BFF or a purpose-built projection. GraphQL is useful when flexible client-selected queries justify its operational cost; adopting it does not repair slow databases or missing authorization.

title: API Design
heading: 18. Validation, precision, and PATCH semantics
text: 18. Validation, precision, and PATCH semantics Validation has layers: transport syntax, schema shape, domain rules, and transactional invariants. Bean Validation can reject a blank address; it cannot prove available stock remains sufficient between a read and a later write. Imagine a profile update containing no address field, an explicit null address, or an empty address object. These can mean “leave unchanged,” “remove,” and “replace with an empty structure,” respectively—but only if the contract says so. Without that distinction, generated clients and default values can silently change data. Validate representation shape first, then cross-field and business rules at the appropriate boundary. Use a decimal representation and a defined currency/unit policy for money rather than binary floating-point assumptions. Pick PATCH semantics explicitly: Merge Patch gives null a removal meaning, while JSON Patch expresses operations. Neither choice makes a stale concurrent update safe without an additional concurrency rule. Input nuance Contract choice Failure to avoid Missing versus null Missing means no change for a partial update; explicit null has documented removal/clearing semantics. A DTO that collapses missing and null can accidentally erase stored values. Money Integer minor units plus currency, or decimal strings plus an explicit scale/rounding policy. Floating-point rounding and assuming every currency has two decimal places. Time UTC instants for events; local date plus IANA zone for future civil-time appointments. A fixed offset cannot describe future daylight-saving rules. Unknown fields Choose strict write validation or tolerant parsing deliberately; document it. Silent misspellings or breaking an older server with a newly added client field. Cross-field rule Validate start before end, permitted currency, and immutable fields at the domain layer. Only validating field types and accepting impossible business state. PATCH /profiles/u7 Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json If-Match: "profile-v12" { "nickname": null, "address": { "city": "Delhi" } } Under JSON Merge Patch, null removes an object member and arrays are replaced as whole values. JSON Patch instead uses explicit operations such as add/remove/replace/test with application/json-patch+json . Neither format grants permission to edit protected fields. Allowlist writable paths and apply validation to the resulting representation. A custom PATCH format is possible, but its rules must be explicit. Spring fragment: @NotBlank , @Positive , nested @Valid , and a class-level validator handle input shape. Use BigDecimal from decimal strings where decimal arithmetic is required; enforce scale and rounding intentionally. Persistence constraints remain the final guard for uniqueness and concurrent invariants.

title: API Design
heading: 19. Concurrency and inventory reservations
text: 19. Concurrency and inventory reservations Definition A race condition occurs when correctness depends on the timing of concurrent operations. An invariant such as available stock ≥ 0 must be enforced atomically at the authoritative store. Idempotency prevents repeating one intention from applying its effect again. It does not resolve two different legitimate intentions competing for the same stock. Both buyers may have distinct valid keys. The service must make the inventory decision atomically at the authority rather than relying on both callers having recently seen available=1. For editing an order representation, a version/ETag can tell the server which state the caller based its change on. For inventory, a conditional decrement can enforce enough stock remains. These are related conditional decisions with different business meanings. After a conflict, the caller must re-evaluate current state rather than automatically replaying a stale overwrite until it wins. Reading stock=1 in two requests and then independently decrementing permits overselling. Use a conditional update rather than a check followed by an unconditional write. UPDATE inventory SET available = available - :quantity WHERE sku = :sku AND available >= :quantity; -- affected rows = 1: reserved; 0: insufficient stock or missing SKU -- Require quantity > 0 and scope by warehouse/tenant where applicable. In one local transaction, create a unique reservation, update inventory, and record the result. A duplicate command must replay the reservation rather than decrement again. For several SKUs, acquire locks/update in a deterministic order, roll back the entire reservation if any item fails, and retry deadlocks only within a bounded policy. Expiry race: payment completion and reservation expiry can arrive together. Make RESERVED → CONFIRMED and RESERVED → EXPIRED conditional transitions. Only the winning expiry transition releases stock. Provider success after expiry needs a defined compensation policy, such as refund or a new reservation; do not silently mark an unfulfillable order confirmed. Mapping: RDS transactions/row locks or optimistic updates; DynamoDB condition expressions and transactions when the access model fits. Redis is useful for fast admission control, but an expiring distributed lock alone does not replace a durable inventory invariant.

title: API Design
heading: 20. Security beyond a valid JWT
text: 20. Security beyond a valid JWT A signed token proves only the claims verified under a trusted issuer and validation policy. Validate allowed algorithms, issuer, audience, expiry and other relevant time claims. Then authorize the requested action on the actual resource. The earlier security section separated identity from permission. Here extend the same reasoning to attack paths. A caller may be authenticated and still submit another tenant’s resource ID, an oversized payload, or a callback URL targeting an internal service. Each input can cross a different trust boundary and needs a specific limit or policy. Do not assume an internal network location proves authority. Validate service identity under the chosen model, constrain delegated capabilities, and authorize the resource operation. For callbacks, inspect destination and redirect/DNS behavior under an egress policy. For tokens, keep issuer, audience, time and algorithm policy explicit rather than merely decoding claims. // Illustrative resource lookup: tenant comes from verified security context. Order order = repository.findByTenantAndId(currentTenant(), orderId) .orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new); policy.requireCanRefund(currentPrincipal(), order); // A scope such as orders:write does not imply ownership of every order. OAuth scopes: express granted capabilities; combine them with tenant, ownership, roles, and business state. Use authorization-code + PKCE for appropriate interactive clients and client credentials for appropriate machine clients. Token rotation: cache trusted signing keys with a rotation strategy; handle unknown key IDs without unbounded issuer fetches. JWT revocation requirements may call for short lifetimes, introspection, or explicit revocation state. mTLS: authenticates peers at the transport boundary. It does not automatically authorize a user's refund or tenant access. SSRF: callback URLs can make a server reach internal services. Validate destinations, DNS/IP results and redirects; restrict egress, block metadata/internal addresses, and account for DNS rebinding. Mass assignment: bind writable DTO fields explicitly. A caller must not set role , tenantId , or payment status by adding JSON properties. Spring/AWS: Spring Security resource-server JWT support supplies token verification machinery; configure audience and authorization policies explicitly. Cognito or another identity provider supplies tokens; API Gateway/WAF can enforce edge controls, while application-level resource authorization remains necessary.

title: API Design
heading: 21. Deadlines, retry budgets, and overload
text: 21. Deadlines, retry budgets, and overload A timeout limits one wait; an end-to-end deadline bounds the caller's useful time. Allocate time for connection acquisition, dependency work, retries, serialization, and returning a response. Cancel work that no longer has a useful consumer where safe, while preserving recovery for already-committed side effects. Now let the payment provider slow down. Each waiting request retains resources; retries add more attempts to the same constrained dependency. A timeout limits one wait, a deadline limits the logical operation, a circuit breaker can stop some future calls, and a bulkhead isolates capacity. These mechanisms protect different boundaries and should be introduced one at a time. Before adding a retry, establish both safe repetition and remaining time/load budget. Three layers each retrying three attempts can multiply calls dramatically. Prefer an explicit owner for retries, bounded attempts with backoff/jitter and a durable recovery path for unknown writes. A shorter timeout without cancellation/resource cleanup can leave the underlying work consuming capacity. Illustrative 800 ms request budget: 50 ms admission/validation 500 ms dependency work (including any retry) 150 ms persistence and response 100 ms safety margin Each downstream deadline must fit the remaining budget. Mechanism Protects against Does not guarantee Timeout/deadline Waiting indefinitely. Cancellation or rollback of a remote side effect. Circuit breaker Repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency. Concurrency isolation or idempotency. Bulkhead/concurrency limit One dependency consuming all worker connections. More backend capacity. Bounded queue Short bursts beyond service rate. Sustained overload; backlog grows if arrival exceeds processing. Retry budget + jitter Retry amplification and synchronized bursts. Safe repetition of an unsafe command. Implementation: Resilience4j offers retry, circuit-breaker, rate-limiter and bulkhead modules; configure HTTP connection/read timeouts separately and verify whether cancellation reaches the client implementation. gRPC supports deadlines. For REST, define an internal deadline propagation convention at trusted boundaries. Gateway throttles are one protection layer, not a complete fair-use policy. Three layers making three attempts each can create 27 leaf attempts. Pick retry ownership and count the initial call consistently. Do not hedge a charge across two providers unless the business protocol guarantees a single effect.

title: API Design
heading: 22. Bulk APIs and partial success
text: 22. Bulk APIs and partial success Batching reduces round trips, but complicates atomicity, authorization, limits, and retries. State whether the batch is one transaction, independently committed items, or an asynchronous job. Do not let a generic batch silently span arbitrary remote services. A bulk request packages several item operations into one transport interaction. It does not automatically turn them into one transaction. Decide whether every item must commit together or whether each item has an independent result. That choice determines response structure, retry granularity, capacity limits and what the caller may conclude after a lost response. For partial success, give each item a stable identity and a machine-readable outcome. Retrying the entire batch must not repeat already-completed effects unexpectedly. Bound item count and total work as well as body bytes; a small JSON body can request an expensive operation. Document ordering, per-item authorization and whether processing stops after one failure. POST /order-imports → 202 with job URI // large import // Example contract for a small independently processed batch: 200 OK { "results": [ { "clientItemId": "a", "status": 201, "id": "ord_7" }, { "clientItemId": "b", "status": 422, "code": "INVALID_CURRENCY" } ] } The outer 200 above means the batch was processed according to this contract; it does not mean every item succeeded. An invalid envelope can fail as a whole. Preserve a stable item identifier and per-item idempotency identity; retry failed items without recreating successful ones. Bound item count, body bytes, response bytes and execution time. Do not adopt WebDAV's 207 without deliberately defining the media type and semantics for your API. Tricky case: a client times out after 60 of 100 items commit. A single batch key with no durable per-item outcomes leaves it unable to recover safely. Store per-item results or expose the job ledger. A database transaction can give local all-or-nothing behavior, but holding it across a huge import can exhaust locks and connections.

title: API Design
heading: 23. File APIs and direct S3 uploads
text: 23. File APIs and direct S3 uploads Large file bodies should often travel directly between the client and object storage. Your API authorizes the intent and tracks the file lifecycle instead of holding an application worker for every byte. A file upload separates control from data transfer. The application authorizes an upload intent and chooses the tenant-scoped storage identity; object storage receives the bytes. This avoids retaining an application worker for the entire transfer, but moves some enforcement into the signed capability and finalization protocol. Uploading bytes is not the same as publishing a safe file. Verify the intended object, size and integrity under the selected mechanism, quarantine for required inspection, and conditionally transition the intent to READY. A presigned URL is a bearer capability that may be reused within its effective lifetime. Do not describe it as one-time authorization without a mechanism that enforces that property. Create an upload intent after checking tenant, file purpose, quota and allowed size/type. Generate a random tenant-scoped storage key. Issue a short-lived presigned upload URL or POST policy with applicable restrictions. The URL is a bearer capability: keep it out of logs and analytics. Client uploads with the required signed headers/checksum. For large objects, use multipart upload and persist upload ID/parts as needed. Verify stored object metadata/checksum and expected ownership. Quarantine until malware/content inspection completes. Publish the file as READY only through a conditional lifecycle transition. Abort abandoned multipart uploads and expire orphaned intents. AWS SDK for Java v2 · illustrative presigning fragment PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder() .bucket(bucket).key(serverGeneratedKey) .contentType("application/pdf").build(); PresignedPutObjectRequest signed = presigner.presignPutObject( PutObjectPresignRequest.builder() .signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) .putObjectRequest(put).build()); // Return signed.url() and signed.signedHeaders() to the authorized caller. A presigned URL can generally be reused until expiry, and an upload to the same key can overwrite an object. Temporary credentials can expire before the chosen URL duration. Do not claim one-time or immutable upload semantics without extra controls. A checksum verifies integrity, not that the file is harmless; a MIME header is not proof of content type. Verify actual bytes and enforce size through an appropriate upload policy and finalization checks.

title: API Design
heading: 24. Webhooks: delivery is a protocol
text: 24. Webhooks: delivery is a protocol A webhook is an outbound HTTP event notification. Network uncertainty means the sender may retry even after the receiver committed. Design event identity, authentication, retention and recovery on both sides. An asynchronous operation now needs to notify another service. The sender sends an event, the receiver persists it, and the receiver’s response can disappear. The sender may retry even though the receiver already committed. Stable event identity is therefore separate from each delivery attempt’s network or trace identity. Define the signed input using the actual protocol, verify it against trusted secret/key material and apply the agreed replay window. Persist accepted work before acknowledging when durable acceptance is promised. Deduplicate business processing, handle out-of-order events and provide a reconciliation/replay path. A valid signature establishes authenticity/integrity under that contract; it does not establish freshness or exactly-once business processing by itself. POST /partner-events Webhook-Id: evt_91 Webhook-Timestamp: 1793275200 Webhook-Signature: v1=... { "eventId": "evt_91", "type": "payment.captured", "resourceId": "pay_7", "resourceVersion": 18 } These header names are an example application contract. Sign a documented canonical input such as timestamp plus the exact raw body bytes using HMAC-SHA256; compare signatures in constant time. Check an allowed clock window and deduplicate the stable event ID. Signature verification after JSON reserialization can fail because whitespace and property ordering changed. Authenticate and validate within strict size/time limits. Persist the event to a durable inbox before returning a successful acknowledgement. Process asynchronously with idempotent business transitions; acknowledge duplicates consistently. Retry transient failures with backoff/jitter and a bounded delivery horizon. Preserve the event ID across attempts; follow the documented retry rules for status codes. Expose delivery history, dead-letter handling and authorized replay. Rotate secrets with overlap and a key identifier if the protocol supports it. Events can arrive out of order. A receiver can apply a version guard or fetch the authoritative current resource. A replay of an old signed event should not roll a payment from REFUNDED back to CAPTURED. Validate callback destinations as SSRF-sensitive input.

title: API Design
heading: 25. Contract lifecycle and safe releases
text: 25. Contract lifecycle and safe releases Contract-first means reviewing the intended interface before implementing it. Code-first can also work when generated contracts are reviewed and checked against behavior. Either approach needs an owner and a compatibility policy. A contract change reaches different clients and server instances at different times. During a rollout, old readers can see new data and delayed messages can carry older schemas. Review that overlap before deploying writers that introduce new fields, values or states. Tests should exercise the transition, not only the final all-new system. Expand the accepted/readable contract first, migrate where required, enable new writes under a controlled policy, and remove old behavior only after evidence permits it. Keep API version support separate from database rollback capability. An image rollback cannot erase facts already committed under a new representation. Stage Artifact / check Useful tools Design Requirements, invariants, OpenAPI examples, failure policies. OpenAPI, Spectral linting, design review. Client development Mock happy/error responses and generated client trials. Prism, WireMock, OpenAPI Generator. Implementation Real DB constraints, auth, duplicate/concurrent request tests. Testcontainers, REST Assured, Karate. Compatibility Schema diff, consumer interactions, semantic review. OpenAPI diff tools, Pact. Release Canary metrics, rollback compatibility, version adoption. CI/CD, gateway routing, feature flags. Migration trap: deploy a server that writes a new database representation, then roll back to code that cannot read it. Use expand/migrate/contract changes and verify both old and new binaries during the transition. API rollback and data rollback are different problems.

title: API Design
heading: 26. SLOs, capacity, load tests, and cost
text: 26. SLOs, capacity, load tests, and cost An SLO is a measurable service target over a time window. Define eligible requests, successful outcomes and measurement boundaries. A health endpoint returning 200 while all checkout attempts fail is not business availability. HTTP availability and business completion are different measurements. An API can return 202 promptly while accepted exports never finish. Define eligible requests and good outcomes for acceptance, then define a completion indicator over accepted operations and their deadlines. Pending work must not disappear from the measurement merely because it has not emitted a terminal result. Use workload estimates to choose a starting capacity, then validate under realistic payloads, hot keys, tenants, cache misses and dependency slowdown. Count useful completions as well as attempts. A retry storm can increase request traffic and cost while business throughput declines. State the measurement window and failure headroom instead of reporting only a best-case maximum RPS. Illustrative targets (validate against product needs): 99.9% eligible checkout requests receive a valid acceptance/outcome per month 95% of status reads complete within 200 ms 99% of accepted exports finish within 5 minutes duplicate business effects = 0 (invariant, not a latency percentile) With average in-flight duration 0.2 s and 1,000 requests/s, Little's Law suggests roughly 200 concurrent requests in steady state. It is an average relationship, not a sufficient connection-pool setting; fan-out, variance, bursts and downstream limits matter. A 1 GB response costs bandwidth even when the compute endpoint is cheap. Load-test realistic payloads, hot keys, tenants, cold starts and cache misses. Measure tail latency and rejection behavior, not only average throughput. Exercise dependency slowdown, DB-pool exhaustion, queue backlog and retry storms. Verify bounded memory and graceful rejection. Budget request charges, compute, database reads/writes, storage, egress, logs and traces. Sampling/retention must preserve required auditability. Separate API acceptance SLO from asynchronous completion SLO; alert on queue age and oldest pending business operation.

title: API Design
heading: 27. Worked design: checkout and payment
text: 27. Worked design: checkout and payment This design combines concepts already introduced: operation identity, atomic inventory decisions, asynchronous progress and unknown provider outcomes. Before reading the implementation list, trace one order and mark each durable commit. Then remove the response after every commit and ask which original identity lets recovery establish the outcome. Treat reservation expiry and late payment success as competing transitions, not merely timeout settings. Decide who owns the final state and what the customer sees while payment is unknown. The code and services are justified only after those intermediate states and business recovery rules are explicit. Functional requirements Create checkout and reserve several SKUs. Authorize payment, expose status, cancel/refund when permitted. Emit confirmation and fulfillment events. Targets and invariants Illustrative: p95 acceptance under 800 ms. No negative stock; one committed capture per payment intent. Recover after worker crashes and unknown provider outcomes. REST checkout → RDS transaction intent + reservation + outbox → Worker + provider → Reconcile outcome The database transaction ends before the remote provider call. Recovery bridges that boundary. POST /checkouts Idempotency-Key: purchase-91 { "items": [{ "sku": "p7", "quantity": 2 }], "currency": "INR" } → 201 { "id": "chk_7", "status": "AWAITING_PAYMENT" } POST /checkouts/chk_7/payment-attempts Idempotency-Key: attempt-1 { "paymentMethodToken": "provider-token" } → 202 { "id": "pat_7", "status": "PROCESSING" } GET /payment-attempts/pat_7 → current durable state Implementation and rationale Derive tenant/customer from verified identity. Resolve current authoritative price; reject changed or unavailable items according to the contract. Within a Spring/RDS transaction, reserve stock conditionally, create checkout and idempotency outcome, and add an outbox record. Commit all or roll back all. Publish outbox events to SQS. A worker uses the durable payment-attempt ID as a provider retry identity when supported. Record success/failure through conditional transitions. Deduplicate provider webhooks and reconcile IN_DOUBT attempts through provider lookup. Confirm inventory and emit fulfillment intent only when business prerequisites hold. Compensation/refund is a new durable action with its own identity. Failure Recovery HTTP response lost after checkout commit Replay the stored outcome using the scoped key/fingerprint. Outbox published, publisher crashes before marking sent Republish safely; consumer inbox/conditional transition prevents duplicate effect. Provider timeout after capture Mark unknown, query with original identity, reconcile webhook; never create a new charge blindly. Payment arrives after reservation expires Conditional transitions detect race; refund or re-reserve under explicit product policy. Validation: concurrent last-item reservations, duplicate keys with mismatched payloads, crashes around every commit, provider timeout then delayed success, duplicate/out-of-order webhooks, and expiry races. Assert database invariants and provider-call identity, not just HTTP statuses. Intermediate Why not hold a transaction open during payment? A local transaction cannot roll back a provider capture, and slow network calls hold database resources. Commit durable intent first and use an explicit state machine and reconciliation across the remote boundary. Architect How do you enforce “one capture” when the provider has no idempotency or lookup? You cannot guarantee a single remote effect through arbitrary timeout/crash windows with local deduplication alone. Require a stronger provider protocol, reconcile through settlement/manual review, or restrict retry behavior and document the residual risk. A distributed lock does not solve the unknown-outcome boundary.

title: API Design
heading: 28. Worked design: large export and download
text: 28. Worked design: large export and download This design reuses pagination, asynchronous status and file capabilities. A cursor bounds traversal, but does not freeze a changing dataset. First decide whether the export is a snapshot or a best-effort live view. Then choose a source/read protocol that can meet that promise under concurrent inserts, updates and deletes. Separate job completion from download authorization. A finished object can remain private while each link request checks current permission. Worker retries need an output-publication protocol so partial objects or competing results do not become the public answer. A successful upload and a successful export are distinct states. Functional requirements Submit a filtered export; poll progress and download. Cancel pending/running jobs; expire output. Restrict access to the requesting tenant. Targets and invariants Illustrative: accept under 300 ms; 99% finish within 5 minutes. Bound worker memory and tenant concurrency. Export consistency is explicitly snapshot or best-effort live. 202 + job ledger → SQS worker bounded chunks → Private S3 object → Authorized download URL Completion and download authorization are independent of the original HTTP connection. POST /exports { "format": "CSV", "filter": { "status": "PAID" } } → 202 + Location: /exports/exp_7 GET /exports/exp_7 → { "status": "RUNNING", "rowsWritten": 50000 } POST /exports/exp_7/download-links → 201 { "url": "short-lived-presigned-url", "expiresAt": "..." } Validate/allowlist filters, record tenant and query specification, reserve quota, and persist job plus outbox atomically. Choose consistency: a maximum-ID watermark bounds new inserts but does not freeze updates/deletes. For a true snapshot, use an appropriate DB snapshot/materialized dataset and budget its cost. Read bounded chunks, stream to multipart S3 upload, and checkpoint only according to a tested resume protocol. Restarting a whole file may be simpler and safer than appending after an uncertain chunk. Complete upload and verify output before conditionally marking SUCCEEDED. Keep partial/failed objects inaccessible and clean them up. Authorize each download-link request using current permissions. A previously issued presigned URL is still a bearer capability until its effective expiry or underlying access changes. Spring/AWS: Spring Batch for chunked jobs/checkpointing where appropriate; ECS workers or a suitable batch runtime for long workloads; SQS for dispatch; private S3 for output. A Step Functions workflow can coordinate phases. Choose execution runtime from actual duration/memory limits rather than assuming every export fits a request handler. Failure walkthrough: a cancellation and completion race uses conditional job transitions. Define whether cancellation is best-effort and whether completed output is deleted. Queue redelivery must not create two published results. CSV exports need spreadsheet-formula injection protection for untrusted cells, plus an explicit encoding/escaping policy. Validation: mutate source data between pages, kill workers mid-upload, retry completion, revoke tenant access, expire links, cancel at each phase, and verify bounded memory and orphan cleanup. Easy Does 202 mean the export will succeed? No. It means accepted for processing. The job resource reports eventual success or failure, and the contract states retention, polling and recovery behavior. Architect Is a cursor enough for a consistent financial export? No. Stable traversal does not freeze changing values. Agree on a consistency point and use a suitable snapshot, ledger cutoff semantics, or materialized export dataset. Explain the storage/DB retention cost and how retries reproduce the same dataset.

title: API Design
heading: 29. Worked design: partner integration
text: 29. Worked design: partner integration The partner journey combines an inbound command and outbound notifications. The command’s idempotency key recognizes one intended order; an event ID recognizes one business notification; a delivery-attempt ID identifies one send. Keeping these separate lets each side retry and diagnose the right boundary. Follow authorization through both directions. A partner credential must be scoped to its own resources, while a callback destination must be controlled as an outbound trust boundary. During an outage, isolate that partner’s backlog and concurrency so retries do not starve every other partner. Recovery ends when business state reconciles, not merely when the last HTTP delivery returns success. Functional requirements Partner submits an order and reads status. Receive signed lifecycle events and request replays. Rotate credentials and migrate contract versions. Targets and invariants Per-partner quota and concurrency isolation. No cross-partner access; durable delivery history. Eventual recovery after partner outages without infinite retries. OAuth partner client → Gateway + service resource authorization → Outbox + delivery ledger → Signed webhook retry / replay Inbound command identity and outbound event identity solve different duplicate problems. POST /partner/v1/orders Authorization: Bearer ... Idempotency-Key: partner-order-781 { "externalOrderId": "781", "items": [...] } → 201 { "id": "ord_7", "status": "ACCEPTED" } Event evt_91: order.shipped, resourceVersion: 4 GET /partner/v1/orders/ord_7 // authoritative reconciliation path Issue machine credentials through the chosen OAuth flow. Map the verified principal to a partner; enforce scopes plus partner/resource ownership in Spring Security and repository access. Scope external IDs and idempotency keys by partner and operation. Rate-limit admission and bound per-partner concurrent work; return documented 429/Retry-After behavior. Persist business change plus outbox; maintain separate event and delivery-attempt IDs. Each retry retains the event ID while timestamps/signatures may be refreshed per the contract. Verify callback ownership, restrict egress, and deliver through bounded workers.
