Durable failed-delivery records allow operator review and authorized replay after the retry horizon. Publish versioned examples and migration dates; track partner version usage. Keep secrets out of audit records while recording actor, resource, action and outcome. Tricky failures: an expired token causes bounded refresh rather than a retry loop; partner 200 before durable persistence can lose events; a slow partner must not exhaust every delivery thread; a valid old webhook cannot revert newer state. Rotate signing secrets with overlap and test both sides before retiring the old key. Spring/AWS mapping: Spring Security resource server, RDS delivery ledger/outbox, SQS dispatch, API Gateway/WAF admission controls, Secrets Manager for signing material, and structured logs/traces for diagnosis. Evaluate EventBridge API Destinations when its auth, retry and delivery contract matches your integration; a managed delivery feature still needs business-level reconciliation. Validation: cross-partner object access, secret rotation, duplicate external IDs, callback SSRF, out-of-order delivery, prolonged outage, quota fairness, version migration and replay auditability. Intermediate Why keep event ID and delivery-attempt ID separate? The event ID deduplicates one business notification; attempt IDs explain retries and delivery diagnostics. Generating a fresh event ID for every retry defeats receiver deduplication. Architect Can webhook delivery guarantee the partner processed an event exactly once? An HTTP acknowledgement proves only the receiver's documented acceptance behavior. The receiver needs durable intake and idempotent effect processing. Provide replay/status reconciliation and state the guarantee at each boundary rather than claiming end-to-end exactly once.

title: Scalability
heading: Overview
text: Follow an order service from one instance to a load-balanced system. Learn to measure demand, find the constraint, and preserve correctness while adding capacity.

title: Scalability
heading: 1. One service meets a sale-day spike
text: 1. One service meets a sale-day spike Keep the contract fixed; change the workload and follow resource use. Keep the API contract from the previous lessons unchanged: the shop accepts an order, enforces inventory rules and lets the caller recover a lost response. Now increase the number of callers. Scaling should preserve those promises under more demand. It is not simply running the same code on more machines, because those machines may compete for the same database, lock or provider quota. Follow one request before following a thousand. It executes some instructions, waits for a database connection, runs statements and possibly waits for another service. Each stage consumes a different resource. CPU capacity helps execution; a query improvement reduces database work; a connection limit bounds admitted pressure. Requests look equally slow from outside even when the required interventions differ. The goal is useful completed work at an acceptable latency and cost. A system receiving twice as many HTTP attempts because clients keep retrying has not doubled business throughput. We will distinguish demand from admission and completion, locate the current constraint, then change one part of the system and measure again.

title: Scalability
heading: 2. Account for where one request spends time
text: 2. Account for where one request spends time Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A service is a collection of finite resources. CPU executes instructions, connections carry requests, memory holds active work, and storage serves reads and writes. Throughput is completed work per unit time. Latency includes execution and waiting. Increasing one resource helps only when it limits the operation or removes work from the limiting resource. At 100 requests per second and 0.2 seconds average time in the measured system, about 20 requests are present on average in steady state. If a dependency slows to one second at the same admitted arrival rate, that becomes about 100. Those requests occupy memory and connections even if CPU is quiet. Once a limit is reached, waiting grows further. This feedback explains why replicas, bounded queues and admission control must be considered together. Check your understanding Foundational Doubling replicas doubles capacity. Only when the divided work and shared dependencies allow it. Two application replicas can contend on the same database lock or overwhelm the same connection limit. Measure useful throughput and tail latency after each change. Intermediate Why might autoscaling make a database incident worse? Each new replica can open more database connections and add retries. If the database is already the constraint, scaling callers increases pressure. Cap fleet-wide concurrency and preserve headroom before scaling.

title: Scalability
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. Imagine ten customers arrive together. If each request needs 100 ms of CPU and there is one available CPU core, they cannot all finish in 100 ms. Some work must wait. If most time is instead waiting for a remote response, there may be spare CPU but exhausted connections. Both look like a slow API from outside, yet need different fixes. First classify service time and waiting; then measure which resource is scarce. Only after that does choosing a larger instance, another replica or a queue become meaningful.

title: Scalability
heading: 4. State demand and success first
text: 4. State demand and success first Describe the demand and allowed degradation before selecting capacity. Write a workload description before a machine count. For the shop, specify reads versus writes, route mix, average and large payloads, requests per second, burst duration and how much work each request triggers. One list request returning 25 rows is not equivalent to a checkout modifying five inventory items. A total RPS number without that mix is difficult to reproduce or use for capacity planning. Next separate a target from a forbidden outcome. A read p95 target means a stated fraction of eligible observations must meet the latency bound over a defined window. No negative inventory remains an invariant even when the latency target is missed. An instance-loss requirement defines a condition under which the system must still meet its stated operating contract; it is not satisfied merely because a second instance exists. Finally define the overload policy. If the system cannot sustainably process the offered work, it must bound waiting, reject/defer some requests, reduce optional work or provide a permitted degraded response. Choose which operations receive scarce capacity first. Durable order acceptance and optional catalog browsing need not have identical admission rules. Functional requirements Accept orders and expose status. Serve product reads and stock checks. Keep already-accepted work recoverable. Targets and invariants Illustrative peak: 1,000 requests/s, 80% reads. Illustrative read p95 below 200 ms. No duplicate order or negative inventory. Continue after losing one application instance. These are example targets, not universal defaults. Measure payload size, read/write mix, dependency fan-out, and burst duration. A peak lasting one second may be buffered; a peak lasting an hour needs sustainable service capacity. Distinguish offered traffic, admitted traffic, and successfully completed business work.

title: Scalability
heading: 5. Connect throughput, latency, and concurrency
text: 5. Connect throughput, latency, and concurrency Define one measurement boundary, then derive average work and inspect waiting. Begin with a stable boundary: from admitting a request until returning its result. Throughput counts completions per second, latency measures elapsed time, and concurrency counts work currently inside that boundary. Little’s Law relates long-run averages in a stable system: average work present equals average arrival rate multiplied by average time present. It does not predict a particular tail percentile. At 1,000 admitted requests/second and 0.2 seconds average time, about 200 requests are present on average. If a dependency slows and average time becomes one second while admissions remain at that rate, the average approaches 1,000 under stable conditions. Those waits retain memory and other resources. If arrivals continue to exceed completions and the queue keeps growing, the steady-state assumptions no longer describe a finite stable queue. Then separate queue time from execution. A controller timer beginning after admission may look healthy while callers spend most of their deadline in a gateway or local queue. Record the boundaries of every timer, use compatible latency distributions across instances, and examine route/cohort differences. An average of per-pod p99 values is not the fleet’s p99. Read a load curve as evidence. At low load, more admissions produce more completions with little waiting. Near saturation, waiting rises faster than useful throughput. Beyond that point, added attempts can reduce useful work through retries, contention or garbage collection. Repeat the measurement after each proposed change: the limiting resource can move. Measure per route: admitted/completed requests per second p50 / p95 / p99 response time active requests and queue wait CPU, GC pauses, DB pool wait, dependency latency rejection and retry rates A percentile describes a distribution: p99 of 800 ms means 99% of measured observations are at or below 800 ms for that window/population. Do not average per-instance percentiles to obtain a global percentile. Scenario Average rate and duration What follows Healthy stable operation 1,000/s × 0.2 s About 200 requests present on average. Stable slower dependency 1,000/s × 1 s About 1,000 present; waiting consumes resources. Arrivals persistently exceed completions Backlog grows over time Do not describe an unbounded growing queue as a finite steady state. One request fans out to five queries HTTP rate differs from query rate Measure downstream work; do not set a DB pool from HTTP concurrency alone.

title: Scalability
heading: 6. Vertical first, then horizontal when justified
text: 6. Vertical first, then horizontal when justified Choose which resource or ownership boundary actually changes. Vertical scaling changes the resources available to one instance. It can be an effective first step when a larger instance removes a measured CPU or memory limit without changing ownership. It remains finite and does not by itself make the instance survive failure. Horizontal scaling adds instances, which helps only if requests can be distributed and shared dependencies can support the resulting work. Now let two application instances accept orders. A Java map of accepted operation keys on instance A is invisible to B and disappears if A fails. A local session also follows that ownership problem. Move durable authority to an appropriate shared store or design explicit partition ownership. “Stateless application” means the instance does not privately own the durable state needed to preserve the contract; it does not forbid temporary local caches. A load balancer distributes eligible traffic but cannot split every coordination point. Both instances may still update the same popular SKU or use the same database writer. Partitioning can distribute different keys, at the cost of cross-partition work, rebalancing and skew. A single last-item claim still needs a coordinated authoritative decision. Choose the scaling dimension from the actual constraint. Choice What changes Constraint Vertical scaling Give one instance more CPU/memory. Simple but finite; failure domain remains large. Horizontal scaling Run more application instances. State, shared dependencies and load distribution must support it. Partitioning Divide data/work by a key. Cross-partition operations and hot keys become harder. Horizontal scaling works best when any healthy instance can process a request. Keep durable order state in the database rather than a Java field. A local cache can still exist, but its contents may differ between instances. Sticky sessions can ease a migration; they do not make session state survive instance loss. Clients → Load balancer → Stateless app fleet → Shared database The shared database remains a common constraint even after application replicas increase. A load balancer routes traffic; health checks determine eligible targets. Readiness should indicate that the instance can handle intended traffic, while liveness answers whether restarting may help. Marking every instance unready for a short shared dependency outage can amplify the outage.

title: Scalability
heading: 7. Implement a bounded scaling change
text: 7. Implement a bounded scaling change Budget the whole fleet, including reaction delay, failure and rollout. Convert the measured limit into budgets across the fleet. If eight instances may each open fifteen database connections, they can request 120 connections collectively, before jobs, operations or rollout surge. Twenty instances with the same setting can request 300. Each local pool can be within its configured limit while the database is overwhelmed by the aggregate. In Spring, measure acquisition waits separately from query time and choose bounded dependency waits. In Kubernetes, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) adjusts desired pod replicas from configured metrics; scheduling and obtaining node capacity are further steps. A CPU-based policy may not react appropriately when the service is waiting on database locks with low CPU. Select a metric that represents the workload and verify its behavior under failure, not just a clean traffic ramp. Autoscaling has a control-loop delay: observe demand, decide, provision/schedule, start, initialize and become ready. Keep enough headroom or pre-scale known bursts when that delay exceeds the workload’s tolerance. Include rollout surge in connection/capacity budgets. During scale-in, drain active requests and reclaim durable queued work; killing a process cannot be the normal completion signal for an accepted order. Illustrative capacity guard: 8 app instances × 15 DB connections = 120 possible connections Reserve DB headroom for operations, jobs, and failover. Scaling to 20 instances without a pool policy → 300 connections. Verify throughput under contention before increasing either limit. Use rolling delivery with graceful shutdown: stop admitting new requests, drain in-flight work, then terminate. Background workers need leases or queue acknowledgement rules so interrupted work can be reclaimed. Configure deployment surge and replica limits against shared-resource budgets. Autoscaling reacts after measurement and startup delay. Pre-scale known events and keep headroom where startup is slow. For queue workers, backlog per worker and oldest-message age may be better signals than CPU alone.

title: Scalability
heading: 8. Choose the next intervention
text: 8. Choose the next intervention Make one hypothesis, change one constraint and compare the same workload. Use the evidence below to choose one hypothesis and a falsifiable intervention. If a query dominates latency, adding callers can increase the same expensive work. An index may reduce it, but increases write/storage cost and needs representative plan evidence. If repeated public reads dominate, caching may reduce source work, provided the miss path and freshness policy remain safe. Keep correctness in the comparison. A read replica can distribute permitted stale reads but cannot automatically serve a read-your-writes promise. A queue can defer work but cannot make sustained arrivals above processing capacity disappear. A quota increase can help only if the downstream system really supplies more useful capacity. After the change, compare the same workload, data distribution, useful completion rate and latency boundaries. Evidence Intervention Check afterward App CPU saturated; database has headroom More/faster app compute, reduce expensive CPU work CPU/request and latency under the same load. Slow query dominates Index/query/model correction Query plan, lock time, write overhead. Repeated read work Cache or read model Freshness contract and miss-path capacity. Remote service limits Concurrency cap, queue, negotiated quota Queue age and completed outcomes. One tenant/key dominates Fair admission or split workload Per-tenant impact and hot partition behavior. A cache hit rate of 95% does not prove resilience: if cache loss sends all reads to the database, the miss path may need 20 times its usual capacity. A read replica may help reads but introduces freshness and failover considerations.

title: Scalability
heading: 9. Worked design: twenty times the traffic
text: 9. Worked design: twenty times the traffic Demonstrate the target under the cold path and lost capacity, not just healthy peak. Start with the twenty-times claim and make it testable. Suppose the baseline completes 100 business operations/second under a recorded mix; the target is 2,000 under that same mix. Keep payloads, data size, hot keys and completion criteria explicit. A test using only cached status reads cannot validate a target that includes concurrent checkouts. Assume measurement shows public product reads dominate. Reuse permitted product descriptions while checkout still validates authoritative price and stock. Separate browsing and order admission so optional reads cannot consume every database connection. Move receipts after a durable outbox handoff. Then increase application replicas while checking that useful throughput still improves and the shared database retains safe headroom. Now remove one failure-domain share of capacity and lose the cache. A system sized exactly for the warm healthy path may fail both tests. Bound refill/fallback concurrency, serve stale data only where the contract allows it, and shed lower-priority work before accepted orders become unrecoverable. Verify database invariants and duplicate-command recovery alongside latency. Report the first limiting resource and the operating margin, not merely the final replica count. Before Change Success evidence Warm cache, healthy fleet Lose cache Bounded refill/source load; allowed freshness; useful checkout completions. All instances available Lose one failure-domain share Latency/rejection under the failure contract; no lost accepted work. Steady traffic Burst arrives before new pods are ready Explicit admission/queue policy and bounded waiting. Normal release Rollout surge and draining Fleet resource budget respected; interrupted work safely recovered.

title: Scalability
heading: 10. Tricky cases and operations
text: 10. Tricky cases and operations Examine transitions and sustained behavior as well as averages. Transitions often matter more than the comfortable steady state. A rollout can create many empty local caches at once. A recovered dependency can receive a synchronized backlog. Scale-in can concentrate hot traffic on fewer instances. Test these changes deliberately because a five-minute healthy peak test may not expose them. Keep a cost measure tied to useful completions and inspect longer runs. If memory, backlog age or retries keep rising under supposedly stable load, the system has not demonstrated sustainable capacity. Fleet averages can hide one slow route or tenant cohort; choose bounded diagnostic dimensions rather than creating a metric series for every customer ID. Case Why it happens Response All replicas start together Empty local caches and connection establishment spike Stagger rollout; bound refill/connections. CPU low, requests slow Waiting for DB locks or remote connections Inspect wait metrics and traces before scaling CPU. Scale-in kills active work Termination occurs before drain completes Drain requests, reclaim durable jobs, test interruption. Average latency looks fine A small customer segment suffers extreme waits Break down route/tenant cohorts without unbounded metric labels. Keep a baseline cost per completed request. More replicas can increase cost while reducing throughput if contention dominates. Use a soak test to find memory leaks and backlog growth that a five-minute spike test misses.

title: Scalability
heading: 11. Interview ladder
text: 11. Interview ladder Foundational Latency versus throughput? Latency measures time per operation; throughput measures completed work per time. High concurrency can raise throughput until contention makes both latency and efficiency worse. Foundational Does a load balancer make a service scalable? It distributes traffic across targets. The targets and their shared dependencies must have capacity, and durable state must survive routing changes. Intermediate Why can HPA make a database incident worse? More pods can create more connections and concurrent queries against the same constrained database. Bound shared-resource use and address the limiting query/lock before raising replicas. Intermediate How do you scale a stateful application? Identify which state must survive instance loss. Move or replicate it with an appropriate ownership/durability model, or partition ownership deliberately. Routing affinity alone is not durable state management. Advanced How would you prove a 20× scaling claim? Use representative data and load, explicit SLOs, steady-state and burst tests, failure injections, and correctness assertions. Report offered/admitted/completed work, saturation, and cost; record the first bottleneck. Advanced What if one key remains hot after sharding? More shards do not split one unsplittable operation. Consider caching, aggregation, salting with merge semantics, a single-writer model, or a product limit, according to the invariant. Intermediate Can Little’s Law choose the database pool size? No. It relates average work over a stated stable system boundary. HTTP requests can wait without holding a database connection and can issue multiple queries. Derive the database budget from its own workload, useful execution concurrency and fleet-wide capacity; then measure acquisition, query and lock waits. Advanced A 95% cache hit ratio looks excellent. Why test cache loss? Normal misses are only 5% of read demand. Losing the cache can send roughly 20 times that usual miss traffic toward the source before refresh amplification. Bound fallback/refill and choose permitted stale responses or load shedding; do not assume application autoscaling supplies database capacity.

title: Scalability
heading: 12. Further reading and practice
text: 12. Further reading and practice Carry the measured database work into the storage lesson. Read HPA and cloud scaling documentation as control-loop behavior, not as a promise that replicas will appear instantly. Check the selected metric, stabilization, limits, startup/readiness and downstream capacity. Use the capacity guide to calculate an initial hypothesis, then replace assumptions with measurements. The next lesson opens the shared database that repeatedly appeared as a constraint here. We will keep the same order workload, identify its exact reads and invariants, then derive keys, indexes and transaction boundaries rather than starting from a database product list. Application Load Balancer : routing and health-check behavior. Kubernetes HPA : replica control and stabilization. AWS target tracking : metric selection and scaling behavior. Exercise: map a service you know to demand, service time, shared-resource capacity and failure headroom. Name one improvement that would reduce work instead of adding machines.

title: Databases
heading: Overview
text: Build an order store step by step: access patterns, keys, indexes, transactions, replication, and partitioning. Follow the data before choosing a database brand.

title: Databases
heading: 1. An order is more than a JSON document
text: 1. An order is more than a JSON document Start with facts, questions and forbidden outcomes, not a database brand. The API lesson defined the contract and Scalability counted the work. Now follow the facts the order service must preserve. An order has identity, a customer, line items and a lifecycle. A reservation changes stock. A retry may represent an already accepted intention. Storing a JSON payload durably does not by itself decide whether two competing changes are legal. Write the questions and mutations separately. “Find the latest 25 orders for this tenant and customer” specifies a filter, ordering and result bound. “Reserve two units if enough remain” specifies a conditional mutation. “Never reuse a partner order ID within a tenant” specifies a uniqueness invariant. These become inputs to access paths, constraints and transaction design. We will first choose the authority for those facts, then make its important operations correct, then reduce their access cost. This order avoids selecting a fast lookup that permits an unsafe update or an attractive storage model that cannot meet the required ownership boundary.

title: Databases
heading: 2. Derive correctness before choosing a storage product
text: 2. Derive correctness before choosing a storage product Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A database stores committed facts, but the application decides which combinations of facts are legal. An invariant is a rule that must remain true after every allowed transition. A constraint checks a rule in the database. A transaction groups changes into one commit. Isolation determines which concurrent observations and outcomes are permitted. These terms solve related but different parts of correctness. Two buyers see stock=1. If both make a decision in Java and later write stock=0, two orders can exist for one item. Begin with one atomic conditional update that subtracts only when enough stock remains. Inspect affected-row count and insert the reservation in the same local transaction. The business decision now happens where competing mutations are coordinated. An index can accelerate access to that row; it cannot replace the rule. Check your understanding Foundational Wrapping check-then-write in a transaction always prevents overselling. Not at every isolation level and not for every read/write pattern. Use an appropriate conditional mutation, lock or serializable protocol, account for conflicts and retry the entire required transaction with stable operation identity. Intermediate Why is a replica a poor default for a post-create lookup? An asynchronous replica can lag behind the committed writer. The absence is then stale evidence, not proof creation failed. Choose the read path according to the promised freshness and use the original identity on retries.

title: Databases
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. Suppose two checkout requests both read the last available item. Each sees stock=1 and each decides the purchase is valid. Storing both orders durably would preserve the wrong business outcome. Durability answers whether committed data survives; isolation and atomic conditional mutation determine whether concurrent decisions can commit safely. This small example explains why database selection starts with invariants as well as query speed.

title: Databases
heading: 4. List operations and invariants
text: 4. List operations and invariants Separate the access pattern, invariant, freshness and recovery promise. An access pattern is a precise operation over data, including its expected frequency, result size and freshness. Record its key distribution as well: one large merchant can dominate traffic even when most tenants are small. Distinguish the authoritative acceptance path from analytics or search views that can be delayed. An invariant describes a forbidden committed state. Uniqueness of a partner reference, nonnegative available stock and a legal order transition are different rules and may need different enforcement mechanisms. A unique constraint guards identity; a conditional update or suitable locking/isolation protocol guards a concurrent stock decision. A fast query is an efficiency requirement rather than a substitute for either rule. Durability and recovery need their own definitions. State what a successful acknowledgement means in the chosen store/configuration, the tolerated data-loss window and the tested restore process. A running replica can reproduce an accidental delete, while an older backup can omit a later external payment. Database correctness includes recovery evidence, not only successful inserts. Functional requirements Create order and line items. Read one order; list recent orders for a customer. Reserve stock and expose payment state. Targets and invariants No duplicate partner order within a tenant. Stock must not become negative. Illustrative p95 order lookup below 100 ms. Durable accepted order; recovery point defined explicitly. An invariant is a condition that must hold after every allowed transition. “Never negative stock” needs an atomic mutation; a fast eventual view is insufficient. “Revenue dashboard updated within a minute” can use an asynchronous projection. Different operations can therefore use different storage paths without changing the source of truth.

title: Databases
heading: 5. Keys and constraints before indexes
text: 5. Keys and constraints before indexes Choose identity and ownership before optimizing how rows are found. Begin with identity. A primary key uniquely identifies a stored row under the database’s constraint semantics. A business key such as tenant plus partner reference recognizes an externally meaningful order. They can coexist because they answer different questions. If two requests race, only an authoritative uniqueness guard can decide which insert may commit; a Java existence check alone has a gap between its read and write. Next decide which facts belong together. Order and line items may need one atomic creation, while a historical customer display name can intentionally be copied into an order. A foreign key can enforce that a referenced identity exists, but cannot decide whether an order may transition from cancelled to shipped. Normalization reduces duplicated mutable facts; denormalization deliberately duplicates data for a read or historical requirement and requires an owner for updates. Before committing to embedding or separate rows, walk an update and a query. Which fields change together? Can a collection grow without bound? Is the copied field a historical snapshot or a current truth? This makes the model’s consistency cost visible before it becomes a production synchronization problem. CREATE TABLE orders ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, external_id text NOT NULL, customer_id uuid NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL, UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_id) ); The primary key identifies a row. The unique constraint enforces one external order ID per tenant even when two requests race. Checking existence in Java first is useful for a friendly error but cannot replace the constraint. Relational foreign keys can enforce referenced identity; domain transitions still require application rules. Normalize when it protects shared facts and useful relationships. Embed or denormalize when an access pattern benefits and you can own the update rules. Duplicating customer display name into an order may preserve a historical snapshot; duplicating live account credit can create an invariant problem.

title: Databases
heading: 6. Derive an index from a query
text: 6. Derive an index from a query Derive an access path from this query, then inspect what the engine actually does. A table stores rows, while an index supplies an additional access structure. For the example query, tenant and customer identify a subset and created_at plus ID order that subset. A suitable composite B-tree index can let PostgreSQL locate the relevant range and traverse it in the required order, rather than examining and sorting the whole table. The ID gives deterministic ordering when timestamps tie. The column order must be justified by actual predicates and ordering. An index optimized for equality on tenant/customer followed by recent time is not automatically the best path for an unrelated status-only query. PostgreSQL planning and multicolumn access have nuances, so inspect the chosen plan rather than treating “leftmost column” as a universal rule that predicts every possible optimization. An index costs storage and mutation work; updates to indexed values may require additional maintenance. Inspect representative data, selectivity, estimated versus actual row counts, sort behavior and buffers. EXPLAIN describes a plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement to collect measurements. Be deliberate about executing writes or expensive queries during diagnosis. A sequential scan can be the right plan when much of the table is needed. SELECT id, created_at, status FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = :tenant AND customer_id = :customer ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 25; CREATE INDEX order_customer_recent ON orders (tenant_id, customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC); An index is an additional access structure. The ordering above lets the engine locate a tenant/customer range and return recent rows without sorting the whole order table. It costs storage and work on inserts/updates. A low-selectivity index or incompatible leading columns may not help the actual query. Use EXPLAIN to inspect the plan; use EXPLAIN ANALYZE carefully because it executes the statement. Compare estimated and actual row counts, scanned rows, sorts and buffer activity with representative data. A sequential scan is sometimes the correct choice for a large fraction of a table.

title: Databases
heading: 7. What a transaction protects
text: 7. What a transaction protects Place the concurrent decision at the authoritative commit boundary. Atomicity means a defined set of changes commits together or not at all. Isolation describes the concurrent observations and anomalies the transaction protocol permits. Durability describes survival under the specified failure/acknowledgement model. These properties are related, but one does not imply every business decision is safe. Follow the last item under PostgreSQL Read Committed. A reads available=1; B reads available=1; both decide in Java that a sale is allowed. Merely putting each read and later unconditional write in a transaction does not make that decision exclusive. Move the check into the authoritative mutation: decrement only where enough stock remains, check affected rows, and insert the corresponding reservation in the same local transaction. Keep quantity validation and duplicate identity explicit. A negative decrement can increase stock; a repeated valid command must not reserve again. For several items, use a consistent acquisition/update order and roll back the intended group when a prerequisite fails. Deadlocks or serialization failures require a bounded retry of the relevant transaction, with stable business identity and no duplicated external effects. In Spring, the transaction boundary must actually be intercepted under the selected transaction mechanism and use the intended resource/manager. A proxied @Transactional method does not enlist an ordinary HTTP payment provider. Keep remote calls outside lock-holding work and persist recovery state across that boundary. Exceptions and JPA flush timing can move when a failure is observed; test the commit outcome rather than assuming a repository call returning means the transaction committed. BEGIN; UPDATE inventory SET available = available - :qty WHERE sku = :sku AND available >= :qty; -- Continue only if exactly one row changed; qty must be positive. INSERT INTO reservations (...); COMMIT; In Spring, a transaction interceptor normally surrounds a proxied method invocation. Self-invocation can bypass proxy interception. Keep the data-source and transaction-manager relationship explicit, avoid long remote calls while holding locks, and understand rollback rules. Catching an exception does not necessarily make a failed transaction usable again. Validate command → Conditional DB mutation → Store reservation + outbox → Commit or roll back The local transaction covers local writes. It does not include a remote payment provider. Timeline step Unsafe read-then-write Conditional mutation in one local transaction A observes last item A decides it may reserve. Decision occurs in UPDATE predicate. B competes B can make the same stale decision. Store coordinates the competing mutation; affected-row result determines success. Reservation creation fails Separate commits can strand the decrement. Rollback restores the intended local group. Response disappears after commit Caller cannot infer failure. Scoped stable command identity recovers the original result.

title: Databases
heading: 8. SQL and NoSQL as access-model choices
text: 8. SQL and NoSQL as access-model choices Compare the same operation and guarantee across storage models. Only now compare storage models. Relational storage makes related rows, constraints and flexible indexed queries natural. Key-value access favors deliberately chosen keys and bounded known operations. Documents can keep aggregate-shaped data together. Search reorganizes derived facts for text retrieval and ranking. These are access/ownership choices, not a ranking from old to modern. For each candidate, express the same operation and its failure boundary. Can the required conditional change be atomic? What is the transaction scope? Which exact read path can be stale? What happens to the busiest key? How are backups restored and migrations verified? SQL systems can partition/replicate, and NoSQL systems can provide transactions; the selected product, topology and access path determine the actual guarantee. A hybrid can be appropriate when ownership is clear: authoritative orders in one write model, search in a derived index, large export bytes in object storage. It becomes dangerous when multiple stores independently act as authority for the same money or inventory fact without an explicit coordination/reconciliation protocol. Model Good fit Boundary to examine Relational (PostgreSQL/RDS) Relations, constraints, transactions, flexible indexed queries Join/query cost, locks, write capacity. Key-value (DynamoDB) Known partition-key access and conditional item changes Key distribution, secondary-index behavior, transaction scope. Document (MongoDB) Aggregate-shaped documents read/updated together Document growth, multi-document invariants and index cost. Search index Relevance and text search Projection freshness; not an automatic authority for orders. Object storage (S3) Large immutable blobs and exports Object lifecycle and metadata/query service. “NoSQL scales” is not a selection criterion. A badly chosen partition key can overload one partition. SQL databases can partition and replicate; NoSQL databases may offer transactions. State the specific operation, transaction boundary, consistency mode and operational cost.

title: Databases
heading: 9. Replication and partitioning solve different problems
text: 9. Replication and partitioning solve different problems Choose where a reader may look and who may accept writes. Another copy and another owner solve different problems. Replication maintains copies of a logical dataset; partitioning divides the dataset or work across keys/ranges. A readable replica may absorb eligible reads but can lag the writer. If order creation commits and the next lookup reaches a delayed copy, not found is stale evidence rather than proof creation failed. Define the promised observation for each journey. The caller retrieving a newly created order may need a writer path or another explicit read-your-writes mechanism. A revenue dashboard may tolerate delay. Do not turn either choice into an assumption that all indexes, replicas or regions behave identically in a managed service. Partitioning introduces locality and distribution trade-offs. Tenant-based routing keeps many queries local, but a giant tenant can remain hot. Splitting it may require fan-out or a new projection. Rebalancing must preserve write ownership while routes change; an old process does not stop acting merely because another node became leader. The dedicated replication lesson develops these protocols further.

title: Databases
heading: 10. Worked design: order store and revenue view
text: 10. Worked design: order store and revenue view Keep correctness local where possible and derive the delayed revenue view. Design the order write model from the earlier requirements: a scoped unique partner reference, an atomic reservation decision, the order facts and a durable outbox intent. Keep the customer/recent-order access path indexed. A response is successful only according to the transaction’s actual outcome; a lost response is recovered using the original operation identity. Now add daily revenue. Its one-minute freshness requirement allows a projection rather than an expensive synchronous scan in every checkout. Each source event needs identity and ordering/version semantics appropriate to the projection. Replaying a paid event must not count revenue again, and a later refund or correction must adjust the view under an explicit rule. Backfill is another concurrent protocol: connect a consistent baseline to subsequent changes using a known position or an equivalent supported mechanism. Otherwise updates during the scan can be lost or overwritten by older copied values. Validate counts and critical business totals, not merely whether the pipeline is running. Keep operational order acceptance independent of a temporarily delayed dashboard. Test unique-key races, concurrent last-item purchases, replica lag after create, transaction deadlocks, and projection replay. Observe pool waits, query latency, locks, slow-query plans and replica lag. Adding an ORM does not remove database behavior: JPA flush timing and N+1 queries still need measurement.

title: Databases
heading: 11. Tricky failures to rehearse
text: 11. Tricky failures to rehearse Classify scan cost, lock wait, pool wait and stale observation separately. Investigate a symptom by separating access cost, contention and freshness. A query can be slow because it scans too much, waits for a lock, waits for a connection, or receives a resource-starved execution plan. An ORM method name does not distinguish those cases. Measure generated SQL, plan, transaction duration and acquisition wait before selecting a fix. Also examine changes over time: index growth, data skew, long-running snapshots, schema overlap and restore compatibility. A clean small dataset can hide an N+1 read pattern or an expensive count. A successful backup job is not a demonstrated restore. Test representative volume, competing mutations and recovery paths against the actual engine/configuration. Failure Common mistake Better response Replica lag after write Treat a missing replica row as a failed creation Use authoritative lookup and retry identity. Schema rollout New writer breaks old readers during rollback Expand, migrate, verify, then contract. Hot partition Add partitions without changing skew Measure key distribution and choose a split/aggregation policy. Backup exists Assume recovery is proven Restore into isolation and measure recovery time/data loss. Record recovery time objective (RTO: acceptable recovery duration) and recovery point objective (RPO: acceptable data-loss window). Availability of a running replica is not the same as recoverability after corruption or an operator mistake.

title: Databases
heading: 12. Interview ladder
text: 12. Interview ladder Foundational Primary key versus index? A primary key identifies a row and enforces uniqueness/non-null semantics. An index is an access structure; databases commonly implement key constraints with indexes, but not every index defines identity. Foundational Does an index always make a query faster? No. Selectivity, column order, result size, data distribution and plan choice matter. Indexes also increase write and storage cost. Intermediate Why is check-then-insert unsafe? Two transactions can both observe absence before either commits. A unique constraint or equivalent atomic conditional operation is the final concurrency guard. Intermediate Can a read replica show stale data? Yes when replication is asynchronous or the selected read path lags. Define freshness requirements and route operations accordingly. Advanced How do you migrate without a write outage? Choose an initial consistent copy plus change capture/catch-up and verification, control the write switch, define rollback and conflict ownership, and test failure windows. The exact protocol depends on source/target capabilities. Advanced When would you avoid a distributed transaction? When a durable state machine, outbox and compensation can meet the business contract with less coordination. That introduces temporary intermediate states and recovery work rather than making cross-system atomicity disappear. Intermediate Why can a transaction still allow an unsafe last-item purchase? A transaction groups changes, but the isolation/protocol may allow both callers to read stock=1 before either writes. Put the stock condition into an authoritative atomic mutation or use an appropriate lock/isolation protocol. Inspect affected rows and commit the reservation with the decrement. Distinct purchase keys still compete; idempotency alone does not solve that race. Advanced The index exists but production is slow. What do you inspect? The actual query and parameters, chosen plan, estimated/actual rows, selectivity/skew, sorts and buffer work, plus lock and pool waits. Verify representative data and query frequency, including ORM-generated N+1 and count queries. An index can be present yet irrelevant to the bottleneck, and a sequential scan may be a rational plan.

title: Databases
heading: 13. Further reading and practice
text: 13. Further reading and practice Know the authoritative read before adding a cached copy. Use the PostgreSQL references to check the exact isolation and plan behavior used in your design. Use Spring’s transaction documentation to check proxy boundaries and rollback policy. For other stores, read the documentation for the specific operation, index and topology rather than transferring guarantees from a different engine. Before moving to Caching, explain which database operation is authoritative and how much it costs. A cache adds a separate copy with its own identity and freshness policy; it should not hide an undefined transaction boundary or turn a stale browse answer into permission to sell stock. PostgreSQL isolation : statement snapshots, anomalies and retry requirements. PostgreSQL EXPLAIN : read real query plans before optimizing. Spring transactions : proxy boundaries and transaction behavior. DynamoDB read consistency : table/index-specific guarantees. Exercise: write three access patterns for your service, derive one index, and identify one invariant that belongs in a constraint or conditional write.

title: Caching
heading: Overview
text: Start with one repeated product lookup. Build a cache, then follow what happens when data changes, entries expire together, or the cache disappears.

title: Caching
heading: 1. Why repeat the same read?
text: 1. Why repeat the same read? The database lesson improved the cost of a query with an index. The same popular product can still cause that query to run thousands of times. A cache keeps an answer for reuse, often nearer the caller. We first save repeated work, then ask what happens when the authoritative product changes while an older answer remains available. Keep browsing and purchasing separate. A customer may tolerate a slightly old description while scrolling, but accepting a purchase at an invalid price or against unavailable stock is a different decision. The right cache policy follows the operation’s correctness and freshness requirements. It does not follow simply from having Redis available.

title: Caching
heading: 2. Derive freshness from the operation
text: 2. Derive freshness from the operation Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. An index finds the authoritative row faster; a cache answers from a separate copy. That distinction introduces time into correctness. A TTL limits how long an entry is reusable under a policy. Eviction removes an entry for capacity or policy reasons. Invalidation reacts to a change. None of those words alone specifies how stale the answer can become during concurrent fills or failed updates. Follow a race. A reader loads product version 7. A writer commits version 8 and deletes the cached entry. The earlier reader then stores version 7 after that deletion. The cache is stale despite invalidation. Depending on the freshness contract, use a bounded expiry, version-aware updates or a coordinated strategy. For checkout, revalidate the price against an authoritative rule instead of assuming a cached browse price is a purchase guarantee. Check your understanding Foundational A high hit ratio means the cache is working correctly. It measures reuse, not freshness, tenant isolation or total cost. Observe stale-answer incidents, source load during misses, refill concurrency, eviction and key distribution alongside hit ratio. Intermediate What must happen when Redis becomes unavailable? The policy depends on the operation. Browsing may use bounded stale data or constrained database fallback. An authoritative safety rule must not silently disappear. Limit fallback concurrency so a cache outage does not become a database outage.

title: Caching
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. Request A reads product version 7 and stores a copy. Request B arrives one second later and can use it without SQL. A merchant then publishes version 8. If B continues reading the copy, the shop has two representations of the product. Decide which operations may see version 7. Browsing can often tolerate delay; charging a price or checking permission may require another policy. This is why freshness belongs in the requirement, before a TTL or Redis command is selected.

title: Caching
heading: 4. Define the freshness contract
text: 4. Define the freshness contract A freshness contract states what observations are permitted, under which conditions and failure modes. “Cache for sixty seconds” describes an entry policy; “no answer more than sixty seconds behind a committed update” is a stronger end-to-end claim. A reader can fetch an old source version and publish it late, or another cache layer can reuse it longer. Explain those intervals before claiming a staleness bound. Define identity before expiry. The same product ID can produce different views for tenants, languages, currencies or permission contexts. Reuse is safe only across callers entitled to the same representation. A fast wrong-tenant hit is a security failure, not a cache-performance improvement. State whether the cache is disposable and what the service will do when it cannot reach it. Functional requirements Read product details and update them as a merchant. Share popular data across application instances. Return a controlled response when a cache read fails. Targets and invariants Illustrative display staleness: at most 60 seconds under the stated policy. Never reuse one tenant’s private representation for another. Checkout revalidates authoritative price/stock. Cache loss must not overload the database. A TTL by itself is not necessarily a bound on staleness relative to the latest write: a slow reader can refill an old value after invalidation. State which races and refresh failures your guarantee covers. If an invariant requires current data, enforce it at the authoritative mutation path.

title: Caching
heading: 5. Walk through cache-aside
text: 5. Walk through cache-aside The freshness requirement defines which answers are reusable; follow the simplest miss path next. Follow a cold lookup: build the complete representation key, ask the cache, and on a miss load the authoritative data and publish a reusable value with its policy. A miss is expected. The source path must therefore be bounded and observable in normal operation, not only during an outage. Distinguish a missing product, an unavailable source and an undecodable cached value. Now let a hundred callers miss the same popular key. The basic pseudocode can send a hundred identical database reads before any fill becomes visible. A local single-flight mechanism lets equivalent callers share one in-progress fill inside that process; other processes may still refill independently. Bound waiting and fill concurrency, and define what happens if the fill fails. Do not let a slow fill hold every caller indefinitely. Fill publication is a separate event from the source read. Carry source/version information when the freshness protocol needs it. A method returning a value does not establish that it is still the latest value when the cache write completes. That is the race explored next. Cache lookup → Miss only: query source → Fill with TTL A hit returns immediately and skips the source/fill path. A miss fills after reading the source; that interval can race with writers. Product getProduct(TenantId tenant, ProductId id) { String key = "product:v2:" + tenant + ":" + id; Product cached = cache.get(key); if (cached != null) return cached; Product value = repository.find(tenant, id); cache.put(key, value, Duration.ofSeconds(60)); return value; } // Teaching pseudocode: add timeouts, missing values, failure policy and metrics. Include every dimension that changes the reusable value: tenant, locale, currency, schema version or permission scope where relevant. Avoid using raw credentials as keys. A user-specific representation often belongs in a private or per-user cache rather than one shared product key.

title: Caching
heading: 6. What happens after a write?
text: 6. What happens after a write? The read path works until the source changes. Now trace a reader and writer together. Place a reader and writer on the same timeline. The reader loads version 7; the writer commits version 8 and invalidates the key; the reader then publishes version 7. The delete was successful, yet an older value reappeared. This is why write-then-invalidate needs an explicit concurrent-fill policy rather than a slogan. A versioned immutable key prevents one version from overwriting another, but the caller still needs a trustworthy way to find the current version. A version-aware publication rule needs durable knowledge or a marker that survives an absent key; comparing only against a cache value that has already been deleted does not preserve that knowledge. A delayed second delete can reduce particular races without proving a general bound. Choose the least coordination that meets the contract. A browse view may tolerate bounded stale answers under documented assumptions. An inventory or permission decision can use the authoritative mutation path. Durable invalidation intent, such as an outbox row committed with the update, helps recover lost invalidations but still does not make a source transaction atomic with all cache readers. Race to reason about: 1. Reader misses and reads DB version 7. 2. Writer commits version 8, then deletes cache key. 3. Reader finishes late and caches version 7. 4. New readers temporarily see version 7 again. Options include tolerating bounded staleness, caching under immutable/versioned keys, and using version-aware conditional publication tied to durable version knowledge. A compare-and-set only against an existing cache value does not solve the absent-key race unless the protocol preserves a newer version marker. “Delete twice after a delay” reduces some races but is not a general proof of consistency. Pattern Useful when Cost Cache-aside Read-heavy data; misses are acceptable Stale copies and refill races. Write-through Writes go through a component that updates cache/source Failure ordering and authority must be explicit. Write-behind Buffering asynchronous persistence is acceptable Loss/durability and ordering become core requirements. No cache on decision path Current state determines permission or stock More source work, but clearer invariant. Step Source Cache consequence Reader loads version 7 Version 7 observed before update Fill is still in progress. Writer commits version 8 Version 8 authoritative Invalidation removes the current entry. Old reader fills late Source still version 8 Version 7 can reappear without a stronger protocol. Choose a policy Define acceptable observation Bounded stale display, coordinated publication, or authoritative decision path.

title: Caching
heading: 7. Local, distributed, and edge caches
text: 7. Local, distributed, and edge caches A local Caffeine cache belongs to one Java process; another process can hold a different copy. A Redis/Valkey cache is shared through a network dependency and serialization contract. A CDN stores HTTP representations under HTTP/cache-key rules. These layers can reduce different costs and can coexist, but every extra copy needs an identity and freshness policy. Trace an update through all layers. If Redis refreshes but a process keeps an older local copy, the shortest TTL does not automatically govern the user’s observation. A freshly fetched lower-layer entry can already contain stale data. Use source/version or age evidence appropriate to the contract and avoid stacking independent TTLs without analyzing the resulting lifetime. Spring’s cache annotation expresses interception and lookup behavior, while the selected provider defines expiry, serialization and operational details. Under normal proxy mode, self-invocation bypasses the cache interceptor. Review key construction and configuration as part of correctness. A cached method result and a shared HTTP response are different layers with different privacy and validation rules. @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#tenant + ':' + #id") public ProductView load(String tenant, String id) { return repository.loadView(tenant, id); } // Provider config supplies expiry/serialization; invoke through the Spring proxy.

title: Caching
heading: 8. Expiration, eviction, and stampedes
text: 8. Expiration, eviction, and stampedes Expiration makes an entry ineligible according to time policy; eviction removes it because of capacity or another policy. Both produce misses, but neither guarantees that a business subscriber receives a durable deletion event. Estimate the working set using realistic key/value encoding, metadata and copies, then measure memory and eviction under the real popularity distribution. A stampede is many callers refilling equivalent data concurrently. Coalesce same-key work where appropriate, spread mass expiry with jitter and cap total source-facing fills. Jitter distributes expiry times; it does not supply capacity for one extremely hot missing key. Coordination needs timeout/ownership rules so a failed filler does not strand future callers. Negative caching stores an intentional not-found result for a defined interval. Use a distinct representation and appropriate invalidation after creation. A database timeout is uncertainty, not proof that the product does not exist. Caching the timeout as absence can turn a transient dependency incident into persistent incorrect answers.

title: Caching
heading: 9. Worked design: catalog during a flash sale
text: 9. Worked design: catalog during a flash sale Combine identity, invalidation and refill protection under one realistic traffic spike. For the flash-sale catalog, define which view is reusable before choosing layers. Public images can use an edge cache; tenant/locale product descriptions can use a shared view; personalized discounts must have a separate representation policy. Checkout independently validates authoritative pricing and stock. Browsing freshness is not permission to commit the purchase. Commit merchant changes and a durable invalidation intent together. The invalidator retries its own work under stable identity. Refill must account for the reader/writer race and protect the database with bounded concurrency. If Redis fails, decide which reads may use a permitted stale copy, which may use constrained fallback, and which must fail/defer. An unconditional “catch exception and query SQL” path can multiply source traffic catastrophically. Prove recovery with more than hit ratio: examine source work, fill latency, age/version, eviction, error rate and useful checkout completions. Repeat with a cold start, a slow old reader, an invalidation outage, a hot key and an intentionally wrong tenant/locale key. These experiments test distinct correctness and capacity boundaries.

title: Caching
heading: 10. Tricky cases and recovery
text: 10. Tricky cases and recovery Cache recovery can be as demanding as cache failure. Reconnecting processes may all refill at once, and a serialization rollout may make old entries unreadable across the fleet. Version representations and roll readers/writers compatibly. Bound fallback and refill before enabling traffic after a cold start. If the cache holds the only copy of an accepted business fact, it is functioning as a primary data store and needs a corresponding durability/recovery design. Likewise, keyspace notifications cannot become the only durable trigger for required work. Choose mechanisms according to what loss or duplication the business can tolerate. Case Risk Policy Redis unavailable All traffic falls through to SQL Bound fallback; shed noncritical reads. Serializer changes Old values cannot be decoded Version key/value format; roll safely. Permission revoked Old cached authorization still allows access Enforce sensitive checks authoritatively or design an explicit revocation bound. Delete notification lost A consumer assumes every expiration is observed Use a durable event mechanism for required business work. Redis keyspace notifications are not a durable business-event log. A disconnected subscriber can miss notifications. Use them for suitable best-effort observations, not as the only proof that an order must be processed.

title: Caching
heading: 11. Interview ladder
text: 11. Interview ladder Foundational Cache hit versus miss? A hit finds a reusable eligible value; a miss requires another source or a controlled fallback. Miss performance matters during normal expiry and incidents. Foundational TTL versus eviction? TTL is time-based eligibility; eviction is capacity-policy removal. Entries can be evicted before TTL. Neither guarantees a reliable deletion event. Intermediate Why delete after DB commit rather than before? Deleting first lets a concurrent reader refill the old DB value before the write commits. Deleting after commit avoids that specific ordering, but a late reader can still refill old data, so state the remaining race. Intermediate Would you cache account permissions? Only with a documented revocation/freshness policy and suitable isolation. For a sensitive mutation, use authoritative validation or a protocol that enforces the required revocation bound. Advanced How do you survive loss of a 99% hit-rate cache? The source may see up to 100 times usual miss traffic. Use bounded fallback/refill, headroom, permitted stale responses, admission control and recovery tests. Advanced Does a distributed lock solve consistency? It only coordinates participants that obey it during its valid lease. Expiry, stale holders, crashes and outside writers remain; durable version/invariant enforcement may still be required. Intermediate Does a 60-second TTL prove an answer is at most 60 seconds behind the latest write? Not by itself. Identify when the source value was observed, when it was published, concurrent invalidation/refill and other cache layers. A late old fill can create a fresh entry containing old data. State the assumptions behind the bound or use an authoritative/coordinated path. Advanced What must a cache outage policy protect? The business invariant, tenant isolation and source capacity. Bound fallback/refill concurrency, use stale data only where permitted, and reject/defer optional reads when necessary. A universal catch-and-query fallback can move the outage to the database.

title: Caching
heading: 12. Further reading and practice
text: 12. Further reading and practice Carry the operation and its guarantee into the next lesson. Read the provider documentation to verify what expiry, eviction, persistence, notifications and coordination actually mean. Read Spring’s cache documentation to locate the interception boundary. Then compare those mechanisms against one precise operation and its failure contract rather than treating @Cacheable as an end-to-end consistency guarantee. The next lesson makes a different kind of copy durable: an intent or fact passed to another process. Unlike a disposable cached view, accepted asynchronous work must survive the producer’s lifetime and have an explicit completion/recovery protocol. Spring cache abstraction : proxy semantics and provider responsibilities. Redis keyspace notifications : delivery limitations and event configuration. Redis eviction : memory policy and eviction behavior. HTTP caching : freshness and validation for edge/client caches. Exercise: draw a cache refill racing with an update. State exactly how long stale data can persist and what evidence supports that bound.

title: Messaging
heading: Overview
text: Begin with a slow receipt email in checkout. Learn queues and event logs, acknowledgements, duplicates, ordering, outbox/inbox patterns, and operational recovery.

title: Messaging
heading: 1. Remove email from the checkout wait
text: 1. Remove email from the checkout wait Checkout already committed the order, but a slow email provider is keeping the HTTP caller waiting. The business can often acknowledge the order before the receipt is sent. Separate those completion points explicitly: order acceptance is one durable fact; sending the receipt is pending work with its own owner and deadline. An in-memory executor changes timing but does not preserve work after a process crash. A durable handoff records the intent independently of the current request thread. This removes one lifetime dependency and introduces new responsibilities: recognizing repeated delivery, measuring delayed completion and deciding when the intermediary may stop retaining work.

title: Messaging
heading: 2. Identify exactly what an acknowledgement proves
text: 2. Identify exactly what an acknowledgement proves Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. An asynchronous message represents work or a fact that another process can handle later. Delivery means the broker made it available to a consumer. Processing means the consumer attempted its handler. Completion means the intended business effect reached its defined durable boundary. An acknowledgement tells the broker when it may stop redelivering; it is not automatically evidence that a remote shipment or payment completed. Commit an order and an outbox row together. A relay publishes the row, then records publication. If it crashes between those steps, it may publish again. A consumer can record the event ID and its local mutation together so a repeat does not apply that mutation twice. If it calls an external carrier, a second boundary remains: the carrier may act before the consumer records success. Carry stable provider identity and reconcile that uncertainty. Check your understanding Foundational Exactly-once delivery eliminates duplicate business effects everywhere. A guarantee has a scope. Broker transactions do not automatically include an external database or provider. Identify which resources participate, how retries are recognized, and what evidence survives a crash. Intermediate When should a consumer acknowledge? After the durable work required by its processing contract commits, with explicit recovery for remote effects. Acknowledging before durable handoff risks loss; acknowledging after a crash can lead to redelivery, which must be safe.

title: Messaging
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. If a Java thread sends the receipt after the HTTP response, a process crash can lose the thread and its pending work. If a queue holds the task, another worker can receive it after the first worker dies. But the queue does not know whether the email provider already acted. Persisting pending work solves one failure window and exposes the next. Keep producer commit, broker delivery, consumer commit and external effect separate throughout the lesson.

title: Messaging
heading: 4. Define acceptance and completion separately
text: 4. Define acceptance and completion separately Name the business acceptance point and the final effect. “No lost receipt intent after order commit” requires a durable connection between the local change and publication; “no duplicate shipment” requires protection at the effect boundary. These are separate guarantees. A broker feature solving delivery does not automatically solve either local atomicity or remote-provider uncertainty. A command requests an action from a responsible owner; an event describes a fact that interested consumers can interpret. SendReceipt is a command, while OrderAccepted is an event. Define their identity, schema, ownership, retry horizon and completion expectations. Independent consumers need independent progress and failure handling so analytics cannot accidentally govern shipping availability. Functional requirements Accept an order and schedule receipt work. Allow fulfillment and analytics to react independently. Retry transient delivery errors and recover failed work. Targets and invariants No lost receipt intent after order commit. Duplicate delivery must not duplicate protected business effects. Illustrative oldest receipt age under two minutes. One broken message must not block all healthy work. A command asks someone to act, such as SendReceipt. An event records a fact, such as OrderAccepted. Events often have several independent consumers. Commands should have clear ownership; events should carry enough identity and contract information for consumers to interpret them safely.

title: Messaging
heading: 5. Queue versus retained event log
text: 5. Queue versus retained event log We know why pending work must survive. Choose how independent readers share or replay it. A work queue assigns pending work among competing workers. Publish/subscribe creates separate delivery paths for independent reactions. A retained log keeps records by policy while consumers track positions. Choose from the reader’s required behavior: one owner processing a job, several independent reactions, or consumers needing ordered replay while history remains available. In a Kafka consumer group, partition assignment constrains parallel progress; adding more consumers than useful partition work does not force additional throughput. Different groups can read independently. In SQS, distinguish standard-queue repeat/ordering behavior from FIFO ordering and send deduplication. In both cases, the application must define when a durable business effect is complete. Ordering also has scope. Grouping by order ID can serialize that order’s events without imposing one global sequence on every order. A hot order/key or a slow handler can still constrain the chosen scope. Preserve the business reason for ordering rather than assuming a globally ordered stream is always safer. Model Reader behavior Use Work queue Workers compete for tasks; successful processing removes/acknowledges work Jobs and independently retried commands. Publish/subscribe Each subscription gets its own delivery path Several independent reactions to an event. Partitioned log Consumers track positions; records are retained by policy Replay, ordered per-partition streams, projections. In Kafka, a consumer group normally divides partition ownership among its members; different groups can independently consume the same retained records. Parallelism within one group is constrained by partitions and assignment. In SQS standard queues, consumers compete and delivery can repeat; ordering is best-effort. FIFO adds specific ordering/deduplication semantics, not automatic atomicity with your database. Order + outbox commit → Relay to broker → Consumer local transaction → Ack / commit position Every arrow is a failure boundary. Follow the stable event identity through all of them.

title: Messaging
heading: 6. Walk through the acknowledgement window
text: 6. Walk through the acknowledgement window The broker can deliver work; next establish what proof lets it stop redelivering. Follow one delivery through receive, local commit and acknowledgement. If the consumer acknowledges first and then dies, the effect can be lost. If it commits first and dies before acknowledging, the message can repeat. Those failure windows are unavoidable when the broker and local store do not share the relevant atomic protocol; the processing contract must tolerate the selected recovery behavior. For a protected local mutation, insert a consumer-scoped event receipt and apply the mutation in one transaction. A unique identity decides whether that work already committed. If it did, the repeat can acknowledge without repeating the effect. If the transaction failed, the receipt must not remain as false proof of completion. Different legitimate consumers need different receipt scopes. A remote carrier or payment provider remains outside that local transaction. The inbox can prove that a local fulfillment task was created once; it cannot by itself prove one remote shipment. Persist the remote intent, reuse its provider identity and reconcile unknown outcomes. Retain receipts for the actual redelivery/replay horizon, not an arbitrary cleanup interval. Safe local-effect pattern: BEGIN; INSERT INTO inbox(consumer, event_id) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; -- If already present, skip the effect and acknowledge. -- Otherwise apply local domain mutation in this transaction. COMMIT; ACK message / commit consumed position afterward; The inbox uniqueness constraint and local mutation must share the same commit. A remote shipment provider remains outside that transaction; it needs its own retry identity/status lookup or reconciliation. Retain deduplication records long enough for the replay/redelivery horizon. Deleting them early permits old events to act again.

title: Messaging
heading: 7. Close the producer dual-write gap
text: 7. Close the producer dual-write gap The producer has its own dual-write problem. Database-first can commit an order and crash before publishing; broker-first can publish a fact for an order that never commits. Record the business change and publication intent in the same local transaction. The relay reads committed intents and publishes them later, so a producer crash leaves recoverable pending work. The relay still has a publish/mark-sent gap. If publication succeeded and the relay dies before recording that result, it can publish again. Keep event identity stable across those attempts. The outbox changes an unrecorded omission into recoverable potentially repeated delivery; the consumer’s effect protocol handles repetition. An after-commit callback can reduce perceived delay but is not a substitute for durable pending intent. Similarly, committing an SQL transaction and a broker transaction in sequence does not erase the failure interval between them. State the exact participating resources and recovery ledger instead of implying an annotation supplies universal atomicity. @Transactional public Order accept(CreateOrder cmd) { Order order = orders.insert(cmd); outbox.insert(new Event(order.id(), "OrderAccepted", 1)); return order; } // Relay publishes committed rows; publish success and "sent" marking can race. // Expect duplicate publication and keep eventId stable. Spring transaction management can cover the local database work. A Spring Kafka or AWS SDK producer sends from the relay. Broker transactions have useful scopes, but do not assume an annotation atomically commits PostgreSQL, Kafka, SQS and a provider. Verify the exact transaction boundary for the chosen client/infrastructure.

title: Messaging
heading: 8. Ordering, schema evolution, and replay
text: 8. Ordering, schema evolution, and replay Arrival order, business event order and effect completion order can differ. One handler may finish slowly while a later event’s asynchronous effect finishes first. Include an aggregate identity and a version/ordering rule where the business requires one. A delayed old state should not blindly overwrite a newer state merely because it arrived later. Schema compatibility must cover retained history and delayed work, not only the newest producer and consumer. Define how readers treat optional additions, unknown event types and incompatible versions. A poison event may require quarantine, but skipping it can let later events for the same aggregate overtake a prerequisite. Choose that ordering/recovery policy explicitly. Replay is safe only for the effects being rebuilt. Reconstructing a search projection can use a replay-specific path that suppresses external email or shipment. Keep stable source identities, define the starting snapshot/log position and verify completeness. Resetting an offset alone does not prove a correct reconstruction or restore history that retention already removed.

title: Messaging
heading: 9. SQS and Kafka operational choices
text: 9. SQS and Kafka operational choices Acknowledge/delete and commit-position APIs expose broker-specific progress. In SQS, visibility temporarily hides received work; expiration can make it available to another worker. In Kafka, consumer positions and group participation have their own poll/processing rules. Neither replaces effect idempotency. Configure the actual Spring listener/client behavior rather than assuming return from a method always means the same acknowledgement boundary. Use bounded retries for transient failures and a deliberate path for deterministic failures. Quarantine preserves the event, error, schema and business identity for diagnosis. A dead-letter queue is a location for unresolved work, not resolution. Fix the reader or data under policy, replay with original identities and prove the business state recovered. Measure age and useful completions alongside broker counters. A decreasing queue can mean successful processing, expiration, quarantine or loss under a bad acceptance contract. Scale consumers only within database/provider capacity and ordering constraints. Backlog per worker is useful only when its relationship to processing cost and the completion target is understood. Concern SQS-style work queue Kafka-style log Progress Message acknowledgement/deletion and visibility Consumer position/offset by partition. Slow consumer Visibility can expire; extend appropriately Poll/processing and group timeouts need correct tuning.
