Retry Redelivery, delayed queues, DLQ policy Retry topics or controlled retry; ordering trade-offs. Replay Explicit retained source/archive strategy Reset positions while records remain retained. SQS visibility timeout is a lease-like hiding period, not exclusive ownership forever. A second worker may receive the message when it expires. Bound processing time, extend visibility when appropriate, and keep effects idempotent anyway. Kafka lag counts how far a consumer is behind; also measure oldest-event age and actual processing failures. A poison message fails repeatedly because of its data or a deterministic bug. After a bounded policy, quarantine it with diagnostics and ownership. A DLQ is not resolution: operators need a fix, replay authorization, and proof the replay cannot duplicate earlier effects.

title: Messaging
heading: 10. Worked design: fulfillment after checkout
text: 10. Worked design: fulfillment after checkout Use the outbox and inbox together, then identify the remote warehouse boundary they do not cover. Commit the confirmed order transition and OrderPaid intent locally. A relay publishes the stable event. A fulfillment consumer commits its receipt and a local fulfillment task together, then acknowledges. A separate runner performs the remote warehouse interaction using a durable fulfillment identity. Each boundary has a ledger that survives the current process. Now lose the warehouse response after acceptance. The local task becomes UNKNOWN until provider lookup, supported repeat-safe retry or reconciliation establishes the result. Creating a fresh shipment because the worker timed out would discard the identity needed to prevent duplication. Analytics and receipt delivery use independent progress so their failures cannot consume fulfillment’s entire budget. Validate every gap: order commit/before publication, publish/before sent mark, local consumer commit/before ack, and remote acceptance/before result recording. Include duplicate, delayed, out-of-order and incompatible-schema deliveries. Assert durable fulfillment identity and state, while monitoring oldest business-state age and unresolved recovery work. Crash window Durable evidence Recovery Before producer commit No committed order/intent Retry under original command identity. After commit, before publish Committed outbox intent Relay publishes it. After publish, before sent mark Intent may be published again Stable event identity and consumer repeat safety. After consumer commit, before ack Inbox plus local task Repeat acknowledges without duplicating local task. After remote acceptance, before result record Durable remote intent; outcome unknown Provider identity/inquiry and reconciliation.

title: Messaging
heading: 11. Backpressure and recovery
text: 11. Backpressure and recovery A queue absorbs a burst only when the system can later process the admitted work within its deadline. Sustained excess arrivals produce backlog age and cost, even if HTTP acceptance stays fast. Bound admissions or provide a declared deferred/rejected response before accepting work the system cannot honor. “Exactly once” requires a scope. Supported Kafka transactions can coordinate selected Kafka writes and consumed positions under the configured model; they do not make an arbitrary external SQL, email or provider effect atomic. Keep the resource boundary, duplicate identity and recovery protocol visible in every design claim. “Exactly once” always needs a scope. Kafka transactional processing can atomically coordinate supported Kafka operations/positions under the configured model; it does not make an arbitrary email or SQL mutation exactly once. State the boundary and prove the effect separately.

title: Messaging
heading: 12. Interview ladder
text: 12. Interview ladder Foundational Why use a queue? To decouple timing, persist pending work and buffer bursts. It introduces delayed completion, consumer operations and delivery semantics. Foundational Command versus event? A command asks for an action and has an owner; an event describes a fact that can have independent consumers. Intermediate Why acknowledge after commit? Acknowledging first risks losing work if the commit never happens. Commit first can cause redelivery, so make the effect idempotent through a shared local transaction or another appropriate protocol. Intermediate What does an outbox guarantee? The local business change and pending event are committed together. Publication can repeat, so consumers still need safe duplicate handling. Advanced How do you rebuild a projection safely? Use retained events/snapshot plus a consistent change position, handle versions, isolate rebuild traffic and suppress external business effects. Verify completeness against the source. Advanced What if FIFO messages still create duplicates? Send deduplication, visibility and redelivery are different boundaries. Protect the consumer effect with stable business identity, conditional transitions and appropriate retention. Intermediate Why does an outbox still require consumer deduplication? The relay can publish successfully and crash before recording publication. Republishing is the safe recovery for that uncertainty. A stable event identity plus the consumer’s atomic receipt/effect boundary handles the repeat. Advanced Can a dead-letter queue prove the business recovered? No. It isolates unresolved work. Preserve identity, establish failure cause and ordering impact, repair under policy, replay safely and verify the intended durable business state. Queue depth alone cannot establish completion.

title: Messaging
heading: 13. Further reading and practice
text: 13. Further reading and practice Carry the operation and its guarantee into the next lesson. Read broker documentation for retention, redelivery, ordering and progress semantics, and framework documentation for listener acknowledgement and transaction boundaries. Compare a specific crash window with those guarantees. Product labels and default configurations do not establish an end-to-end business effect. Then connect messaging to distributed consistency: separate local durable facts, delayed observations and independent service commits. The next lesson explains which states users may see while the workflow is between those commits. SQS at-least-once delivery : why consumers must tolerate repeats. SQS visibility timeout : processing leases and redelivery. Apache Kafka documentation : partitions, consumer groups and transaction semantics. Spring for Apache Kafka : listener acknowledgement, error handling and transactions. Exercise: mark each commit/ack in a flow you own. At every gap, kill the process in a test and explain the recovery identity.

title: Reliability
heading: Overview
text: Follow a checkout request through slow services, lost responses and process crashes. Derive deadlines, retries, idempotency, circuit breakers and recovery from those failures.

title: Reliability
heading: 1. A slow provider consumes the whole service
text: 1. A slow provider consumes the whole service The earlier lessons made local state correct and pending work durable. A dependency can still be slow, unreachable or uncertain. Reliability asks whether the required business function remains correct and recoverable under those conditions. Availability of a process is only one part: an HTTP 202 with permanently stranded orders is not successful completion. Follow one payment call. The provider can reject it, accept it and respond, or accept it while its response disappears. A timeout stops the caller’s wait without distinguishing those outcomes. Resource protection and business recovery therefore need different mechanisms, introduced below before combining them.

title: Reliability
heading: 2. Follow an unknown outcome through recovery
text: 2. Follow an unknown outcome through recovery Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A timeout bounds waiting; it does not roll back a remote operation. A retry makes another attempt; it does not prove that repeating is safe. A circuit breaker limits calls to a failing dependency; a bulkhead isolates capacity. Learn these responsibilities separately before composing them. Capture payment with operation ID pay_7. The provider acts, but the response is lost. Store or retain an UNKNOWN state and look up pay_7 using the provider contract. If another attempt is allowed, reuse that identity within the provider retention rules. Never create a fresh operation merely because a socket timed out. Meanwhile release local resources according to deadlines; recovery must survive beyond that HTTP request. Check your understanding Foundational Every failure should trigger three retries. Only transient failures with safe repetition and remaining time/load budget should be retried. Layered retries multiply traffic. Validation errors, exhausted deadlines and ambiguous unsafe writes need different policies. Intermediate Why is a circuit breaker insufficient for a slow database? Calls already in progress can consume the pool before it opens. Bound connection acquisition, statement execution and admitted concurrency. Measure cancellation behavior and lock/transaction cleanup.

title: Reliability
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. A request sends capture to a payment provider. The provider may reject it, complete it, or complete it while the response disappears. A timeout distinguishes none of those by itself. The local application must both stop waiting within a budget and preserve enough identity to find the real outcome later. The first is a resource-control problem; the second is a business-correctness problem. Different mechanisms are needed for each.

title: Reliability
heading: 4. Identify what must remain correct
text: 4. Identify what must remain correct Define eligible requests, acceptance and completion targets, and forbidden effects. State which work can be delayed and which facts must survive a crash. A payment operation may become pending/unknown without being declined; the caller needs a durable status path and an owner for reconciliation. Include finite resource and recovery budgets. How long may requests wait, how many may wait together, how much retry traffic is allowed, and how old may unresolved operations become? These choices connect reliability to capacity. A policy that retries forever can preserve neither latency nor bounded cost. Functional requirements Accept checkout, expose payment status and reconcile uncertain attempts. Keep status reads usable during provider problems. Let operators recover failed/unknown work safely. Targets and invariants One capture per payment intent under the provider protocol. Illustrative p95 status read below 200 ms. Bound dependency concurrency and queue length. Explicit RTO/RPO and durable intent retention. An SLO is a measurable reliability target over a window. An invariant is a condition that must hold, such as not shipping an unpaid order. A fallback can preserve availability while violating an invariant if chosen carelessly. Serving a stale product description can be acceptable; fabricating payment success cannot.

title: Reliability
heading: 5. First bound waiting time
text: 5. First bound waiting time Bound the resources consumed by one wait before considering another attempt. A timeout usually bounds a particular wait according to a client/library’s semantics. A deadline bounds the useful lifetime of a logical operation across waits and attempts. Allocate remaining time for admission, connection acquisition, dependency work, local commit and response handling; do not give every nested call a fresh original budget. Cancellation may stop local interest without undoing work already accepted elsewhere. Verify whether the underlying client releases connections/tasks, and preserve durable recovery for possible side effects. A shorter future timeout that leaves network work running can hide resource consumption instead of limiting it. Example 800 ms total budget: validation/admission: 50 ms provider + any allowed retry: at most 500 ms persistence/response: 150 ms safety margin: 100 ms Do not reset to a fresh 800 ms at every downstream hop. Configure connect, pool-acquisition and response/read timeouts for the actual HTTP client. Cancellation may interrupt local waiting without stopping remote work. A timeout cannot roll back an already-committed provider action. Use durable state and status lookup to resolve it.

title: Reliability
heading: 6. Retry an identity, not a new intent
text: 6. Retry an identity, not a new intent Retry only after establishing safe repetition, a potentially transient failure and remaining time/load budget. Validation errors need corrected input, while an ambiguous unsafe write needs identity/inquiry rather than a new intention. Keep attempt identity separate from the stable business identity. Backoff and jitter spread attempts; they do not make an unsafe effect safe. Multiple retry layers can multiply downstream calls, so choose an owner and count the initial attempt consistently. Reconciliation may continue durably after the original HTTP deadline, under its own bounded policy and unresolved-tail handling. Persist intent → Call with stable identity → Known outcome: store result → Unknown: reconcile Reconciliation queries or receives evidence about the original attempt; it is not another blind charge.

title: Reliability
heading: 7. Add circuit breaking and bulkheads
text: 7. Add circuit breaking and bulkheads Safe retries still add load. Isolate that load so one dependency cannot consume the service. A circuit breaker can stop some future calls after observed failure behavior; a bulkhead limits how much shared capacity one dependency or workload can occupy. Neither automatically cancels calls already in flight. Bound connection acquisition, execution and admitted concurrency together so a slow provider cannot exhaust the service first. Choose degradation from the operation. A stale catalog description may be permitted; a fabricated payment success is not. Separate critical and optional work, keep recovery/admin capacity, and avoid retry loops that overwhelm a recovering dependency. A breaker’s recovery probes must also fit the downstream budget. Mechanism Meaning What it does not do Circuit breaker Temporarily stop calls after evidence of dependency trouble; probe recovery It does not make a command idempotent. Bulkhead Limit resources assigned to one dependency/work class It does not increase downstream capacity. Rate limiter Bound arrivals over time It does not necessarily bound concurrent slow work. Bounded queue Limit waiting work and expose overload It does not solve sustained excess demand. Circuit breakers usually move among closed, open and half-open states. Half-open probes should be bounded; releasing every waiting caller when one probe succeeds can overwhelm a recovering dependency. Choose thresholds from real traffic, not arbitrary defaults. Separate payment-call concurrency from status-read resources. Reject early with a documented response when a budget is exhausted. Keep fallback behavior visible in metrics; a service can report 200 while returning unusable substitute data.

title: Reliability
heading: 8. Spring and AWS implementation boundaries
text: 8. Spring and AWS implementation boundaries Configure HTTP timeouts in the actual underlying client, and compose resilience libraries according to their scope. Retrying inside versus outside a circuit breaker changes observed attempts and load; applying a time limit without resource cancellation can leave hidden work. Test the configured composition rather than assuming annotations are interchangeable. For remote business actions, persist intent and stable provider identity before relying on the result. Use conditional state transitions and a durable worker/workflow where needed. Spring local transactions, SQS dispatch and a managed orchestrator can implement parts of the protocol; none chooses the business policy for late success, expiry or an unavailable inquiry endpoint. // Teaching pseudocode: explicit semantic order, not a library API signature. requireRemainingDeadline(); return boundedPaymentConcurrency.execute(() -> retryBudget.executeSafeAttempts(() -> breaker.call(() -> provider.capture(stableIntentId, request)))); // HTTP client timeouts and durable UNKNOWN-state recovery remain separate. Use Spring transaction management for durable intent and outcome updates, with remote calls outside long-held DB transactions. RDS holds the ledger; SQS can schedule retry/reconciliation work; Step Functions can coordinate explicit states when its execution model fits. ALB/API Gateway limits and SDK retry policies must be included in the end-to-end budget. A multi-AZ deployment addresses a failure domain; it does not protect against a bad release, corrupt writes or region-wide dependency failure. Test backup restoration and failover routing, and define who can initiate recovery.

title: Reliability
heading: 9. Worked design: provider outage during checkout
text: 9. Worked design: provider outage during checkout Combine bounded waits, stable identity and a durable UNKNOWN state into a recovery protocol. Payment intent pay_7 is submitted; the provider accepts it and the response is lost. Retain UNKNOWN and reconcile the original identity through the supported provider contract. A second fresh key would create a different intention and can charge again. If retention or inquiry constraints prevent establishing the outcome, surface that limitation and route the unresolved case under business policy. While recovery runs, release finite request resources and expose the durable state. Test crashes around intent creation, provider acceptance and result recording; repeat callbacks and race cancellation/expiry with late success. Recovery is proven by a known correct business outcome or a clearly owned unresolved state, not by the circuit breaker closing.

title: Reliability
heading: 10. Failure drills and recovery evidence
text: 10. Failure drills and recovery evidence Failover and hedging can duplicate irreversible work if they create independent effects. Use them only under a protocol that preserves the required business identity and guarantee. Similarly, treating every HTTP 500 as retryable can amplify deterministic bugs or replay work whose result is unknown. Observe useful completions, pending age, resource waits and recovery backlog alongside HTTP errors. A service can appear fast because it rejects everything or because it acknowledges work it never completes. Define the eligible population and success boundary so the reliability claim matches the customer journey. Drill Assertion Kill worker immediately after provider capture Attempt becomes resolvable with original identity. Provider stays slow for an hour Pools/queues stay bounded; status reads remain usable. Duplicate success after refund Conditional state/version policy prevents regression. Breaker recovers at traffic peak Probe and release policy avoids a new surge. Restore ledger backup Measured RPO/RTO meet the declared recovery contract. Track timeout rate, attempt count, retry amplification, breaker state, rejected concurrency, oldest unknown age and business discrepancy count. A green CPU chart is insufficient if payments remain unknown for hours.

title: Reliability
heading: 11. Interview ladder
text: 11. Interview ladder Foundational Timeout versus failure? A timeout means the caller did not receive a result in time. The remote side effect may have completed, so classify the outcome as unknown when appropriate. Foundational Circuit breaker versus retry? Retry performs another attempt. A circuit breaker suppresses attempts when a dependency appears unhealthy and probes for recovery. Their composition must not amplify overload. Intermediate Why use both a rate limit and a concurrency cap? A rate limit bounds arrivals per time; slow operations can still accumulate. A concurrency cap bounds simultaneous resource use. Intermediate What makes a fallback safe? Its result and side effects must preserve the operation’s business contract. Stale display data can be acceptable; invented payment success is not. Advanced What if the provider has no key or status inquiry? Local coordination cannot prove a single remote effect across arbitrary lost-response windows. Require a stronger protocol or explicitly accept bounded retry/manual-settlement risk. Advanced How do you prevent recovery from causing another outage? Bound probes, retry/reconciliation rate, queue drains and concurrency. Keep resource headroom and separate critical paths, then test a prolonged outage and synchronized recovery. Intermediate Why can a shorter timeout still leave the service exhausted? The caller may stop waiting while underlying network/task work continues to hold resources. Verify cancellation and cleanup, bound admitted concurrency and pool waits, and preserve recovery for already-accepted remote effects. Advanced Can recovery continue after the HTTP deadline? Yes, through a durable intent and separately bounded recovery policy. The response deadline limits the caller wait; it must not erase the identity and evidence needed to resolve a possible committed effect.

title: Reliability
heading: 12. Further reading and practice
text: 12. Further reading and practice AWS Builders’ Library: retries : timeout budgets and retry amplification. AWS Builders’ Library: idempotency : caller intent and uncertain outcomes. Resilience4j circuit breaker : states, thresholds and interaction with other mechanisms. gRPC deadlines : deadline propagation and cancellation. Exercise: identify one remote write you call. Write a recovery action for the exact moment after the remote commit but before your local outcome is saved.

title: Observability
heading: Overview
text: Start with a customer asking where an order went. Build a useful evidence trail from logs to metrics, traces, asynchronous work, audit records and actionable alerts.

title: Observability
heading: 1. The endpoint is green, but the customer has no order
text: 1. The endpoint is green, but the customer has no order The order API returns acceptance, messaging handles later work, caches serve copies and payments can be unknown. A generic health check cannot explain which state a customer encountered. Observability connects emitted evidence to hypotheses about those states; it does not make the evidence a substitute for the authoritative ledger. Begin with one question: why did a paid order not ship? Identify the expected transitions and the evidence needed to distinguish publication failure, consumer failure and a remote unknown outcome. Add signals for those decisions rather than collecting every possible field without a question or retention policy.

title: Observability
heading: 2. Connect evidence to a customer question
text: 2. Connect evidence to a customer question Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A metric summarizes measurements over dimensions; a log records an event; a trace relates timed operations through propagated context. A business ledger records durable facts needed for correctness and recovery. These are complementary. A trace can be sampled out, while a ledger entry still proves an accepted order exists. A customer asks why a paid order never shipped. Start with order identity, verify payment state, locate the outbox event, inspect consumer receipt and quarantine state, then find the shipment transition. A trace may shorten the search but must not be the only evidence. Measure age from paid to shipped; HTTP success rate would count the earlier acceptance as healthy even while fulfillment is broken. Check your understanding Foundational A correlation ID provides idempotency. An ID that links logs does not coordinate concurrent writes or remember a prior result. Idempotency needs a recognized operation identity and durable atomic enforcement over the effect being protected. Intermediate Why not put every order ID in a metric label? Unbounded identity creates unbounded series and cost. Use bounded labels for aggregate detection and controlled logs/traces/ledgers for individual diagnosis. Redact credentials and sensitive payloads.

title: Observability
heading: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns
text: 3. Follow one operation before adding patterns Carry this concrete operation through the later mechanisms. An API returns 202 for order ord_7. The HTTP request succeeded at acceptance, but the order may still be waiting for a message consumer. A request ID finds the initial HTTP attempt, an order ID finds the durable business state, and an event ID follows the notification. A trace can show timings where it was recorded. These identifiers answer different questions; treating them as interchangeable makes both diagnosis and duplicate prevention unreliable.

title: Observability
heading: 4. Decide the questions evidence must answer
text: 4. Decide the questions evidence must answer Define detection and investigation separately. Aggregate indicators should reveal customer-impacting delay or failure, while controlled identities let an operator investigate one journey. Specify retention, sampling, redaction and audit integrity according to purpose. A sampled trace cannot be the only record needed for business recovery. Measure acceptance and completion over explicit eligible populations and deadlines. Pending work must not disappear from the indicator merely because it has not finished. Also observe the telemetry pipeline itself: exporter failures or dropped data can make an unhealthy service look quiet. Functional requirements Find an accepted order and its current lifecycle state. Locate latency/error causes across services and workers. Audit who changed a sensitive business state. Targets and invariants No credential/card payload in telemetry. Bound metric cardinality and storage cost. Illustrative accepted-to-fulfilled SLO measured separately from HTTP. Essential audit evidence survives trace sampling. A service-level indicator (SLI) is the actual measurement, such as the fraction of eligible orders completed within five minutes. An SLO is the target for that measurement. Specify eligible events, time windows, missing evidence and where timestamps come from. Otherwise teams can appear reliable by dropping failed requests from the denominator.

title: Observability
heading: 5. Use the right signal for each question
text: 5. Use the right signal for each question The customer question spans acceptance and completion. Choose which signal supplies each part of the evidence. Metrics summarize measurements over bounded dimensions; logs describe events; traces relate timed execution through propagated context. Profiles can show where runtime resources are spent. A durable order/event ledger records facts required for correctness. Choose the signal that can establish the required evidence, and connect them with appropriately scoped identifiers. For latency, align boundaries before comparing values: gateway time, local queue wait, handler execution and provider work can measure different intervals. Aggregate compatible histograms/distributions instead of averaging pod percentiles. Use bounded route/failure/version cohorts to expose skew without creating an unbounded metric series for every customer. Signal Good question Limitation Metrics Is error rate rising? How old is the backlog? Aggregates do not reconstruct every request. Logs What error/state transition was recorded? Unstructured text and missing context make joins difficult. Traces Where did elapsed time go across this path? Sampling or missing propagation can leave gaps. Audit records Who approved this refund and what changed? Need deliberate integrity, access and retention policies. A span is one timed operation in a trace, such as an HTTP handler or database call. Parent/child relationships explain a call path. Metrics summarize populations; labels split those populations into dimensions. A trace ID belongs in a log field or exemplar, not a metric label that creates one series per request.

title: Observability
heading: 6. Separate request, trace, and business identity
text: 6. Separate request, trace, and business identity Signals become useful together when identities have precise meanings and lifetimes. An order ID identifies a durable entity; an operation key recognizes one intended mutation; an event ID recognizes one fact; an attempt ID distinguishes one execution; a trace context connects recorded spans. A retry can have another trace while retaining the same business identity. Treating these as one identifier makes both diagnosis and duplicate protection ambiguous. Propagate trace context across supported HTTP/message carriers and validate untrusted incoming metadata. Keep durable business references where recovery needs them even when traces expire. Context is not authority: a caller-supplied trace ID cannot grant access, prove a committed effect or dictate unlimited sampling cost. { "service": "checkout", "route": "/orders/{id}", "requestId": "req_82", "traceId": "trace-example", "orderId": "ord_7", "eventId": "evt_91", "operation": "payment.confirm", "outcome": "SUCCEEDED", "durationMs": 42 } Request ID identifies one ingress attempt; trace context connects observed execution; order/payment/event identity identifies durable business work. A retry may have a new request/trace while acting on the same payment intent. Using trace ID as an idempotency key confuses these different lifetimes. W3C traceparent carries standard trace context between HTTP services. It is metadata, not authentication. Validate untrusted incoming context and apply your sampling policy. Do not accept a client-provided tenant or actor as authoritative simply because it is in a header. HTTP server span → Outbound HTTP / SQL spans → Queue carrier metadata → Consumer processing span Cross-process context needs injection/extraction. Message identity remains durable even when a trace is not retained.

title: Observability
heading: 7. Java context and structured logging
text: 7. Java context and structured logging Logging context such as MDC is commonly associated with execution threads. An executor handoff, reactive pipeline or message boundary may lose it unless the supported framework/instrumentation captures and restores context. Cleanup matters too: reused threads must not retain another request’s identity. ScopedValue provides scoped in-process value access under its runtime rules; it does not create spans, inject HTTP headers or decide sampling. Use instrumentation suited to the actual stack and verify propagation through custom executors and manually constructed clients. Business identity remains separate from logging convenience. // Illustrative synchronous logging scope; use your logging API correctly. MDC.put("requestId", validatedOrGeneratedId); try { handler.process(); } finally { MDC.remove("requestId"); } // This alone does NOT propagate context to another thread or message. OpenTelemetry Context provides execution-scoped trace propagation abstractions; Spring Boot Micrometer Tracing integrates with supported instrumentation. Use configured HTTP client builders/instrumentation so outbound context is injected. Verify executor, Reactor and messaging boundaries explicitly. Java ScopedValue provides lexically scoped immutable context binding in supported Java versions, useful for deliberate request-context design. It is not a logging adapter or distributed propagation protocol. MDC integration, instrumentation and task-boundary behavior still require an explicit strategy; do not assume replacing ThreadLocal changes every library.

title: Observability
heading: 8. Build metrics that stay affordable
text: 8. Build metrics that stay affordable Start with a precise numerator, denominator and measurement window. An acceptance SLI might count eligible valid requests durably accepted within a deadline. A completion SLI might count accepted orders reaching fulfillment within their target age. These populations differ; HTTP success alone can hide a broken asynchronous flow. Choose bounded labels such as route template, operation class, release or controlled error category. Order IDs and raw URLs can create unbounded cardinality. Preserve essential audit/ledger facts separately when sampling or telemetry retention would discard individual execution details. Measurement Useful interpretation HTTP latency + DB pool wait Distinguish slow execution from waiting for a connection. Accepted-to-completed duration Capture asynchronous user experience. Retry attempts / original commands Detect amplification hidden by final success. Outbox age / DLQ count Find durable work that is not progressing. Sampling can keep traces affordable, but head sampling may miss rare errors and tail sampling has buffering/collector cost. Keep essential operational metrics and required audit outcomes independently of sampled traces.

title: Observability
heading: 9. Spring and AWS instrumentation map
text: 9. Spring and AWS instrumentation map Instrument inbound and outbound boundaries using configured Spring/Micrometer/OpenTelemetry support appropriate to the stack. Check custom HTTP clients, message attributes, executor handoffs and exporter failure behavior. Seeing one local span does not prove end-to-end propagation. On AWS, map the complete collection/export path and its trust/retention rules. Telemetry is workload and cost too: bound payloads, redact credentials and avoid putting sensitive data in baggage that travels to unrelated services. Core business metrics and recovery records should not depend on every trace being retained. Work the boundary through a failure Trace one Spring request through HTTP, a durable message and a worker as separate execution spans. At each boundary, inject/extract the supported trace context using the instrumentation contract rather than inventing a private header. Keep the stable business operation identity as a separate correlation field: a retry, replay or reconciliation may have a new trace while still belonging to the same order. Signal Useful fields Avoid Trace span Operation, dependency, outcome and bounded error classification Recording secrets or complete customer payloads. Structured log Trace/span correlation where present, business identity, release and state transition Assuming thread-local context automatically crosses every executor boundary. Metric Low-cardinality route/operation/outcome and latency distribution Order IDs or trace IDs as unbounded metric labels. Validate propagation with a controlled request whose producer completes before the consumer starts, and with a retry after the original request has ended. Check that the trace explains execution and the durable operation identity connects all attempts. Sampling can omit a trace; the business status and recovery record must still exist. A dashboard showing only successful sampled requests is not evidence that the unresolved tail is healthy.

title: Observability
heading: 10. Worked design: missing fulfillment investigation
text: 10. Worked design: missing fulfillment investigation Investigate a missing shipment using durable identity even when a sampled trace is unavailable. For an accepted paid order, inspect the durable order state, its outbox event, relay evidence, consumer receipt/quarantine and fulfillment task. If the consumer rejected an unsupported schema, a healthy broker delivery graph does not mean shipping completed. The missing state transition explains the customer impact. Repair the reader compatibly and replay under the original event identity with conditional/repeat-safe effects. Confirm the final fulfillment state and audit the recovery action. A trace may speed the investigation, but the procedure must still work when that trace was sampled out or expired.

title: Observability
heading: 11. Alerts and tricky interpretation
text: 11. Alerts and tricky interpretation Alert on actionable customer symptoms and risk to a defined SLO, with a responsible owner and diagnostic path. Queue depth alone can fall because events moved to quarantine; CPU can be low while the database pool is exhausted. Combine outcome/age signals with evidence useful for the likely causes. Error-budget burn compares observed bad-event consumption with the allowed budget over the selected window. Use appropriate short and long perspectives to distinguish sudden and sustained problems. Recovery proof needs restored business outcomes, not merely an alert returning green after its data pipeline failed. Trap Why it misleads Better practice All 202 responses counted as success Background work may never finish Measure acceptance and completion separately. p99 from averaged pod p99 values Percentiles are not additive Aggregate compatible histograms/distributions. Every trace sampled Cost and sensitive-data exposure grow Intentional sampling plus independent core metrics/audits. No logs means no errors Exporter or pipeline may be broken Monitor telemetry delivery/drop health. Alert on actionable symptoms and SLO risk, then attach diagnostic context. Error-budget burn compares observed bad-event consumption to the allowed budget. Use suitable short and long windows so fast incidents and slow persistent degradation are both visible. A runbook should name the invariant, safe mitigation and evidence needed to confirm recovery.

title: Observability
heading: 12. Interview ladder
text: 12. Interview ladder Foundational Logs versus traces? Logs record events; traces connect timed operations across execution boundaries. Shared IDs can link them, but neither automatically replaces the other. Foundational What is an SLO? A target over a defined SLI and measurement window, such as 99% of eligible accepted orders completing within five minutes. Intermediate Why did MDC disappear in an async task? Thread-bound logging state does not automatically cross executor/reactive/message boundaries. Use scoped context capture/restore through supported mechanisms and test cleanup to avoid leakage. Intermediate Why not label metrics with order ID? It creates a growing time series for every order and can expose sensitive identity. Put it in controlled logs/traces; metrics need bounded dimensions. Advanced How do you investigate with no retained trace? Use durable business state, event IDs, structured outcomes and audit records. Traces are sampled evidence, not the only recovery ledger. Advanced Does ScopedValue replace distributed tracing? No. It can carry scoped in-process state. HTTP/message propagation, span creation, sampling, logging integration and durable business identity are separate responsibilities. Intermediate Why can all HTTP requests succeed while the business SLO fails? Acceptance may be prompt while asynchronous completion is delayed or stranded. Define and measure completion over accepted operations with explicit deadlines and pending-state handling. Advanced How do you investigate when the trace is missing? Follow durable business, operation and event identities through authoritative state, outbox/inbox and controlled outcome/audit records. Traces are sampled execution evidence, not the only recovery ledger.

title: Observability
heading: 13. Further reading and practice
text: 13. Further reading and practice OpenTelemetry signals : metrics, logs, traces and their roles. OpenTelemetry propagation : context carriers and boundaries. W3C Trace Context : interoperable headers and trust considerations. Spring Boot tracing : supported integration and client instrumentation. Java ScopedValue : scope and inheritance rules for context. Exercise: trace one asynchronous business outcome with IDs from HTTP acceptance through outbox, broker, inbox and final state. Identify what survives when traces are sampled out.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: Overview
text: Understand the layers beneath an API call before diagnosing connection failures, slow requests and gateway timeouts.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 1. Why “the API is slow” is not a diagnosis
text: 1. Why “the API is slow” is not a diagnosis Start with the destination and the request. No transport vocabulary is assumed. Begin with a status read rather than a payment mutation: GET https://orders.example.com/orders/42. The URL gives a scheme, a host name and a path. HTTPS selects a secure HTTP connection; the host identifies the intended authority; the path identifies the requested resource within that authority. The client cannot send bytes to a Java controller by naming the path alone. It first needs a route to a listening process. Think of the request as work passing through several owners. The resolver supplies an address, the network carries packets, the server accepts a connection, a TLS endpoint establishes trust, and an HTTP endpoint interprets the request. A load balancer can terminate one connection and create another. Consequently, the “server” that acknowledges bytes need not be the application that commits the order. We will keep those boundaries visible when interpreting failures.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 2. Follow the time, not just the URL
text: 2. Follow the time, not just the URL Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. You know that an API receives an HTTP request. Before its controller can run, the caller must find a destination and establish a usable connection. DNS translates a name into an address; a connection joins endpoints; TLS authenticates the peer and protects traffic; HTTP describes the operation. These layers have separate state and separate failure signals. A successful DNS lookup therefore proves neither that a port is reachable nor that the certificate is trusted. Consider an order lookup taking two seconds although its controller timer records 30 ms. First ask what that timer excludes. The client may have waited for a pooled connection, performed DNS resolution, negotiated TLS, or waited at a proxy before the controller began. Reusing a connection avoids some setup work, but does not make its lifetime unlimited. Idle connections can be closed by either endpoint or an intermediary. Diagnose the stage before changing the read timeout. Check your understanding Foundational An HTTP timeout means the server did not execute the operation. No. The response can disappear after the database commits. Connection failure before sending and timeout after sending convey different evidence, and even client instrumentation may not establish the remote outcome. Use business identity and reconciliation for a mutating operation. Intermediate Why can a connection pool be exhausted while CPU is idle? Connections remain occupied while requests wait on downstream work. Inspect lease wait, active connections and remote latency. More CPU cannot release those connections; bound waits and concurrency before increasing the pool.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 3. Write connectivity and user-facing requirements
text: 3. Write connectivity and user-facing requirements Turn the customer promise into measurement boundaries and bounded waits. Before choosing timeout values, separate the user promise from the engineering limits. A user promise might be “most status reads finish within 200 ms.” The limits describe how much time or capacity each stage may consume. p95 is the 95th percentile: 95% of the measured observations are at or below that latency. It is measured over a defined population and window, not a per-request cancellation mechanism. A deadline is the boundary for one operation. We need both measurement and enforcement. Write the boundary of the deadline explicitly: from the caller starting the logical lookup until it receives a usable result. Include local queueing, connection acquisition, setup when needed, request/response transfer and any retry. If each nested call receives a fresh full budget, total latency can exceed the caller’s promise. Record which stages the chosen HTTP client actually times; similarly named “read timeout” settings can have different semantics. Functional requirements Reach the intended provider and send a valid HTTP request. Reuse suitable connections and return meaningful failures. Drain connections safely during deployment. Targets and invariants Verify TLS peer identity; no disabled certificate checks. Bound connect, pool-wait and response time within a total deadline. Illustrative p95 status call below 200 ms. Never infer remote rollback from a connection failure. The user cares about an outcome, but operators need a layer-specific error: DNS resolution, connection refusal, TLS validation, pool exhaustion, HTTP rejection or application timeout. Preserve that distinction without leaking credentials.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 4. Walk through the layers
text: 4. Walk through the layers Follow a fresh connection; identify which layer creates each piece of evidence. The Domain Name System (DNS) answers a naming question. A process normally asks its resolver for records, and cached answers may avoid a new upstream lookup. An address can be stale or point to a healthy machine with an unhealthy application. Multiple addresses also require a client selection/fallback policy. The name remains important after resolution because the TLS and HTTP layers still need to know which authority was intended. On a new Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connection, the endpoints establish transport state before HTTP application data can be exchanged. TCP delivers an ordered byte stream; it does not preserve your Java method boundaries or mark a database commit. Transport Layer Security (TLS) then negotiates protected communication and verifies the expected peer according to trust and identity rules. The client must validate both the trust chain and the intended hostname; accepting any certificate or any hostname removes a different part of that protection. Finally, HTTP carries the method, target, headers and representation. GET /orders/42 asks the application to return an authorized representation. A 404 is an HTTP response with application semantics; a TLS certificate failure occurs before that response exists on the failed connection. This ordering is why the next diagnostic step should depend on the layer that produced the evidence, rather than treating every exception as an HTTP 500. Resolve name → Connect IP:port → Establish TLS → Exchange HTTP This is a conceptual new HTTPS connection. Reuse, proxies and protocol choices can change which steps occur on a call. Layer What it establishes What it cannot prove DNS A name-to-record answer, subject to caching and resolver behavior That the returned address is healthy or the application is authorized. TCP A connection and reliable ordered bytes while viable That the business operation executed exactly once. TLS Encrypted transport and peer identity under configured validation That an authenticated user may refund a particular order. HTTP Methods, representations, status and metadata That a timeout means the remote side effect did not happen. A port selects a listening service on a host; an IP identifies a network destination, not a specific Java object. A Kubernetes Service routes to eligible endpoints; a pod may listen on 8080 while the Service exposes port 80. Keep listener, Service and externally exposed ports distinct. Observed evidence What you may conclude What remains unknown DNS returned an address A resolver supplied a record answer. Whether that destination serves this application. TLS negotiation succeeded with configured verification A protected channel to the expected peer under that policy exists. Whether the user may read order 42. Server returned 202 The operation was accepted under its contract. Whether asynchronous fulfillment completed. Response deadline expired after send The caller stopped waiting. Whether the remote mutation committed.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 5. Connection pools and HTTP versions
text: 5. Connection pools and HTTP versions Now reuse the connection and see what begins waiting locally. Once a connection is established, the client may keep it for later eligible requests. Reuse saves setup work, but the client must decide whether the connection is still usable and which requests may share it. A connection pool owns this lifecycle. “Waiting for a connection” means waiting locally for access to that managed resource; it is not the same interval as waiting for the remote handler. Follow three requests through a small pool. A obtains a connection and waits on the provider. B consumes the remaining eligible capacity. C now waits before it sends anything. If C’s total deadline expires there, a larger read timeout cannot help because the response-reading stage never began. Increase the pool only after establishing that the provider, network and fleet-wide resource budgets can sustain more work. For HTTP/2, a connection can carry multiple streams, so connection count alone does not describe concurrency. Stream limits and the client’s scheduling policy matter. A stream is not an extra CPU core at the server. Protocol selection can remove some connection overhead while the same application, database or dependency remains the limiting resource. HTTP/1.1 commonly uses multiple reusable connections for parallel requests. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a connection, reducing some connection overhead; TCP packet loss can still delay streams sharing that connection. HTTP/3 uses QUIC and has different transport behavior. Neither protocol automatically fixes an overloaded handler or an N+1 query. DNS records may change while connections remain open. Idle timeouts on clients, ALBs and proxies can disagree, creating stale-connection failures. Configure reuse, idle eviction and connection lifetime deliberately; retry only when the operation’s semantics permit it.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 6. Implement clear budgets and trust
text: 6. Implement clear budgets and trust Map the measured budget to the actual underlying client and each network hop. Translate the earlier deadline into a budget, then map each part to supported client controls. An illustrative 600 ms logical budget might allow bounded pool acquisition, connection setup if required, and response handling, with reserve for serialization and returning to the caller. These numbers are a starting hypothesis. A fresh TLS connection and a reused connection consume different portions, so measure both paths rather than summing one best-case trace. Configure the underlying client used by Spring, not only the controller or a wrapper future. A timeout on a future may release the caller while network work continues; cancellation and resource cleanup must be verified for that client. Share appropriately configured clients to reuse pools rather than constructing a new pool for every request. Keep per-destination limits separate when dependencies have different capacities. An edge proxy adds another hop and potentially another TLS boundary. If the ALB receives HTTPS but forwards HTTP internally, only the first hop is encrypted by that TLS session. Decide the internal-hop protection intentionally. Forwarded host/scheme/client-IP headers are metadata from a trusted proxy contract, not facts any internet caller may assert. This becomes an identity and authorization concern in the Security lesson. Conceptual client configuration (client-specific APIs differ): pool acquisition timeout: 50 ms TCP connect timeout: 100 ms response/read timeout: 400 ms total logical-call deadline: 600 ms including any retry TLS: verify certificate chain AND intended hostname connection pool: bounded per destination Spring RestClient/WebClient uses an underlying HTTP client whose pool and timeout configuration must be inspected. Construct clients through configured/instrumented builders where appropriate. A WebClient reactive return type does not guarantee every invoked dependency is nonblocking. Do not put a blocking SOAP call on an event-loop thread. On AWS, map client → DNS → ALB/API Gateway → ECS/EKS/Lambda → provider. Distinguish security-group routing/access from application authentication. If TLS terminates at the ALB, decide explicitly how the next hop is protected. Trust forwarding headers only from your controlled edge.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 7. Worked diagnosis: intermittent gateway timeouts
text: 7. Worked diagnosis: intermittent gateway timeouts Use those boundaries to test competing explanations for one slow request. Build the timeline before changing configuration. Suppose a gateway allows 800 ms for a request; the application records 40 ms of local work and reports a provider call lasting 700 ms. The provider records 80 ms of processing. These figures do not yet contradict one another: the application timer may include pool waiting and transfer, while the provider timer begins only after admission. Establish start/end events and clock assumptions for each measurement. Test two hypotheses: local pool saturation and slow remote admission. A long acquisition timer with few newly transmitted requests supports the first; prompt transmission followed by a long server-side queue supports the second. Then consider why scaling changed demand. Twenty pods with independent pools can multiply aggregate pressure even if each pod respects its own limit. A safe fix must bound the fleet’s effect, not merely improve one pod’s graph. If the failed operation were a capture rather than a status read, the same latency diagnosis would be necessary but insufficient. You would also need the durable payment intent and provider result inquiry. A transport repair restores communication; it does not retrospectively prove what the earlier write did. Keep operational recovery and business reconciliation as separate steps. Next separate a 504 generated by the gateway from an exception generated by the client. Compare gateway access records, application trace and provider request reference. If capture may have committed before the gateway timed out, reconcile using the original intent; do not fix the symptom by blindly increasing every timeout. Validate with fresh and reused connections, idle gaps, DNS rotation, certificate rotation and controlled packet/delay faults in a nonproduction test environment. Confirm hostname validation remains enabled throughout.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 8. Pitfalls and selection rules
text: 8. Pitfalls and selection rules Check how a proposed repair changes retries, trust and resource pressure. Use the table below as a hypothesis guide, not an automatic diagnosis. A reset after an idle interval can involve client eviction, an intermediary closing a connection, a server restart or another fault. Correlate timing and ownership before changing policies. Reproduce with a safe read first; then test write recovery using stable identity in an appropriate test environment. Be especially careful with retries. A request that definitely never left a local acquisition queue is different from one whose body was transmitted and whose response vanished. Client retry behavior can depend on method, body replayability and failure stage. Document the behavior of the exact underlying library and preserve the business-level rule even if the client automatically retries some failures. Symptom First evidence Likely action Pool wait high, provider fast Active/idle pool and pending acquisitions Bound concurrency and size pools within provider limits. TLS fails after rotation Trust chain, hostname, expiry and time Repair trust/identity; do not bypass validation. Only first call slow DNS/connect/TLS phase timings Evaluate connection reuse and startup warmup. Connection reset after idle Client/proxy idle policies Align eviction/reuse and safe retry rules. Client disconnect or cancellation does not undo work already accepted by the server. Connectivity and idempotency are related operationally but solve different problems.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Define the concept, follow the request, then name what the evidence cannot prove. Foundational What does DNS do? It resolves names to records through a resolver/cache hierarchy. It does not guarantee application health or authorization. Foundational Is HTTPS simply HTTP on another port? HTTPS adds TLS protection and peer validation. Port conventions alone do not create encryption or prove identity. Intermediate Why can pool wait dominate latency? Connections are finite. Slow calls or excessive concurrency can exhaust them, making later requests queue locally before reaching the provider. Intermediate Does HTTP/2 eliminate head-of-line blocking? It multiplexes HTTP streams but runs over TCP; loss can delay all streams on that connection. Application queues and downstream contention also remain. Advanced How do you distinguish a gateway timeout from an application timeout? Use phase timing, gateway logs, trace boundaries and provider references. Identify which component ended its wait and preserve unknown write outcome recovery. Advanced Should certificate validation be disabled during an incident? No. Diagnose the chain, hostname, clocks and trust configuration. Disabling validation removes the peer-identity guarantee and creates a different failure/security mode. Intermediate A provider call is slow, but the provider reports fast handling. Is one timer wrong? Not necessarily. The boundaries can differ: local pool acquisition, transfer and remote admission may be excluded from the provider timer. Align stage boundaries and clocks, then test competing explanations before tuning. Advanced A request timed out before a client observed response bytes. Can it safely send a fresh payment intent? No. The remote effect may have committed. Reconcile or retry with the original identity under the provider contract. A transport observation alone cannot establish that the business action did not happen.

title: Networking & HTTP
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice Carry the HTTP boundary into the API contract lesson. Read specifications to answer a concrete question. Use HTTP semantics to interpret method and status behavior; use transport and TLS documentation to understand the underlying channel; use the client’s own documentation to learn which settings it exposes. A Spring abstraction does not make all supported clients share identical timeout or pool behavior. Before moving to API Design, explain this journey without product names: resolve the authority, obtain a viable connection, establish trust, send a request, receive a response—or identify where evidence stops. The next lesson starts at that final HTTP boundary and defines what a caller may conclude from it. HTTP semantics : methods, intermediaries and status meanings. HTTP/2 : streams and connection behavior. Spring WebClient configuration : client transport configuration. AWS ALB : listeners, routing and targets. Exercise: diagram your application’s actual TLS termination points and list where a timeout can originate.

title: Security & Identity
heading: Overview
text: Build from one private order lookup to tokens, delegated access, tenant isolation, credential rotation and auditable decisions.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 1. A valid login can still access the wrong order
text: 1. A valid login can still access the wrong order The channel is protected. Now establish who may perform this resource operation. Networking established that the caller reached an endpoint over a protected connection. Now ask a different question: who is making this particular request, and why may they read order 42? A server certificate authenticates the expected server under the client’s trust model. It does not establish the customer’s identity, and it does not grant the customer permission over an order. Start with two legitimate customers, Alice and Bob, in the same application. Both can sign in successfully. Alice requests Bob’s order ID. If the service checks only that a token is valid, the request may leak Bob’s data despite successful authentication. This is the simplest way to see why authorization is a decision over identity, action, resource and relevant context, rather than a synonym for login. Start with a rule: this caller can read orders in their tenant only when the relevant role/relationship permits it. Express that rule before choosing JWT or a gateway. The token supplies verified inputs; the application makes the resource-specific decision.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 2. Follow identity into one authorization decision
text: 2. Follow identity into one authorization decision Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. Begin with GET /orders/42. A credential answers who the caller is or which client is acting. That still leaves a separate question: may that caller read order 42? Authorization is the decision over subject, action, resource and context. A role such as customer is insufficient if it grants access to every customer order. Tenant membership and resource ownership are part of the decision. Walk through the checks in order. Validate a token using an explicitly trusted issuer and expected audience; check its time validity and permitted algorithm through the security library. Establish the subject. Query the order within the authorized tenant or verify ownership before returning it. Shape the response so forbidden fields are absent. Repeat equivalent checks for updates, background jobs and exports. An authenticated internal request is not a universal exemption. Check your understanding Foundational A signed JWT makes its claims safe to use for any API. A valid signature only establishes integrity under a key. The receiving service must also establish trust in issuer, intended audience and claim semantics. A token intended for another service may be correctly signed and still unacceptable here. Intermediate Where should tenant isolation be enforced? At every authoritative data access or mutation boundary. Derive the tenant from trusted security context and authorized delegation, then constrain queries and writes. UI filtering and a tenant header chosen freely by the caller are insufficient.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 3. Threats become requirements
text: 3. Threats become requirements Write a concrete policy before translating it into scopes, roles or annotations. A tenant is a logical isolation boundary, such as a partner organization. Write an allow/deny rule for one operation before selecting roles or claims. For GET order, the customer may need to own that order within the authenticated tenant. For refund, a partner may need an explicit capability, ownership of the order, an amount bound and a refundable state. Some checks are security policy; others protect business-state correctness. They must all hold at the authoritative operation boundary. Next identify the entry paths that can reach that operation: REST controller, scheduled task, queue consumer, batch export and support tooling. A secure controller is insufficient if another path bypasses the same rule or acts with excessive authority. Background work should carry a deliberate authorization/actor model, not blindly reuse an arbitrary user token indefinitely. Non-functional security requirements need observable policies too. Define how quickly a revoked permission must stop working, what happens during identity-provider or signing-key discovery failure, which audit facts must survive and how credentials are excluded from logs. These choices affect availability, caching and operational recovery; “use JWT” does not choose them. Functional requirements Authenticate browser, mobile and partner clients. Authorize order read, refund and administration separately. Rotate credentials and audit sensitive actions. Targets and invariants No cross-tenant access or secret leakage. Reject invalid issuer/audience/signature/time policy. Bound credential/key discovery load. Define revocation and audit-retention expectations. Threat modeling asks what an attacker can submit, observe or influence. Include an authenticated malicious user, a compromised partner credential and a forged callback, not only anonymous traffic. Give every trust boundary an owner.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 4. Sessions, tokens, scopes and claims
text: 4. Sessions, tokens, scopes and claims Distinguish credential format, protocol and application permissions. A credential is evidence presented under a protocol. A session cookie may refer to server-side session state; an access token grants access under its issuer and audience contract. JWT is a representation format that can carry claims. Its use does not by itself choose an OAuth flow, decide token storage or define resource permissions. A bearer credential can be used by whoever possesses it, so exposure in logs is a meaningful security failure. OAuth addresses delegated access to protected resources. OpenID Connect adds an authentication layer, including an ID token intended for the client’s sign-in context. The API should receive the appropriate access token rather than assuming an ID token is interchangeable. Scopes express granted capabilities, but a broad orders:read scope still needs a resource-level rule to distinguish Alice’s orders from Bob’s. Choose the flow from the client and trust boundary. An interactive user-facing client commonly uses authorization code with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), which binds the code exchange to a client-generated verifier, under a complete supported protocol. A machine acting on its own behalf may use client credentials when the provider supports the required model. Do not put a secret in a mobile app and treat it as proof that only your app can call the API: distributed client software cannot keep that shared secret from its users. Concept Meaning Boundary Session cookie Browser sends a session reference/cookie under browser rules Requires CSRF/session-lifecycle policy. Access token Credential presented to a resource server Must be intended for this API and validated. JWT Signed/encoded claim format, not an authorization policy Decoded text is not verified identity; encryption is separate. Scope Granted capability such as orders:read Does not imply ownership of every order. ID token OIDC token for the client’s authentication context Not a substitute for the API’s access token. For an appropriate user-facing client, authorization code with PKCE protects the code exchange; validate redirect URIs and the complete flow. Client credentials fits machine identity where supported. Do not invent a token protocol from base64 JSON or store a client secret in a distributed mobile app.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 5. Walk one request through policy
text: 5. Walk one request through policy Follow the evidence from token receipt to the final resource decision. Follow an incoming bearer token through distinct stages. First extract it from the supported location without logging it. Establish its integrity and issuer/audience/time policy through a configured security library and trusted key source. Then map validated claims to a principal understood by this application. Finally, authorize the requested operation on the specific resource. Successful completion of one stage is not a shortcut past the later ones. Consider a correctly signed token issued for an analytics API. The order service may trust the same organization as issuer and still need to reject that token because the audience is wrong. Likewise, a token with a valid signature can be expired. The signed data remains readable and integrity-protected while its use is unacceptable. This distinction explains why “I decoded the JWT” and “the signature verified” are incomplete security checks. After identity is established, load or mutate the order within the permitted tenant scope and apply the action policy. Do not fetch an arbitrary record, serialize it, and only then filter it in the UI. If permission or business state can change concurrently, locate the decisive checks close enough to the mutation to enforce the required rule. Preserve a consistent existence-hiding policy for unauthorized IDs without treating a 404 as the authorization mechanism itself. Verify transport/token → Establish principal → Load scoped resource → Authorize and audit Rejecting a token and denying access to a valid principal are different outcomes. Order order = repository.findByTenantAndId(verifiedTenant(), orderId) .orElseThrow(NotFoundException::new); policy.requireCanRefund(principal(), order); // Check business state and record the authorized transition. // tenant supplied in the body is not authority. Verify allowed signing algorithms, trusted issuer, expected audience, expiry and relevant time claims. Plan key rotation and clock tolerance. Fetch keys only from configured trusted discovery endpoints; an untrusted token must not choose an arbitrary key URL. Choose 401/403 and any existence-hiding 404 policy consistently.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 6. Spring and AWS mapping
text: 6. Spring and AWS mapping Separate framework verification from domain policy and storage enforcement. Use framework support for the token protocol and keep domain policy in an explicit application boundary. Spring Security resource-server machinery handles configured token validation; a route rule can require authentication or a coarse capability. The service and repository must still enforce resource ownership and tenant scope. Choose one authoritative mapping from validated principal/delegation to tenant; an unverified tenantId in the request body is merely caller input. An API Gateway authorizer can reject unsuitable credentials before application work, which reduces exposure and load. It does not know every order’s current ownership, refund balance or state unless that information is deliberately part of its policy. Keep the responsibility boundary explicit. IAM authenticates and authorizes AWS resource access under its model; it does not automatically encode the shop’s customer-order policy. For browser sessions, understand why CSRF and CORS solve different problems. Browsers can automatically attach cookies to requests under applicable rules, so a state-changing cookie-authenticated endpoint needs an appropriate CSRF defense. CORS governs browser cross-origin access behavior; a nonbrowser client is not constrained by it. For outbound callbacks, destination URLs are SSRF-sensitive input: signing an outbound request does not make an attacker-chosen internal destination safe. Cognito or another identity provider issues credentials; API Gateway can validate suitable tokens at the edge. Application authorization remains necessary. mTLS authenticates a peer connection, not the end user’s refund rights. Store signing material/provider secrets in managed secret storage with least-privilege access and tested rotation. For browser cookie authentication, assess CSRF because browsers attach cookies automatically. CORS controls browser cross-origin access; it does not stop a nonbrowser caller and is not authentication. For callbacks, prevent SSRF with destination validation and restricted egress, including redirect/DNS behavior.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 7. Worked design: partner refunds
text: 7. Worked design: partner refunds Apply the policy and recovery rules to one refund, then vary the failure. Work one refund from request to provider. A partner asks to refund an order. Establish the partner principal and required capability, resolve the order inside that partner’s scope, validate current refundable state/amount, and create a durable refund intent under a stable operation identity. The external provider call happens under its own credential and idempotency/recovery contract. Do not hold a database lock while waiting merely because every step belongs to the same business operation. Now vary one condition at a time. A token for another audience fails credential validation. A valid partner token requesting another partner’s order fails authorization without disclosure. A valid authorized request exceeding the remaining refundable amount fails the business rule. A provider timeout after accepting a refund creates an unknown remote outcome. These failures need distinct internal evidence and documented external responses; calling all of them authentication errors hides the real recovery action. Finally rotate a signing key or provider secret. During an intentional overlap, allow only the defined old/new material, observe errors and verify consumers refresh according to their supported configuration. Retire the old key only after the migration policy permits it. Test recovery from unavailable discovery endpoints and avoid an unbounded refresh on every attacker-supplied unknown key ID. Audit actor, action, resource, decision, time and stable request/business references without storing bearer tokens or card data. A short-lived token can reduce revocation exposure, but the actual revocation contract may require introspection or explicit state. During signing-key rotation, overlap trusted keys and observe unknown-key errors before removing the old key. Test a valid token for another audience, another tenant’s order ID, expired tokens, unknown key IDs, mass assignment of tenant/role fields, and a rotated key. Verify both allowed and denied decisions; happy-path login tests cannot prove tenant isolation. Input variation Expected decision Correctness assertion Valid customer, own tenant, own order Allow the permitted read. Only permitted fields are returned. Valid customer, another customer’s order Deny or hide existence under policy. No sensitive fields or side effects. Valid signature, wrong audience Reject credential for this API. No domain mutation runs. Authorized refund, amount exceeds remaining balance Reject business transition. Refund ledger remains unchanged. Valid request repeated after lost response Apply documented idempotency policy. No second provider effect.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 8. Pitfalls and operational decisions
text: 8. Pitfalls and operational decisions Check what stays valid when permissions, keys or dependencies change. Security decisions can become stale. If an allow decision is cached for ten minutes, a permission removal may take that long to affect that path unless another mechanism intervenes. Short-lived credentials reduce some exposure but do not create immediate revocation. State the exact promise for each path, including long-running exports and already-issued download capabilities. Operational shortcuts can change the trust model. Disabling certificate validation, accepting arbitrary issuers or granting every internal caller an administrator role may hide an incident while exposing data. Prefer diagnosis and constrained recovery. Audit the actor, action, resource and outcome without retaining bearer tokens, sensitive request bodies or provider secrets. Issue Reasoning JWT revocation Stateless verification does not automatically learn revocation. Define lifetime and any revocation/introspection state. Authorization caching Cached allow decisions can outlive permission changes. State the revocation freshness bound. Secret rotation Replacing a value is not sufficient if clients keep old pooled/configured credentials. Verify rollout and overlap. Overprivileged service Internal network location is not sufficient authority. Validate identity and scope at the resource boundary.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Defend the boundary: authentication success alone is not resource permission. Foundational Authentication versus authorization? Authentication establishes identity; authorization applies action/resource policy to that identity. Foundational Is a decoded JWT trustworthy? No. Validate signature and trust/claim policy before using its contents as identity. Intermediate OAuth versus OIDC? OAuth delegates access to resources; OIDC adds identity/authentication semantics on top of OAuth flows. Intermediate Why is a scope check insufficient? A broad capability does not prove tenant membership, resource ownership, amount limits or current business state. Advanced How do you revoke JWT access quickly? Choose short lifetimes and, if required, introspection/revocation state or another explicit protocol. State latency/availability trade-offs rather than promising immediate stateless revocation. Advanced How do you prove isolation? Exercise valid credentials across tenant/resource combinations at every entry path, inspect query scoping, and assert denied requests cause no side effects or sensitive disclosure. Intermediate Why must an export be authorized separately from its creation? Creation, background processing and later download are distinct paths. Current permissions, the chosen delegated authority model and already-issued bearer capabilities need explicit policies. A successful creation check does not define indefinite download access. Advanced How can a valid scope still allow a cross-tenant breach? The scope may grant a broad capability without proving ownership of the specific object. Constrain authoritative access by a verified tenant/delegation mapping and apply domain policy at every entry path; test valid credentials against another tenant’s resource.

title: Security & Identity
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice Return to one API endpoint and prove both allowed and denied behavior. When reading the primary references, keep four questions separate: What protocol establishes the credential? What does this API validate? Which resource policy decides the operation? How is a change in permission or keys propagated? A library example answering the second question does not settle the other three. To connect this lesson back to API Design, take an endpoint from that lesson and write a policy matrix: caller type, action, tenant/ownership, business state and expected allow/deny result. Then test the same matrix through every entry path. This is a stronger demonstration of isolation than showing a successful login screen. OAuth security best current practice : flow and attack mitigations. OIDC Core : identity and token semantics. Spring Security JWT : validation and resource-server configuration. OWASP API Security : object authorization, resource use and SSRF. Exercise: write an authorization matrix for one resource: caller class × action × ownership × business state.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: Overview
text: Move from one transaction to replicated reads and multi-service workflows without confusing local atomicity, consistency models and business compensation.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 1. The order exists on one copy but not another
text: 1. The order exists on one copy but not another The order transaction committed, but a status read from another copy says not found. Keep the write outcome and the read observation separate: the writer may be correct and the replica delayed. The missing agreement is which observation the caller was promised after acceptance. Read-your-writes is a user-journey guarantee, not something implied by the existence of replicas. Now let inventory and payment belong to independent services.
