A fresh inventory read does not make both services commit together. Reader freshness and multi-resource atomicity are different dimensions. We will first specify permitted observations, then explain coordination and the intermediate states it must recover.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 2. Separate fresh reads from atomic workflows
text: 2. Separate fresh reads from atomic workflows Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. Consistency describes the observations and histories an operation permits. Transaction atomicity describes whether grouped changes commit together. You can atomically commit an order on the writer and still read an older value from a replica. Conversely, a fresh single-row read does not make a multi-service checkout atomic. State which property the user journey actually needs. A customer pays and immediately opens order status. A stale view may briefly say pending, which could be acceptable if documented. Using that stale view to start another charge is a different decision with a stricter correctness requirement. Keep the authoritative payment transition in a controlled write path. Use a read model for display only when its delay does not authorize an unsafe action. Check your understanding Foundational A saga is an ACID transaction spread over services. A saga coordinates local commits and recovery actions. Intermediate states are visible and compensation can fail or be semantically incomplete. It requires durable progress, repeatable steps and reconciliation. Intermediate Can a refund compensate every payment failure? No. Refunds can fail, take time, incur fees or be forbidden in a particular state. Model irreversible effects and business recovery explicitly rather than treating compensation as a mathematical inverse.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 3. Choose guarantees by operation
text: 3. Choose guarantees by operation Choose guarantees per operation. Browsing and analytics may tolerate delayed copies; authorizing a financial transition may require authoritative current state. A customer’s immediate post-create lookup can need read-your-writes without requiring every reader worldwide to observe one real-time order. State the boundary rather than saying all data must be “strongly consistent.” Also define what a write acknowledgement means under the store/topology and which failures the contract covers. A local durable commit, replicated acknowledgement and completion of a remote workflow are not interchangeable. Under lost communication, describe whether an operation waits, rejects, accepts pending work or permits a domain-defined conflict. Functional requirements Create order and immediately retrieve its accepted state. Reserve inventory and authorize payment across services. Expose workflow progress and reconcile partial completion. Targets and invariants Read-your-writes for the order-creation experience. Never confirm fulfillment without its prerequisites. Permit delayed analytics/search projections. Define behavior when components cannot communicate. Uniform “strong consistency everywhere” can impose cost without solving a business need. Define current-state reads for money decisions, session guarantees for a user experience, and bounded/documented lag for projections. State whether a write acknowledgement represents local durability or replicated commitment.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 4. Explain the observations
text: 4. Explain the observations A consistency model describes which histories of observations are allowed. Linearizability makes the specified operations appear to take effect at points between invocation and response while respecting completed real-time order. Read-your-writes promises a caller visibility of its own completed writes. Causal guarantees preserve causal relationships, while unrelated concurrent changes still need a conflict policy. Eventual convergence alone gives no maximum staleness interval. Serializable transaction isolation is about equivalence to a serial execution, not automatically real-time ordering across clients. Apply these names to the actual operation and system boundary; a correct guarantee for one key or transaction cannot silently be extended to an entire multi-service purchase. Guarantee Intuition Nuance Linearizability Each operation appears to take effect at one point between invocation and completion Requires the specified operation/system scope, not merely a replica count. Read-your-writes A caller sees their own completed writes Does not imply every caller sees one global order. Causal consistency Causally related operations are observed in causal order Concurrent unrelated operations need additional conflict policy. Eventual consistency Copies converge if updates stop and the protocol progresses Does not by itself specify maximum lag or conflict meaning. Serializable isolation concerns equivalence to a serial transaction order; it does not automatically imply real-time ordering across clients. Name the guarantee and scope rather than using “consistent” as an unexplained adjective.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 5. Quorum, partitions and split-brain
text: 5. Quorum, partitions and split-brain A network partition means some participants cannot communicate even though they may still be running. If a rule needs one authoritative order of conflicting writes, isolated groups cannot independently invent that same order without additional coordination assumptions. The system may need to reject/wait for some work or explicitly permit reconcilable conflicts. A quorum supplies an overlap argument under a membership and protocol model. The inequality R+W>N is not a complete correctness proof: concurrent writers, versions, failures and reconciliation determine what the reader can actually observe. Likewise, electing a replacement leader does not stop an old paused process from acting. Protected resources must reject obsolete authority through an enforced ownership/fencing protocol.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 6. Atomic commit versus saga
text: 6. Atomic commit versus saga Prefer one local commit boundary when it naturally owns the invariant. Independent services may instead need atomic coordination supported by their participants, or a workflow allowing visible partial progress. A saga coordinates local steps and recovery actions; it does not turn them into an invisible ACID transaction. Compensation is a new business action after an earlier commit. A refund may be delayed or fail; a reservation may already be reassigned; an email cannot be unread. Record progress and identities durably, define meaningful recovery for irreversible steps, and do not choose a saga when the required invariant cannot tolerate its intermediate states. Approach Use when Trade-off One local transaction All critical data can share an appropriate store/owner Simpler invariant; less independent ownership. Two-phase commit Participants/protocol support atomic commit and its operational cost is acceptable Coordinator/participant failures can block progress in relevant designs. Saga Business permits visible intermediate states and compensation Compensation can fail and is not an automatic rollback. Reserve stock → Authorize payment → Confirm order → Recover or compensate Each saga step is a durable local transition. A later failure creates new work, not time travel. Refunding a charge is a new financial operation; it may have fees, timing constraints or fail. Releasing a reservation is only valid while its state allows it. Store step identity, status and retry/compensation evidence durably. Avoid a saga for an invariant that the business genuinely requires to be invisible and atomic.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 7. Spring and AWS boundaries
text: 7. Spring and AWS boundaries Write a durable state machine before selecting an orchestrator. Record the order, current step, stable command/provider identity, state version and unresolved outcome. A conditional transition prevents two workers independently deciding incompatible next states. Recovery must resume from those facts instead of restarting the purchase with fresh identities. Spring transactions protect configured resources, while an ordinary provider call remains another authority. A database-backed coordinator or a managed workflow can run the protocol, but retry settings do not choose the business recovery rule. Event choreography still needs ownership, deadlines and an inspectable explanation of overall progress. Verify exact consistency behavior for the chosen table, index and regional topology. Workflow ledger (illustrative): orderId, step, commandId, state, version, lastError conditional transition: RESERVED -> PAYMENT_PENDING remote call: stable payment intent identity unknown outcome: reconcile before compensation decision outbox: publish only committed local transitions Spring @Transactional covers the configured local resources. It does not make calls to unrelated payment and stock services atomic. A durable orchestrator can use RDS plus workers, or AWS Step Functions when its state/retry model fits. Choreography uses events instead; it still needs ownership, timeouts and a way to inspect the full workflow. For DynamoDB, verify the selected consistency mode and exact access path, including secondary indexes and global-table configuration. Never infer multi-region money invariants from a generic product label or from a local strongly consistent read option.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 8. Worked design: payment succeeds, stock expires
text: 8. Worked design: payment succeeds, stock expires Follow a reservation racing expiry while payment is in flight. If confirmation wins the authoritative RESERVED transition, expiry must not release that same reservation. If expiry wins, a late payment success cannot simply overwrite the state and promise fulfillment. Resolve it through the declared re-reserve, void or refund policy. Keep UNKNOWN separate from DECLINED. Before compensation or another irreversible attempt, reconcile the original provider operation. Test duplicated callbacks, stale coordinators, repeated expiry and provider failure during recovery. The customer-visible pending state and operator-owned unresolved tail are part of the design, not exceptional details outside it.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 9. Pitfalls and decision criteria
text: 9. Pitfalls and decision criteria Stale observations become dangerous when used to authorize mutations. A delayed display can be acceptable while a second charge based on that display is forbidden. Separate the source used for a view from the authority used for the decision and state their freshness explicitly. When comparing alternatives, identify the invariant owner, coordination participants, availability/latency cost and recovery burden. A named consistency model or workflow product is not evidence that every boundary is protected. Introduce a partition and one crash at each commit point to test the argument. A compensating action is not guaranteed to restore the exact original world. Emails have been read, stock may have been sold, and refunds can be delayed. Define domain recovery rather than saying “roll back the saga.” Choose one owner for the invariant when possible. Use replicas/projections for permitted lag. Require atomic coordination only where the contract needs it, and budget the availability/latency cost. Review the design under partitions, not only clean sequential failures.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 10. Interview ladder
text: 10. Interview ladder Foundational Eventual consistency versus immediate visibility? Eventual convergence permits temporary differences; immediate visibility/read-your-writes requires a stronger selected path or protocol. Foundational Is compensation a rollback? No. It is a new domain action intended to offset an earlier effect and can itself fail or be incomplete. Intermediate Does R+W>N prove linearizability? No. It describes overlap under assumptions; versions, concurrent writes, membership and failure/reconciliation semantics determine the real guarantee. Intermediate Can @Transactional span arbitrary microservices? Not automatically. It covers configured transactional resources; remote business calls need an explicit coordination/recovery protocol. Advanced When is a saga inappropriate? When required invariants cannot tolerate visible intermediate states or meaningful compensation is impossible, unless the contract is changed or a different coordination boundary is chosen. Advanced How do you handle late payment success after expiry? Use conditional durable states, reconcile provider identity, and follow a documented re-reserve/void/refund policy. Never infer outcome solely from timeout or overwrite a newer state. Intermediate Does a fresh read make checkout across two services atomic? No. Freshness constrains an observation, while atomic commitment constrains a set of changes. Identify the authorities and commit protocol; independent local commits require explicit intermediate states and recovery. Advanced Why can payment succeed after a reservation expires? The remote operation and expiry have independent timing/commit boundaries. Conditional reservation transitions establish the winning local state; reconcile the original payment identity and apply the declared re-reserve, void or refund policy.

title: Consistency & Distributed Transactions
heading: 11. References and practice
text: 11. References and practice PostgreSQL isolation : transaction-level guarantees. AWS saga orchestration : steps and compensation. DynamoDB consistency : read-path-specific support. Raft research : replicated logs, leadership and safety. Exercise: mark which order operations need local atomicity, read-your-writes, delayed projection or explicit compensation.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: Overview
text: Grow a modular order application into independently owned services without creating a distributed monolith.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 1. One change requires six coordinated deployments
text: 1. One change requires six coordinated deployments The application now has orders, inventory, payment and fulfillment behavior. Those names do not require four deployable services. Start with who owns each rule, which facts change together and which team needs independent change. A module can create a useful boundary without adding a network or separate deployment. Extracting a module changes failure semantics. A method call becomes remote admission, serialization, communication and an uncertain response. If an inventory reservation was formerly part of the order transaction, extraction introduces a visible interval and recovery protocol. The service boundary must justify that cost through ownership, scaling or deployment needs.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 2. Find an ownership boundary before adding a network call
text: 2. Find an ownership boundary before adding a network call Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A module groups behavior behind an interface. A service adds independent process, deployment and operational boundaries. A bounded context supplies a consistent domain model and vocabulary. Those boundaries can align, but they are not identical. First ask which team owns a rule and which facts it must change atomically. Orders and inventory may begin as modules sharing a local transaction. Extracting inventory creates an interval between accepting an order and confirming a reservation. The API must now represent that interval and recover when the reservation response is lost. If the product cannot tolerate the intermediate state, splitting processes requires more coordination or a revised boundary. Network separation does not erase the original invariant. Check your understanding Foundational Each database table should become a service. A table is a storage detail. Splitting by tables can force every business operation into chatty distributed coordination. Group by domain responsibility, change patterns, invariants and team ownership. Intermediate When is a modular monolith a reasonable endpoint? When coherent modules, acceptable release coupling and one operational unit meet the workload and team needs. Extraction should solve a measured ownership, scaling or deployment problem with a sustainable operational cost.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 3. Define autonomy and invariants
text: 3. Define autonomy and invariants Collect change patterns as well as request rates. Which features repeatedly modify the same business rules? Which operations must commit atomically? Which team can operate and evolve the behavior independently? Those answers often reveal a more coherent boundary than a table-by-table split. Include operating constraints: on-call ownership, contract evolution, identity, telemetry and data migration. Independent deployment is useful only when the team can preserve compatibility and diagnose failures across the new boundary. A diagram with many small boxes can conceal tightly synchronized releases and a shared database that nobody owns. Functional requirements Own checkout, catalog, payment and notifications explicitly. Change receipt behavior without deploying checkout. Expose supported contracts instead of shared-table writes. Targets and invariants Each critical invariant has an owner. Bound synchronous fan-out and failure propagation. Independent delivery requires compatible contracts. Teams can observe and operate what they own. A bounded context defines a model in which terms have precise meaning. “Customer” in billing may differ from “customer” in marketing. A domain boundary is not inferred from matching noun names alone. Analyze workflows, shared invariants and reasons for change.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 4. From modules to service ownership
text: 4. From modules to service ownership A bounded context supplies a consistent domain model and vocabulary. The word customer may mean a payer in billing and a delivery recipient in fulfillment; forcing one universal entity can couple unrelated changes. Define the facts each context owns and the interfaces through which others learn or request changes. In a modular monolith, enforce module interfaces and data access discipline before distributing execution. Private data ownership makes later extraction safer. If every module can mutate every table, adding REST endpoints does not create independent domain ownership. Keep business invariants cohesive even when the storage representation spans several tables. Evidence Boundary implication Two operations must commit together for a hard invariant Keep an appropriate common transactional owner or design explicit coordination. A capability changes independently and has distinct load/lifecycle Candidate for independent deployment. Every request needs many chatty calls across the boundary Revisit boundary or introduce a suitable projection/BFF. Another service directly updates its tables Ownership is bypassed regardless of repository layout. Start with module interfaces and restricted data access in the monolith. Integration tests enforce allowed calls. Extract only when deployment, scaling, fault isolation or organizational autonomy benefits exceed extra operational complexity. A well-structured monolith is not a failure state.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 5. Synchronous decisions and asynchronous facts
text: 5. Synchronous decisions and asynchronous facts Follow one customer journey across proposed services and count sequential dependencies. Every required synchronous response contributes latency and availability constraints. A call from orders to inventory may be justified for reservation, while email or analytics may use durable asynchronous progress. Choose from completion semantics rather than a blanket “everything is an event” rule. An event records a fact owned by its source, not permission for any consumer to rewrite that source’s data. A command has a responsible action owner. Publish stable domain contracts rather than leaking internal table schemas without an evolution policy. Consumers needing local views must own their freshness, backfill and replay behavior. Checkout owner → Committed order + outbox → Notification owner → Delivery provider The receipt boundary is independent only if delivery delays do not invalidate checkout acceptance. Avoid sharing one giant DTO/entity jar across all services. A schema contract or generated client can be useful, but forced lockstep dependency updates undermine compatibility. Publish versions and behavioral guarantees at the boundary.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 6. Modular Spring and AWS choices
text: 6. Modular Spring and AWS choices Place an application interface around a cohesive module, test its contract and identify its data authority. Then extract a bounded path if independent operation is needed. Spring controllers and messaging listeners adapt transport; they should call explicit domain/application boundaries rather than exposing repository methods as the public service contract. For AWS/EKS deployment, separate scaling and identity policies by the actual service responsibility, and propagate evidence across calls/events. Network access is not domain authorization. Each new service needs bounded dependencies, rollout compatibility and a recovery runbook. Sharing a library can reduce boilerplate, but shared domain schemas can also force lockstep upgrades. Boundary contract: Checkout publishes OrderAccepted(eventId, orderId, receiptAddressRef) Notifications owns delivery status and retry policy Notifications cannot UPDATE checkout.orders Checkout does not wait for email provider completion Store only the data a consumer needs under the applicable privacy rules. A replicated reference is not permission to treat stale copied data as authority for another owner’s invariant.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 7. Worked migration: extract notifications
text: 7. Worked migration: extract notifications Extract fulfillment first when delayed shipping work can proceed independently of order acceptance. Commit an order-side event durably; fulfillment creates its own task and uses a stable warehouse identity. Orders exposes progress under the agreed contract without directly mutating fulfillment tables. If inventory is extracted later, model reservation, expiry and late payment before cutover. Migrate write ownership deliberately and avoid two active authorities for the same stock. Compare the extra intermediate states with the organizational/scaling benefit. It is reasonable to retain a cohesive local boundary where distribution does not solve a measured problem.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 8. Trade-offs and tricky cases
text: 8. Trade-offs and tricky cases A distributed monolith has network-separated processes that still require coordinated releases or chatty shared-state access for ordinary work. Diagnose change coupling and critical-path fan-out rather than counting services. A shared database can be a migration stage, but independent uncontrolled writers undermine the claimed boundary. Review failure and cost after extraction. More telemetry, deployments, contracts and on-call paths are real obligations. Keep rollback compatible with data already produced by the new service, and retire old jobs/routes only when no supported path depends on them. Trap Consequence Response One service per entity Chatty distributed transactions Model business capability/invariant ownership. Shared DB without ownership Independent deployments break each other Restrict writes and migrate through explicit contracts. Event choreography everywhere Workflow state/ownership becomes invisible Use an orchestrator or an explicit end-to-end ledger where useful. Premature extraction Operations overhead exceeds benefit Enforce module boundaries first. Measure lead time, coordinated deployments, dependency failures and operational workload. Service count is not a success metric. A shared team can operate several services, but ownership and on-call capacity must be credible.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Foundational Monolith versus microservices? A monolith deploys as a unit; microservices make selected responsibilities independently deployed/operated. Internal modularity is a separate property. Foundational What is data ownership? One capability controls authoritative mutation and invariants for its data; others use supported contracts or projections. Intermediate When should you keep a modular monolith? When clear modules deliver change isolation and there is no sufficient need for remote deployment/scaling autonomy to justify its cost. Intermediate Why can shared entity jars cause coupling? Persistence changes and lockstep versions can spread across services, exposing internals rather than a stable contract. Advanced How do you extract a side-effecting capability safely? Establish durable intent/identity, shadow without effects, switch ownership deliberately, preserve compatibility and test rollback/duplicates. Advanced How do you detect a distributed monolith? Frequent coordinated releases, shared writes, synchronous chatty chains and inability to tolerate one component’s outage indicate boundaries lack autonomy. Intermediate Why can splitting by tables create a distributed monolith? One business rule can require several tables and atomic decisions. Splitting them into separate owners without changing the protocol creates chatty coordination and lockstep releases rather than coherent autonomy. Advanced What should an extraction prove before routing all traffic? Clear write ownership, compatible contracts/data, recovery for new remote boundaries, acceptable critical-path capacity/latency and an operating owner. Test cutover and rollback with facts already committed by the new path.

title: Microservice Boundaries
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice Spring Modulith : module boundaries and verification. ArchUnit : executable code dependency constraints. AWS decomposition guidance : migration patterns and boundary choices. Exercise: choose one candidate extraction and describe the invariant owner, data migration, contract and rollback before drawing new services.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: Overview
text: Protect checkout from noisy clients and slow dependencies by distinguishing request rate, concurrency, queues, quotas and downstream demand.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 1. A fast caller can consume a slow service
text: 1. A fast caller can consume a slow service Scalability showed that finite dependencies can be overwhelmed before new capacity arrives. Rate limiting decides which arrivals may enter under a policy; backpressure/admission control align accepted work with processing capacity. Protecting a service therefore involves both usage allocation and overload behavior. Keep rate, quota and concurrency separate. A rate bounds arrivals over time, a quota bounds accumulated use over an allocation period, and concurrency bounds active work. Fifty requests per second can be safe at 100 ms and exhausting at two seconds. A fixed rate policy alone does not bound the latter wait population.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 2. Distinguish arrivals from work already in progress
text: 2. Distinguish arrivals from work already in progress Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A rate limit bounds arrivals over time. A quota bounds total usage over a longer allocation period. A concurrency limit bounds active work. If requests become slower, an unchanged arrival rate can still produce too much simultaneous work. This is why a request-per-second rule is only one part of overload control. Suppose 50 requests arrive each second and complete in 100 ms: average in-flight work is about five. A dependency slowdown to two seconds raises that figure toward 100 under steady admitted traffic. A concurrency gate can reject or defer work before the scarce pool is exhausted. A bounded queue absorbs a short burst but cannot sustainably absorb arrivals above service capacity. Check your understanding Foundational A queue solves overload without rejecting callers. Only for bursts or work whose demand can eventually be served within its deadline. Sustained excess arrivals grow backlog, delay and cost. Bound queue capacity or age and define admission, expiry and recovery policies. Intermediate How do you protect small tenants from a large tenant? Combine tenant-aware allocation with global capacity limits and bounded concurrent work. A global counter alone can be monopolized; independent per-tenant limits alone can exceed total capacity.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 3. Define fairness and overload semantics
text: 3. Define fairness and overload semantics Define who shares capacity: user, tenant, credential, endpoint or service. A global limit can be monopolized by one tenant; independent tenant limits can collectively exceed total capacity. Combine allocation with a global resource budget and decide how bursts and priorities are handled. State the response and recovery contract. Rejected work must not secretly commit a business effect. Deferred work needs durable acceptance and an age/deadline policy. A Retry-After hint should be compatible with the client’s overall deadline; it is not permission for synchronized unlimited retries. Functional requirements Apply per-partner and global admission limits. Protect payment-call concurrency and queue size. Tell rejected clients how to recover. Targets and invariants One tenant must not starve others. No unbounded queues or retries. Distributed limit precision is specified. Limiter outage behavior is explicit per operation. A business command rejected before acceptance should cause no side effect. Once accepted durably, responsibility changes: the service must complete or report its terminal failure through the stated protocol. Do not count a queued 202 as successful completion.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 4. Choose an algorithm from burst behavior
text: 4. Choose an algorithm from burst behavior A token bucket accumulates permits up to a capacity and replenishes them at a rate. It permits bounded bursts after idle time while constraining sustained admission. A fixed window is simple but can admit bursts at adjacent boundaries; a sliding approach smooths that behavior at additional state/coordination cost. Choose the unit carefully. Requests with radically different cost should not always consume identical permits. Consider payload/query work and downstream resources. A concurrency semaphore protects active work, while a bounded queue absorbs some waiting. Specify acquisition timeout, release behavior and cancellation so an abandoned request does not leak a permit. Algorithm Behavior Trade-off Fixed window Count requests in aligned periods Can admit a double burst around a boundary. Sliding log/window Account over a moving interval More storage/work or approximation. Token bucket Tokens refill; capacity permits a bounded burst Refill, capacity and cost units need definition. Leaky bucket Drain at a controlled rate Queue delay/overflow policy matters. A token bucket with capacity 100 and refill 10/s allows a saved burst of 100, then roughly 10/s over time. It does not guarantee a limit of ten requests in every individual second. Assign weighted cost if an export is more expensive than a tiny status read. Atomic token-bucket decision (conceptual): elapsed = max(0, now - lastRefill) tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillRate) if tokens < cost: reject without mutation/effect else: tokens -= cost; admit Persist balance + refill timestamp atomically. Validate clocks and numeric bounds. Concurrent read-modify-write from Java without an atomic store operation can overspend tokens.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 5. One limit across many replicas
text: 5. One limit across many replicas With several application instances, independent local counters can admit several times a purported global limit. A shared atomic counter/script can coordinate a chosen scope but adds latency and an availability dependency. Hierarchical or approximate local budgets trade precision for reduced coordination; expose that trade-off instead of calling it an exact global guarantee. Choose failure behavior by operation. Failing open can preserve availability while losing abuse/resource protection; failing closed can block legitimate work during a limiter outage. Keep sensitive invariants elsewhere at their authority. Clock, expiry, hot-key load and retry races need testing in the actual shared-state implementation. Edge admission → Tenant budget → Dependency concurrency → Bounded work queue Passing one budget does not bypass the others. Each protects a different resource.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 6. REST, Spring and AWS mapping
text: 6. REST, Spring and AWS mapping At the edge, apply coarse body/rate controls to avoid spending application resources on obviously excessive traffic. In the application, enforce tenant/resource-aware admission and bound costly downstream concurrency. Gateway throttling and WAF rules do not automatically provide fair scheduling inside a shared worker or database pool. Spring can integrate limiter and bulkhead libraries, and Redis can support selected shared algorithms, but configure the scope and failure policy explicitly. Measure attempted, admitted, rejected and completed work separately. Keep counters bounded and avoid a distinct metric time series for every unbounded identity. Work the boundary through a failure For a token bucket shared across instances, the authoritative operation must read the last refill time, compute available tokens, conditionally debit and persist the new state as one serialized mutation under the chosen store contract. Splitting a read and write across requests lets concurrent callers spend the same token. Use the authority’s time model consistently and bound elapsed-time arithmetic; clock behavior and idle-key expiry must not mint unexpected bursts. Define the unavailable-store policy per operation. Allowing through protects availability but can breach a dependency budget; rejecting protects the budget but denies otherwise valid work. A bounded local fallback partitions or weakens the original guarantee, so explain its limit. Return an appropriate rejection signal and retry guidance, while still requiring clients to use backoff and a deadline. Test Required evidence Parallel callers across replicas Total admitted burst respects the declared shared budget. Tenant changes a caller-supplied identifier Authorization-derived tenant identity still chooses the limit key. Limiter becomes unavailable Observed admission matches the documented fallback policy. Scale-out doubles pods Local buckets do not silently double a supposedly global budget. A rate limit bounds admissions over time; it does not bound concurrent slow operations. Pair it with concurrency/queue limits when service time can grow, and measure rejects separately from admitted requests that later fail.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 7. Worked design: noisy export partner
text: 7. Worked design: noisy export partner For a flash sale, reserve capacity for checkout and bound catalog refill separately. Give tenants a declared allocation and cap total database-facing work. When processing slows, the concurrency gate prevents indefinite accumulation even if arrival rate remains within its ordinary limit. Test a burst at a window boundary, one noisy tenant, shared-limiter failure and a dependency slowdown. Verify rejected requests cause no business mutation, accepted durable work remains recoverable, and retry guidance does not amplify overload. Measure queue age and useful completions rather than celebrating a low rejection percentage alone.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 8. Pitfalls and observability
text: 8. Pitfalls and observability An unbounded queue can make acceptance look successful while deadlines become impossible. Recalculate backlog drain using completion capacity minus new arrivals; if there is no positive margin, waiting will not resolve itself. Reject/defer according to the contract before accepting work without a viable completion path. Fairness is a business and scheduling choice, not just a counter. Separate limits, priorities and queues can help, but starvation and bypass paths still need analysis. Protect administrative/recovery capacity so an incident does not prevent the operations required to repair it. Trap Fix Return 429 after committing a side effect Make admission precede acceptance or return the accepted identity/outcome. Use IP as user identity behind a proxy Resolve trusted identity and proxy boundary; shared IPs can penalize unrelated users. Retry every rejection immediately Honor backoff/deadline and cap attempts. Global limit hides one noisy tenant Track bounded tenant cohorts or controlled diagnostics plus per-tenant policy. Monitor admitted/rejected work, concurrent operations, wait time, oldest job and limiter latency/errors. Confirm the limiter improves completed work and fairness rather than simply moving the queue into the client fleet.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Foundational Rate versus concurrency limit? Rate bounds arrivals over time; concurrency bounds simultaneous resource use. Slow calls can exhaust concurrency even under a modest rate. Foundational What does backpressure mean? A mechanism that reduces or bounds upstream demand based on downstream capacity, instead of allowing indefinite accumulation. Intermediate Why can fixed windows burst at boundaries? A client can spend one full allowance just before reset and another just after, concentrating two windows of traffic into a short interval. Intermediate Can per-pod buckets enforce a strict global limit? Not by themselves. Replicas multiply budgets unless the protocol partitions or coordinates a global allowance. Advanced Fail open or fail closed when Redis fails? Choose per operation from abuse/cost/correctness and availability requirements; use a bounded tested fallback if allowed, not an improvised universal rule. Advanced How do you prevent lost permits after worker death? Use bounded leases/reclamation with correct ownership/expiry and, where protected effects require it, fencing. Test paused workers as well as clean process termination. Intermediate Why can a service overload while requests stay below its rate limit? Service time can increase, so the same arrival rate produces more simultaneous work. Bound active work and waiting at scarce dependencies separately from rate/quota allocation. Advanced How do you combine tenant fairness with total capacity? Allocate tenant-aware budgets while enforcing a global resource/concurrency budget. Independent local or per-tenant limits alone can collectively exceed capacity; a global limit alone can be monopolized. State precision and limiter-outage policies.

title: Rate Limiting & Backpressure
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice API Gateway throttling : limits and behavior. HTTP 429 : Too Many Requests semantics. Bucket4j : token buckets and integrations. Reactive Streams : bounded asynchronous demand contracts. Exercise: name the unit, scope, burst allowance, enforcement precision and outage policy for each limit in one API.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: Overview
text: Follow a growing order store through read replicas, failover, sharding keys, hot partitions and safe rebalancing.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 1. The order database reaches two different limits
text: 1. The order database reaches two different limits The database lesson introduced additional copies for reads and partitions for distribution. Now make ownership explicit. A replica maintains a copy of logical data; a partition owns a subset of data/work. Neither mechanism removes the need to coordinate conflicting decisions or recover from an old owner returning. Follow an order write, a replica read and a failover separately. The write’s acknowledgement policy determines known durability; replication mode affects what a reader may see; failover chooses who may accept later writes. A product offering “replication” does not answer all three questions without its configuration and protocol.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 2. Ask whether you need another copy or another owner
text: 2. Ask whether you need another copy or another owner Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. Replication makes copies of a logical dataset. Partitioning assigns subsets to different storage or execution owners. Copies can improve failure tolerance or read distribution; partitions can distribute capacity. Both introduce coordination. The routing key determines locality, while the distribution of real keys determines whether load is balanced. Partition orders by tenant. Most queries stay local, but one merchant generates half the traffic. Adding partitions for other tenants does little for that merchant. Splitting it by time or an additional bucket distributes work while making some reads fan out. During rebalancing, establish which owner may accept writes and how old owners are fenced. Routing changes without ownership control can create conflicting writers. Check your understanding Foundational A replacement leader is safe because the old one is unreachable. Unreachable to the coordinator does not mean stopped. The old process may still reach storage or clients. Use an ownership protocol and fencing token or storage mechanism that rejects obsolete authority. Intermediate Why can a good average partition load hide an incident? One hot key can dominate tail latency while most partitions are idle. Measure skew, busiest partitions and per-key classes, then choose a split that the workload can actually use.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 3. List routing and recovery guarantees
text: 3. List routing and recovery guarantees Define read freshness, acknowledged-write survival and recovery-time expectations per operation. A dashboard can tolerate lag that is unacceptable for a new order lookup. A low data-loss objective may impose coordination or replication costs that differ from a best-effort browse view. For partitioning, record query locality, cross-key invariants, data size and real key popularity. Tenant count alone does not predict load balance. Plan rebalancing and failure capacity before the dataset or workload outgrows one owner. Functional requirements Route order lookup and recent-order queries. Continue or recover after writer loss. Move data when partitions grow. Targets and invariants Define RPO for acknowledged writes. Read-your-writes for critical user paths. Prevent stale writers after promotion. Avoid hotspots and preserve tenant isolation during movement. Measure data volume, key-frequency distribution and access locality. A partition containing 10% of rows can receive 90% of requests. Equal row counts do not imply balanced load.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 4. Follow a write to its replicas
text: 4. Follow a write to its replicas In asynchronous replication, the writer can acknowledge before a follower applies the change. Routing a fresh post-write lookup to that follower can produce stale absence. Synchronous acknowledgement can strengthen selected durability/visibility properties but increases coordination and needs a precise failure policy. During failover, distinguish choosing a new leader from preventing obsolete writes. The old process may be paused or isolated rather than dead. Terms, epochs or fencing must be enforced at the protected resource. A coordinator’s lease expiry is not a physical stop signal to code still running elsewhere. Writer accepts change → Replicate log/state → Replica applies change → Eligible read or promotion An asynchronous replica can lag; a write acknowledgement may precede its application. Synchronous replication waits for specified replica acknowledgement before returning under the configured policy. It can reduce certain loss windows at a latency/availability cost. Asynchronous replication improves decoupling but can leave a lagging promotion candidate missing acknowledged writes. Exact durable/apply guarantees depend on the engine and settings. Failover must establish one authority, update routing and handle in-flight clients. Fencing prevents the old writer from continuing protected writes after recovery. A successful DNS change does not instantly replace every pooled connection.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 5. Derive a partition key
text: 5. Derive a partition key A partition key determines where work is routed. A tenant key makes many tenant queries local, yet one large tenant may dominate a partition. Splitting by time or another bucket can distribute work while requiring fan-out, aggregation or additional projections. Evaluate the busiest keys, not just average partition utilization. A single coordinated inventory claim may remain hot regardless of partition count. Splitting its authority changes the business protocol, such as allocating bounded stock to separate owners. Consistent hashing can reduce movement under membership changes, but does not by itself solve skew, replication, write ownership or the semantics of concurrent rebalancing. Key strategy Strength Risk Range/time Efficient range scans and lifecycle management Newest range can become hot. Hash of order ID Distributes independent order operations Customer history may scatter across partitions. Tenant ID Keeps tenant-local work together One large tenant remains a hotspot. Tenant plus bucket Splits oversized tenant load Queries/transactions may need fan-out or another index. Choose access paths and transaction locality together. A globally unique external order ID may require a coordinating index/owner if uniqueness spans shards. Do not assume each shard’s local unique constraint enforces a global rule. Consistent hashing reduces key movement when membership changes relative to a simple modulo mapping under common assumptions. Virtual nodes can smooth assignment; replication placement, weighted capacity and hot keys still require design. The hashing algorithm does not move data safely by itself.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 6. Rebalance with explicit ownership
text: 6. Rebalance with explicit ownership Rebalancing moves ownership while traffic continues. Establish a source baseline plus subsequent changes, route reads/writes under a controlled protocol and fence obsolete writers at cutover. A copied dataset that looks complete at one instant can still lose updates made during transfer. Verify critical identities, versions and invariants, and define rollback after new-owner writes begin. Pointing clients back is insufficient if the old owner lacks committed target facts. Budget the load of copy, catch-up and repair so movement does not overload the system it is meant to expand. Conceptual shard move: record migration epoch and source owner copy a consistent dataset / record change position catch up writes while source remains authoritative verify checksums/business counts and lag switch ownership with fencing and routing epoch retain rollback evidence; retire source only after policy permits Dual writes can diverge if either destination fails. Prefer a tested change-capture/replication protocol with an authoritative writer, or define conflict handling and reconciliation explicitly. During cutover, a stale router must not commit to the old owner. A forwarding layer may help, but it needs epoch and retry semantics. Spring Data does not choose a safe shard key automatically. RDS read replicas and engine partitioning have distinct capabilities. DynamoDB partition-key design distributes access under service behavior; verify key/index limits and adaptive behavior rather than assuming capacity is uniform for any key.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 7. Worked design: one oversized merchant
text: 7. Worked design: one oversized merchant Partition order history by a key matching its access pattern and keep the live inventory authority separate where its invariant requires coordination. Use replicas only for operations whose freshness contract permits the selected path. Track hot partitions and lag alongside aggregate throughput. Exercise leader loss, a paused old leader returning, lagging reads and migration during writes. Confirm that acknowledged facts survive under the declared policy and obsolete authority cannot commit protected effects. A successful routing change is not proof of data reconciliation or safe write ownership. Work the boundary through a failure Consider a client that receives a committed order version 18 from the write authority and immediately reads through a lagging replica at version 17. The older read does not reverse the write; it violates read-your-writes if that session was promised it. One possible protocol carries a minimum observed version and routes/waits until a replica can satisfy it, with a bounded fallback to the authority. This requires a real comparable version/freshness mechanism, not an arbitrary wall-clock delay. Now lose the writer. Before promoting another replica, establish the supported fencing and durability protocol: which acknowledged facts can be absent, and how is the old writer prevented from continuing? Promotion alone cannot create missing committed history or revoke an isolated writer’s authority. If the offered replication mode permits an acknowledged-write loss window, expose it as part of the recovery guarantee and reconcile related external effects. Check Why it matters Read after write under injected lag Proves the session contract, not just normal-case speed. Old writer resumes after promotion Proves stale ownership cannot mutate protected state. A hot partition exceeds capacity Shows whether extra unrelated partitions actually help. Rebalance interrupts a consumer Checks duplicate work and ownership transitions during movement.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 8. Failure cases to rehearse
text: 8. Failure cases to rehearse Redundancy is not backup: an accidental delete or corrupt write can replicate successfully. Retain independent recoverable history and rehearse restore/reconciliation. Also test failure-domain concentration; copies sharing one dependency may fail together. Large aggregate capacity can hide a hot key, lagging follower or exhausted failover target. Make ownership, skew and lag observable. More shards or replicas are useful only when they address the measured operation without weakening its required guarantees. Case Required reasoning Promote a lagging replica Quantify possible lost writes and reconcile acknowledged intents. Old primary returns Prevent split authority with fencing/epoch policy. Hot key after adding shards A single key is not split by more partitions alone. Global query across shards Budget fan-out, partial failure and pagination/ordering. Track per-shard latency, traffic, storage, replication lag and rebalancing progress. A fleet average can hide one overloaded shard. Backups remain essential because corruption/deletion can replicate correctly.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Foundational Replication versus partitioning? Replication copies; partitioning divides. A partition can itself have replicas for availability. Foundational Does a read replica scale all writes? No. It can serve suitable reads, while the primary write path may remain the bottleneck. Intermediate Why is tenant ID sometimes a poor key? It gives locality but can concentrate a very large tenant on one partition. Evaluate actual size and traffic skew. Intermediate What does consistent hashing not solve? It does not guarantee hot-key balance, transaction locality, replica placement or correct migration/fencing. Advanced How do you prevent stale writes during a shard move? Use an authoritative ownership/epoch protocol enforced at the write boundary, then copy/catch up/verify and switch with defined retries. Advanced How do you enforce uniqueness across shards? Assign a suitable global owner/index or coordination protocol, or redefine the uniqueness scope. Independent local constraints do not enforce a global rule. Intermediate Why does another replica not automatically fix stale post-create reads? The selected replica may not have applied the acknowledged write. Define read-your-writes and route/use a protocol that supplies it for that journey; do not infer freshness from replica count. Advanced What prevents an old leader from writing after failover? An enforced ownership/fencing protocol at the protected resource, using terms/epochs or equivalent authority checks. Election or lease expiry elsewhere does not physically stop a paused process from returning.

title: Replication & Partitioning
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice PostgreSQL replication : standby and failover behavior. PostgreSQL partitioning : table partitioning scope and limitations. DynamoDB partition keys : distribution and hot-key considerations. RDS read replicas : replication and promotion semantics. Exercise: choose a shard key, then describe how one large tenant and one global uniqueness rule challenge it.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: Overview
text: Connect Java process behavior to container lifecycle, Kubernetes routing, rolling delivery and data-compatible rollback.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 1. A healthy rollout loses a background task
text: 1. A healthy rollout loses a background task A deployment is a transition through overlapping execution and data versions. For a period, old and new instances may both serve requests, consume events and write state. A green health endpoint proves little about whether an old reader can interpret a new status value. Follow one order through a rollout and termination. The application must stop admitting work, finish or durably hand it off, and recover if termination becomes abrupt. Container packaging and orchestration make lifecycle controllable; they do not replace compatible contracts or crash-safe business protocols.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 2. Treat a rollout as overlapping versions
text: 2. Treat a rollout as overlapping versions Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A container packages a process; a deployment controller manages its lifecycle. During a rolling update, old and new versions often coexist. Readiness determines eligibility for traffic. Liveness decides when restarting may help. Graceful shutdown coordinates stopping new work and finishing or handing off existing work. None replaces application compatibility. Version B writes a new order status while A is still serving reads. If A rejects that status, the rollout fails even when every health probe is green. First deploy readers that tolerate the future state, then enable writers, and only later remove old behavior. For shutdown, remove readiness, account for routing propagation and drain active work within the platform grace period. Check your understanding Foundational Rolling back an image rolls back the data. Committed schema and business-state changes survive an image change. Define rollback compatibility and a forward-repair route for writes old code cannot understand. Intermediate Should liveness fail whenever a dependency is down? Usually that creates restart storms without repairing the dependency. Distinguish a stuck process from temporary downstream unavailability; readiness and admission policies require their own capacity analysis.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 3. Define release safety
text: 3. Define release safety State what a successful release preserves: supported clients keep working, committed facts remain readable, accepted work survives interruption, and failure capacity stays within target. Define canary signals and rollback/forward-repair boundaries before enabling new writers. Budget resources during overlap. Deployment surge can create more database connections and cold-cache fills than the ordinary replica count. A rollout losing one availability-zone share also differs from a healthy steady state. Capacity and compatibility are both release requirements. Functional requirements Roll out a Spring service and route to ready instances. Drain in-flight HTTP and reclaim interrupted jobs. Roll back code when necessary. Targets and invariants No lost accepted intent or duplicate protected effect. Keep enough capacity during rollout/failure. Use least-privilege runtime identity and bounded resources. Old/new code must coexist with schema changes. A release may change code, database schema, configuration and message contracts. These components do not automatically roll back together. Plan the compatibility interval explicitly.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 4. Startup, readiness and liveness
text: 4. Startup, readiness and liveness Readiness controls eligibility for traffic; liveness asks whether restart is appropriate; startup handling gives initialization its intended conditions. A shared dependency outage does not automatically mean every process should be restarted. Choose probes that distinguish a stuck process from unavailable external capacity. For shutdown, stop advertising readiness, allow routing state to propagate and drain bounded active work. New requests can arrive briefly while intermediaries update. A worker must finish a durable unit or let repeat-safe redelivery recover it, not acknowledge unfinished work. Graceful termination is an optimization over a crash-safe design, not permission to ignore crash windows. Probe/state Question Pitfall Startup Has initial startup completed? Aggressive liveness restarts a legitimately slow startup. Readiness Should this instance receive intended traffic now? Marking all pods unready for a shared temporary outage can worsen recovery. Liveness Is restart likely to repair this process? Restarting healthy processes because a database is down creates churn. A pod can be alive but not ready. A process can also be ready for status reads but unable to accept a costly operation; coarse readiness cannot express every route’s admission policy. Use application-level rejection where needed. Start and initialize → Become ready → Serve within limits → Drain and terminate Durable jobs can outlive the process. In-memory tasks need an explicit loss policy.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 5. Requests, limits and graceful shutdown
text: 5. Requests, limits and graceful shutdown CPU and memory requests/limits influence scheduling and runtime behavior under the chosen platform. A Java heap is only part of process memory: native buffers, thread stacks and runtime metadata also consume resources. Choose headroom from representative measurements rather than setting heap equal to the container limit. Capacity policies must consider startup, garbage collection, connection acquisition and dependency waits. More pods can remain pending without node capacity; more runnable pods can overload a shared database. Inspect useful completions and saturation rather than assuming a desired replica count has already become usable capacity. Illustrative shutdown protocol: stop admitting new application work allow endpoint/routing changes to propagate drain in-flight requests within a bounded grace period commit/abandon work with a durable reclaim protocol close clients and exit before forced termination Termination hooks, endpoint updates, load-balancer deregistration and application shutdown can overlap. Test their ordering in the actual platform; a fixed sleep alone is not proof of graceful draining. Worker acknowledgement/leases must tolerate hard termination as well as polite shutdown.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 6. Spring and deployment strategies
text: 6. Spring and deployment strategies Use explicit deployment configuration for readiness, shutdown grace, resource budgets and rollout strategy. In Spring, verify server and worker shutdown behavior for the actual runtime. HTTP draining does not automatically stop every scheduled task or safely transfer every consumer lease. Apply expand/migrate/contract sequencing to schema and state changes: make readers compatible, migrate under a restartable protocol, enable new writes, and remove old behavior after the support/rollback window. Feature flags can control exposure, but disabling a flag does not erase new data already committed. Strategy Benefit Risk Rolling Incrementally replaces replicas Old/new versions coexist; surge consumes shared DB/provider budget. Blue/green Switch between complete environments Extra capacity; routing rollback does not undo new data writes. Canary Expose a subset and compare outcomes Small samples can miss rare failures or tenant-specific paths. On EKS/ECS, account for node/task startup, AZ placement, connection pools and dependency quotas. A PodDisruptionBudget constrains certain voluntary disruptions; it is not a universal guarantee against node failure, overload or every rollout behavior.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 7. Worked design: add an order state safely
text: 7. Worked design: add an order state safely Version B adds a payment state while A still serves reads. First deploy readers that understand or deliberately tolerate the future value. Then enable B’s writers for a controlled population and compare customer outcomes, errors and completion age. A probe that never reads the new state cannot validate this compatibility. Interrupt the rollout and exercise rollback against data already written by B. If A cannot handle it, image rollback is not a safe recovery. Disable unsafe new writes if supported and use a compatible reader or forward repair. Also kill a worker after a local commit but before acknowledgement to prove interruption recovery remains correct.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 8. Operational pitfalls
text: 8. Operational pitfalls A rollout can fail without a process crash: enum interpretation, default changes, incompatible serializers or a new scheduled job can break older instances. Test mixed versions and delayed messages, and identify every writer rather than only the web deployment. A restart storm, synchronized cold fills or an oversized surge can turn a small problem into fleet-wide saturation. Keep a safe mitigation path, operational capacity and observable release identity. Declare success from the intended business journeys over an appropriate interval, not solely from all pods being Ready. Failure Mitigation OOM during warmup Budget heap plus native memory; observe real startup/steady-state. All pods restart together Separate dependency health from process liveness. Surge exhausts DB connections Include deployment replicas in shared-resource budgets. Rollback breaks data readers Expand/migrate/contract with tested compatibility windows. Deploy immutable versioned artifacts and track image digest, config version and schema/event compatibility. Store secrets outside image layers and source. Know the difference between restarting, replacing an instance, rolling back code and restoring data.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Foundational Readiness versus liveness? Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness indicates whether restarting may recover a process. They should not be identical dependency checks by default. Foundational Does a container limit equal JVM heap size? No. Native allocations, stacks, metaspace, buffers and instrumentation also consume memory. Intermediate Why can a rolling deployment overload a database? Surge replicas open extra pools and startup/cache-fill work. Count peak rollout resources, not only steady-state replicas. Intermediate Does a PDB prevent outages? It governs specified voluntary disruptions under its semantics; it does not prevent all failures or ensure application correctness. Advanced Why is code rollback not data rollback? New versions may have committed states/schema/events older code cannot interpret. Plan compatibility before enabling writers. Advanced How do you verify graceful shutdown? Exercise real routing/endpoint propagation and hard/soft termination under load, assert bounded draining and durable job recovery, and inspect client-visible outcomes. Intermediate Why is image rollback not necessarily safe? The newer version may have committed states or representations that old readers cannot interpret. Verify mixed-version/data compatibility and retain a forward-repair route; changing the binary does not reverse those facts. Advanced What must a shutdown test include? Late routed requests, bounded drain, forced termination after grace, worker commit/ack gaps and repeat-safe reclamation. Graceful shutdown should improve behavior while abrupt interruption remains recoverable.

title: Deployment & Runtime
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice Pod lifecycle : termination and lifecycle states. Deployments : rollout and availability controls. Kubernetes probes : distinct probe responsibilities. Spring graceful shutdown : server and lifecycle configuration. Exercise: test termination during a request and a background job, then verify the business ledger rather than only the pod status.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: Overview
text: Derive backup, failover, reconciliation and failback choices from acceptable downtime and data loss.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 1. The replica copied the accidental delete
text: 1. The replica copied the accidental delete Replicas help some availability failures but can faithfully copy an accidental deletion. A backup supplies recoverable history; recovery must restore a usable business state. Keep recovery point objective (RPO: tolerated data-loss window) separate from recovery time objective (RTO: tolerated restoration duration). The database is not the whole business world. A restored order ledger may be older than a completed provider payment, message delivery or shipment. Recovery therefore includes reconciling external facts and preventing unsafe replay, not only starting a database process in another region.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 2. Define recovery in business terms
text: 2. Define recovery in business terms Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A backup is a recoverable representation of data at some point. RPO is the tolerated data-loss window; RTO is the tolerated recovery duration. A replica can copy accidental corruption, so redundancy and recovery are distinct. A successful restore must recover a usable business state, not merely a running database. Restore an order database to 10:00 after an incident at 10:05. A payment completed at 10:03 in an external provider may now have no matching local order transition. Before resuming charges, compare provider identities, outbox/inbox state and ledger records. Decide the authoritative source for each fact and prevent replay from issuing a second effect. Recovery includes the reconciliation interval. Check your understanding Foundational An available secondary region means regional recovery is proven. Failover still depends on routing, secrets, capacity, replication lag and write ownership. Failback introduces another transition. Measure the entire rehearsal rather than counting deployed resources. Intermediate What should a restore drill prove? Usable data, application compatibility, dependency access, observed data-loss window, recovery time and business reconciliation. Preserve evidence and repeat after significant topology or schema changes.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 3. Agree on recovery objectives
text: 3. Agree on recovery objectives Define the service scope and failure scenario: instance loss, region loss, corruption and malicious/accidental change may need different recovery paths. State which facts may be lost, which customer journeys must become usable first and which operations must remain paused until reconciliation. Include identities, keys/secrets, routing, capacity, dependencies, audit history and access controls. A backup is unusable if the required decryption key or identity path cannot be recovered. Measure RTO through the actual usable-service boundary and RPO against recoverable committed business facts. Functional requirements Restore the order/payment ledger after corruption or regional loss. Reconcile external provider outcomes and accepted messages. Return safely to the primary operating model. Targets and invariants Example ledger RPO: five minutes; RTO: one hour, validated by drills. No dual active authority for protected writes. Recovery artifacts and keys available during the scenario. Audit evidence and explicit incident ownership. Those objectives are illustrative. A payment ledger may need stricter loss handling than a rebuildable search index. Inventory each data class, dependency and contractual obligation rather than imposing one target on the whole estate.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 4. Select a recovery posture
text: 4. Select a recovery posture Backup/restore, pilot-light, warm standby and active regional operation trade cost, readiness and coordination. Choose from tested requirements rather than ranking the most duplicated topology as automatically best. Extra live writers create ownership and conflict obligations that a standby design may avoid. Failover includes proving the old writer cannot continue protected mutations, ensuring the new path has current-enough data and usable capacity, and directing clients under a controlled protocol. Failback is another migration with target-only facts to reconcile; it is not simply reversing a DNS record. Posture What exists before disaster Trade-off Backup/restore Backups and reproducible infrastructure Lower steady cost; slower recovery and restore work. Pilot light Essential data/core components ready More startup and orchestration at incident time. Warm standby Reduced running environment Faster recovery; scaling/quotas still need proof. Active/active Multiple serving environments Data ownership, conflicts and split authority become harder. Choose from measured recovery duration, cost and correctness, not prestige. Replication lag influences RPO; routing, scaling, validation and operator decisions influence RTO. Active/active does not eliminate recovery from bad writes or compromised credentials.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 5. Back up enough to reconstruct a valid system
text: 5. Back up enough to reconstruct a valid system Confirm what each backup contains, its consistency point, retention, encryption and restore prerequisites. A successful backup job is not a successful restore. Restore into isolation, start compatible application versions and verify critical identities and invariants using representative data. Compare the restored point with external providers and retained message history. A provider charge after the restore point may need to reconstruct local state or trigger a governed recovery action. Replaying an older pending intent with a fresh provider identity can create a duplicate effect. Stable business references make reconciliation possible. Detect and scope incident → Choose recovery point → Restore and validate → Switch authority safely Failback is a further planned transition, not simply pointing DNS back.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 6. AWS and Spring recovery boundaries
text: 6. AWS and Spring recovery boundaries Automate reproducible infrastructure and configuration while keeping credentials and recovery access governed. Ensure the alternate environment can reach required identity providers, KMS keys, queues, object stores and external integrations. Dependency and quota readiness can dominate the recovery timeline. Write a runbook with evidence gates: protect/fence old authority, restore/catch up, validate critical state, enable selected writes, reconcile the unresolved population and observe business outcomes. Each step needs an owner and a safe stop/repair condition. Exercise the procedure rather than assuming infrastructure-as-code proves recoverability. Recovery checklist (workload-specific): incident scope + write-stop/authority decision restore target and time/source position schema/config/key availability ledger invariants + provider reconciliation routes, credentials, quota and capacity validation controlled reopen + monitored failback plan Spring services restarting against a recovered database must tolerate schema/state and replayed messages. Reconcile inbox/outbox positions: a restored ledger may have forgotten an effect a provider already performed. Stable external identity is crucial here; replaying everything as new commands can multiply damage.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 7. Worked drill: recover checkout after regional failure
text: 7. Worked drill: recover checkout after regional failure Restore the order ledger to 10:00 after failure at 10:05. Provider payment pay_7 completed at 10:03 and the restored ledger still shows pending. Before resuming irreversible work, match durable provider identity, available event history and order state. Decide the authority for each fact and record the reconciliation result. Validate orders accepted near the boundary, duplicate/replayed events and already-completed shipments. Measure time until the required journeys are usable and the unresolved tail is governed. Retain evidence of observed loss, restoration duration and discrepancies so the next drill can test improvements rather than repeat assumptions.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 8. Recovery mistakes to avoid
text: 8. Recovery mistakes to avoid An available secondary can still lack secrets, usable capacity, current data or compatible readers. A cross-region copy does not protect against every corruption history. Test the declared disaster scenario and the shared dependencies that may fail with it. Prematurely enabling both writers can create conflicts while operators are trying to recover. Preserve ownership and distinguish safe read-only access from write readiness. Restoration success must include business reconciliation and failback planning, not just a healthy endpoint. Mistake Consequence Untested backup Restore/key/schema dependencies fail under pressure. Failover without fencing Two writers can commit conflicting protected state. Forget third-party effects Restored local state can retry already-completed payments. Failback as DNS flip Old data and pooled connections can reintroduce stale authority. Run drills with realistic data size, not an empty database. Measure restore throughput, replay time, DNS/connection behavior and quota approvals. A successful exercise must prove business invariants and the return path, not only that a web page responds.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 9. Interview ladder
text: 9. Interview ladder Foundational RTO versus RPO? RTO bounds acceptable recovery duration; RPO bounds acceptable data-loss time window for the specified scenario/workload. Foundational Why is a replica not a backup? It may quickly copy deletes/corruption. Historical recovery needs retained points and a tested restore protocol. Intermediate What must be restored besides rows? Schema, configuration, access to keys/secrets, event positions, dependencies and enough evidence to reconcile external effects. Intermediate Does active/active remove DR? No. Bad writes, compromise and cross-region dependencies can affect every active copy; recovery and ownership still require design. Advanced How can restoring create duplicate charges? The restored ledger may lack a completed external effect. Preserve/query provider identity and reconcile before retrying unknown work. Advanced What proves a DR plan works? A realistic timed drill demonstrates the declared RPO/RTO, invariants, dependency readiness, controlled authority switch and tested failback. Intermediate What does a successful restore fail to prove? That the application and dependencies work, keys/secrets are usable, acknowledged business facts meet RPO, and external effects reconcile. Measure the entire required recovery journey. Advanced Why can replay after restore create another payment? The restored local state may predate a provider completion. Replaying with a fresh identity discards the connection to the existing effect. Reconcile original provider references before issuing another action.

title: Disaster Recovery
heading: 10. References and practice
text: 10. References and practice AWS DR strategies : postures and trade-offs. RDS point-in-time recovery : restoration mechanics and boundaries. AWS Backup : protection and recovery features. Exercise: write a one-page runbook for corruption and another for region loss. Identify which steps and recovery points differ.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: Overview
text: Follow committed order changes into search and analytics, then handle duplicates, old events, backfills and rebuilds.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 1. A database filter is not relevance search
text: 1. A database filter is not relevance search The order database is authoritative, but product search needs relevance, text analysis and retrieval shapes different from the write model. A projection derives a read representation from source facts. It can make queries useful without becoming the authority for inventory, current price or permission. Follow one source change until it is searchable. There is an interval between commit and projection visibility, and failures can extend that interval. Define freshness and recovery before adding a search engine; otherwise a fast search result can be mistaken for a current business decision.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 2. Treat a projection as a derived answer
text: 2. Treat a projection as a derived answer Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. The order database records authoritative transactions. A search index reorganizes facts for retrieval, ranking or filtering. A projection is a derived representation maintained from source changes. CDC captures changes from a source mechanism; event time is when the business event happened, while processing time is when the pipeline handled it. An order changes from pending to paid. If a delayed pending event arrives after paid, a blind overwrite moves the projection backward. Carry source versions or an equivalent ordering rule, handle deletion records and define replay identity. For a backfill, connect the snapshot to a change position so updates during the scan are not lost. Refresh delay is visible in search even when the source commit succeeded. Check your understanding Foundational Replaying all events always reconstructs the correct view. Only with complete retained history, compatible interpretation, correct ordering/deduplication and a defined starting state. Some sources retain only a bounded log.
