Schema evolution and external enrichment can also change replay results. Intermediate Can search results authorize a purchase? Use the authoritative path for current inventory, price and permissions when the invariant requires it. A stale projection can suggest candidates without authorizing the final business mutation.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 3. Define freshness and authority
text: 3. Define freshness and authority Write both the retrieval need and the freshness contract. Text ranking, filters, facets and exact lookups are different operations. Bound result size and query cost, enforce tenant/security policy, and identify which decisions must be rechecked authoritatively after search returns candidates. For the pipeline, define source identity, versions, deletion handling, retained history and recovery ownership. A backfill must coexist with live updates, and replay must not repeat external side effects. Measure age/version lag and reconciliation errors alongside indexing throughput. Functional requirements Index product/order views for search. Build daily totals and support correction/backfill. Rebuild projections while changes continue. Targets and invariants Authoritative writes remain in the owning system. Duplicate/out-of-order data must not corrupt derived state. Illustrative search freshness under one minute. Deletes, privacy rules and schema evolution propagate. A source row appearing in a search result does not authorize access. Include tenant/visibility filtering and enforce sensitive access at the appropriate authoritative boundary. A search result is not proof of current price or stock.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 4. Understand the search representation
text: 4. Understand the search representation A search index reorganizes documents and terms for retrieval. Analysis/tokenization changes what queries mean; an exact identifier lookup and a relevance-ranked description search need different field/query choices. Model filters, sorting and access control explicitly rather than indexing raw database rows without a retrieval contract. Index publication and refresh can delay visibility after ingestion. That is separate from source commit success. A search hit is evidence from a derived view; authorize the final resource operation and validate current inventory/price through the required authority. Restrict fields and query complexity so one flexible search cannot create unbounded work or disclose other tenants. Committed source change → CDC / outbox → Transform and validate → Versioned projection The projection can be rebuilt. Its progress and errors need durable evidence.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 5. Snapshot plus changes without a gap
text: 5. Snapshot plus changes without a gap Change data capture (CDC) obtains changes through a supported source mechanism. It is not automatically a complete domain event contract: row changes may require interpretation, ordering and transaction-context handling. State which source position and identity let the consumer recognize progress and repetition. Join a consistent baseline to subsequent changes using a known position or equivalent supported protocol. A bulk scan followed by an arbitrary later subscription can miss intervening updates; applying an old copied row after a newer event can regress the projection. Carry version/ordering guards, handle deletions and verify reconciliation under concurrent source writes. Illustrative projection event: eventId, aggregateId, aggregateVersion, operation, occurredAt, payload apply only when the version/order policy permits record durable progress after committed projection work include tombstones/deletes and schema version handling CDC can expose low-level row changes, while an outbox can publish intended domain events. Select based on what consumers need and which producer coupling is acceptable. Neither eliminates duplicate delivery. Retention and source-log cleanup must exceed expected outages/catch-up time or require a resnapshot plan.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 6. Event time, windows and corrections
text: 6. Event time, windows and corrections Event time describes when the business event happened; processing time describes when the pipeline handled it. A delayed event can arrive after a later business fact. Windowed aggregates need an explicit late-data and correction policy rather than treating arrival order as business order. Choose what a watermark or lateness threshold means for your source and result contract. Closing a window is a policy decision, not proof that no earlier event can ever appear. Retractions/corrections, deduplication and replay must preserve the intended aggregate when historical data changes or arrives late. Work the boundary through a failure Suppose a five-minute event-time window closes at 10:05, but an event timestamped 10:03 arrives at 10:08. A watermark is a progress estimate used by the processing system; it does not prove that every older event has arrived. Choose an allowed-lateness and correction policy based on source disorder and the business result. Processing time tells when the worker handled the event, which answers a different question. Policy Trade-off Drop beyond the bound Final results arrive sooner, but omitted facts need a declared tolerance and a count. Update/retract a published aggregate More correct under late data, but consumers must support revisions and identities. Send to a correction path Keeps the fast path bounded; requires an owner and a deadline for corrections. Replaying a source can resend an old fact after a newer update or deletion. Use source identity and a supported ordering/version rule at the projection boundary; arrival order alone can resurrect stale data. A tombstone must survive the replay/correction window or be replaced by an equivalent durable deletion rule. Test duplicate, delayed, reordered and deleted facts, then rebuild the projection from a known source position and compare business invariants.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 7. Spring, AWS and pipeline tools
text: 7. Spring, AWS and pipeline tools Use a pipeline with explicit source positions, repeat-safe writes and observable failure/quarantine state. On AWS, managed stream/search services can supply parts of ingestion and storage; framework connectors can manage checkpoints. Verify the actual retention, delivery, ordering and schema behavior rather than transferring guarantees between services. For Spring consumers, keep local processing and acknowledgement boundaries clear. Separate a projection rebuild from external business effects, budget its load and support compatible schema evolution. If retained changes are insufficient for replay, establish another baseline instead of assuming an offset reset can reconstruct lost history.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 8. Worked rebuild: change product search mappings
text: 8. Worked rebuild: change product search mappings Rebuild order search while customers continue updating orders. Establish a source baseline and continuation position, populate an isolated target view, then apply subsequent changes with the chosen version/deletion rules. Compare critical identities, counts and sampled/domain-specific results before routing reads. Exercise an update during the scan, a delete, duplicate events, old schemas and a lagging consumer. Confirm that no older copy overwrites a newer fact and no deleted/unauthorized resource leaks through the final access path. After cutover, retain an explicit rollback/reconciliation plan and observe freshness under real load. Test duplicate events, out-of-order updates, deletion during snapshot, connector outage beyond retention and a corrected refund. A low consumer lag can coexist with a broken projection if bad records are silently discarded. Measure end-to-end source-to-query freshness and reconciliation differences.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 9. Backfills and failure recovery
text: 9. Backfills and failure recovery A healthy ingestion process can still produce wrong search: stale permissions, missing deletes, incompatible analysis or silent rejected documents can all escape a throughput graph. Inspect failure records, result correctness and source-to-view reconciliation. Do not make a projection the accidental authority for an invariant merely because it is fast. Rebuilds, lag and retention gaps must have declared behavior, and expensive queries need admission/limits independent of source-write capacity. Case Required policy Backfill replays old side effects Separate projection rebuilding from email/payment execution. Late event changes a closed report Define correction, versioning and re-publication semantics. Source log expires Detect the gap; resnapshot/reconcile rather than claiming continuous progress. Deleted data reappears Preserve delete/version ordering and purge derived/retained copies per policy. Budget backfill I/O, source reads and write load separately from live traffic. Throttle and pause safely. Record source position and transformation version so a result can be reproduced and compared.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 10. Interview ladder
text: 10. Interview ladder Foundational What is a projection? A derived representation optimized for a use case, with its own freshness/update behavior and an identified authoritative source. Foundational Event time versus processing time? When the fact happened versus when the system handles it. Late delivery can make them far apart. Intermediate Why is snapshot plus CDC tricky? A consistent relationship between snapshot contents and the change position is needed to avoid gaps/duplicates and stale overwrite races. Intermediate Does low consumer lag prove search is correct? No. Records may be dropped, mis-transformed or invisible due to mappings/refresh. Check end-to-end freshness and reconciliation. Advanced What does a watermark guarantee? It supports the engine’s configured event-time progress/late-data policy; it is not a universal assertion that older events cannot arrive. Advanced How do you rebuild without an outage? Build a versioned projection, combine snapshot/change capture correctly, validate/catch up, switch routing, and retain a tested rollback/freshness plan. Intermediate Why can a backfill lose an update even when every scan query succeeds? The source changes while scanning. Without a baseline/change-position protocol and correct apply ordering, an intervening update can be missed or overwritten by an older copied row. Verify concurrent changes, deletes and versions. Advanced Can a retained log alone guarantee a correct projection rebuild? Only under explicit assumptions about complete retained history, starting state, compatible interpretation, ordering and deduplication. Retention gaps or changed external enrichment can require another baseline and reconciliation.

title: Search & Data Pipelines
heading: 11. References and practice
text: 11. References and practice Debezium : source-specific snapshot and change semantics. OpenSearch : mappings, indexing and search behavior. Flink event time : timestamps, watermarks and late data. Kafka Streams : stateful processing and guarantees. Exercise: design a correction for a duplicated and then refunded order in yesterday’s revenue view.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: Overview
text: Apply the V4 foundations to six systems. Make each decision traceable to a requirement, invariant, failure or operating constraint.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 1. Start with the user outcome, not a box collection
text: 1. Start with the user outcome, not a box collection You now have mechanisms for contracts, state, copies, delivery and recovery. A design exercise asks you to assemble only the mechanisms required by one problem and defend their boundaries. Begin with a user journey, functional behavior, measurable targets, invariants and constraints before drawing products. Follow a normal transition, then interrupt it at each commit or remote call. State what the caller sees, which fact is authoritative and what identity lets recovery continue. Capacity estimates and implementation mappings come after that argument so the diagram explains a solution rather than disguising missing requirements.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 2. Build an argument, not a product diagram
text: 2. Build an argument, not a product diagram Read this slowly: it establishes the distinction used in the implementation sections. A design starts with required behavior, measurable targets and invariants. An invariant rules out an unsafe outcome; a target allows a measured degree of degradation. Constraints include team skills, existing infrastructure and migration cost. A diagram is useful only after these choices explain why each boundary exists. Take booking one remaining seat. A fast browse projection can show availability, but acceptance needs an atomic claim. A payment timeout creates an unknown external outcome, while a reservation expiry changes local ownership. Define who wins that race and how late payment success is refunded or reconciled. Only then select SQL conditional updates, a durable coordinator and messaging for side effects. Check your understanding Foundational A named pattern is a complete design justification. An outbox explains reliable publication from a local commit; it does not decide reservation duration, payment uncertainty or authorization. Tie every mechanism to a requirement and name the boundary it leaves uncovered. Intermediate How should you answer an unfamiliar design prompt? Clarify one user journey and its invariants, estimate workload, define authoritative state and trace a happy path. Then introduce concurrency and one crash at each commit boundary before scaling or selecting products.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 3. Use one review template
text: 3. Use one review template Ask questions that change a decision: must a booking be final immediately, may search be stale, how long can notifications be delayed, and what must never be duplicated? Separate illustrative load assumptions from known requirements and identify the busiest key or tenant, not only aggregate volume. Include failure, migration and operating constraints. Who owns unresolved work? How are contracts rolled out? What data loss and recovery time are acceptable? A design that works only when every dependency responds promptly has not answered a distributed-systems prompt. Functional requirements Define core operations and access patterns. Choose authorities, identity and state transitions. Explain errors, recovery and rollout. Targets and invariants Set workload, latency/availability and retention targets. State invariants and acceptable staleness. Identify dependency/resource budgets and cost. Plan security, observability and recovery ownership. Interview sequence: 1. clarify users, scope and invariants 2. estimate workload and data shape 3. define APIs/state and authoritative model 4. explain read/write paths 5. pressure-test concurrency/failure/abuse 6. choose scaling and operating policies 7. state trade-offs and unresolved assumptions During an interview, answer the actual follow-up before adding another technology. A small correct design with a clear evolution path is more useful than a large diagram with unexplained guarantees.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 4. Case 1: URL shortener
text: 4. Case 1: URL shortener A short link maps a public identifier to a destination. Begin with unique creation, lookup latency, destination validation, expiry and abuse handling. Choose an identifier-generation/collision protocol and define what a caller may observe if a new mapping has not reached a read copy. Caching can reduce popular lookup cost, but update/deletion and malicious-destination policy affect freshness. A redirect is an HTTP contract with client/cache behavior, not just a database row. Rate-limit creation and investigate hot links, skew and invalidation before adding partitions merely because total link count is large. Work the boundary through a failure Define code uniqueness and redirect mutability separately. For random codes drawn uniformly from an alphabet of size A with length k, the space is A^k. An illustrative 62-symbol, seven-character space has about 3.52 trillion candidates. This is not a collision-free guarantee: enforce uniqueness at the write authority and retry a bounded number of generated candidates. Two different destinations can intentionally receive different codes; duplicate commands should follow the chosen request-identity policy. Redirect caching depends on the edit and revocation contract. If a destination can be corrected or disabled promptly, a long-lived permanent redirect in an uncontrolled client cache can outlast the server change. Choose response/cache policy from the tolerated staleness, and define how malicious or expired links are blocked. Authorization for editing a mapping is distinct from public permission to follow it. Decision Evidence to defend Random versus allocated codes Collision handling, enumeration resistance needs and allocation availability. Cache TTL and invalidation Maximum allowed stale redirect, including browser/CDN behavior. Analytics delivery Whether lost/duplicate clicks are tolerated and whether redirect availability depends on analytics. Keep analytics off the critical redirect commit path if approximate reporting is acceptable. If billing requires exact counted events, specify an identity and durable accounting protocol; client retries, prefetches and bots make a raw HTTP request count different from a human click.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 5. Case 2: notification service
text: 5. Case 2: notification service A notification system separates durable business intent from delivery attempts. The event identifying a required notification differs from provider attempts and user/channel preferences. Define whether completion means accepted by a provider, delivered to a device or acknowledged/read by a person; those are different evidence boundaries. Use durable handoff, per-channel retry policy and stable provider identity where supported. An accepted send with a lost response can repeat; an inbox at the local consumer does not necessarily prevent a second external message. Record residual duplicate risk and recovery policy rather than promising exactly-once delivery to a human. Durable notification intent → Channel queue → Provider attempt → Callback / reconciliation A provider acceptance timeout creates uncertainty; queue acknowledgement does not prove delivery. Baseline: use an outbox from business producers, stable notification/event identities, a per-channel worker budget and a durable delivery ledger. Resolve templates/preferences under an explicit policy; do not replay historical marketing sends blindly after a rebuild. Failure: provider accepted but response vanished. Reuse provider identity or query delivery evidence; where unsupported, document residual duplicate risk. Rate-limit by tenant/channel and quarantine invalid destinations. Spring consumers plus SQS/SNS/SES or another provider can implement selected pieces; inspect each provider’s actual delivery semantics. Test: duplicate event, provider outage, opt-out change before delayed delivery, secret rotation and bounded backlog drain. Audit delivery without storing unrestricted personal message bodies in logs.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 6. Case 3: chat with offline delivery
text: 6. Case 3: chat with offline delivery A persistent WebSocket carries live interaction but does not by itself store a message or guarantee delivery after disconnect. Define the durable acceptance point, message identity, conversation ordering and what a reconnecting client uses to resume. Receipt states should say precisely whether data reached the server, device or reader. Partition by access/locality needs while considering very large groups and fan-out. Bound slow-client buffers, enforce conversation membership at authoritative access and handle duplicates/out-of-order arrivals. Presence is often an expiring observation, while durable message history needs a different retention/recovery contract. Work the boundary through a failure Separate message acceptance, delivery and read status. On send, authorize membership and durably append a message with a stable sender command identity. Return the accepted identity after that boundary; a WebSocket write alone proves neither persistence nor receipt. If the response disappears, the sender retries the same command and obtains the same accepted message rather than producing a second message. Choose ordering scope explicitly. A conversation-scoped authority can assign a monotonic sequence, while unrelated conversations progress independently. Clients reconnect with a last-seen sequence and fetch the durable missing range. Push is a low-latency hint over that history: it may be delayed, repeated or absent. Bound slow-client buffers and reconnect storms rather than retaining unlimited socket work. Injected failure Expected behavior Connection drops after commit Retry resolves the original message identity. Push for sequence 42 arrives before 41 Client fetches/merges the missing range; it does not infer deletion. Member is removed during reconnect History and new delivery enforce the current chosen authorization policy. Offline client returns after retention Protocol explains the gap and supplies an allowed snapshot/history boundary. Delivery receipts and read receipts are separate facts with defined identities and privacy rules. A successful server push should not be labeled “read.” Measure acceptance latency, catch-up lag, dropped slow connections and unresolved gaps as different outcomes.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 7. Case 4: booking scarce inventory
text: 7. Case 4: booking scarce inventory Browsing availability can use a delayed view; confirming the last seat requires an authoritative atomic claim. Model reservation identity, expiry and allowed transitions before adding payment. Distinct legitimate customers can compete even when each request is individually idempotent. Payment completion can race reservation expiry. Conditional transitions decide which state wins, and late success needs the declared re-reserve/void/refund policy. Persist unknown provider outcomes and recovery identity. A distributed lock or queue cannot replace the business rule for an already-reassigned seat. Work the boundary through a failure Two buyers request the final seat. A read that reports one available seat is only an observation; both buyers can see it. Define the authority as a seat row or equivalent serialized owner. A conditional transition from AVAILABLE to HELD records a reservation identity and expiry together; only the successful transition grants a hold. A unique command identity prevents a retry from creating another reservation. General admission counters require their own atomic invariant, not this exact seat schema. Step Durable fact Failure question Acquire hold Seat, reservation identity, owner and expiry Can two successful holds name the same seat? Begin payment Stable provider identity associated with the reservation Can a timeout be recovered without charging a new intention? Confirm or expire Conditional transition from the expected reservation state What happens if expiry races a late payment success? Choose the late-success policy before implementation. If expiry won and the seat was resold, payment success cannot silently recreate the old hold. Reconcile and refund or offer an alternative under a durable, repeat-safe process. Test the race with controlled interleavings: pause after provider acceptance, expire the hold, sell the seat, then deliver the original callback twice. The result must preserve seat ownership and assign the financial recovery to a known owner.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 8. Case 5: private file storage
text: 8. Case 5: private file storage Separate file authorization/lifecycle control from bulk byte transfer. The API issues a scoped upload intent, storage receives bytes, and finalization verifies the intended object before making it usable. Integrity checks, content inspection and ownership are different validations. Handle abandoned multipart uploads, overwrite/reuse behavior and publication races. A download capability has an effective lifetime and may outlive a permission change unless the access protocol prevents that. Keep private objects inaccessible until the required lifecycle state and authorize each new capability request. Work the boundary through a failure Create an upload session only after authorizing the tenant and intended object. Allocate a server-controlled object identity and record an expected size/type policy; a client filename is display metadata. A signed upload capability has its own expiry and scope. Receiving a successful browser response is not sufficient evidence that the service should expose the file to other users. State Allowed behavior Recovery PENDING Upload to the allocated staging identity Expire abandoned sessions and clean up staging objects. UPLOADED / VERIFYING Inspect actual stored metadata and required integrity/security checks Retry verification by session identity; handle duplicate notifications. READY Serve only through the required authorization and delivery policy Treat deletion, retention and revoked access as explicit lifecycle rules. Finalize using a conditional transition and verified object/version identity. A delayed notification for an old object must not approve a replacement. Keep unverified data outside the trusted download path. Test a client that finalizes before upload completion, changes metadata, retries completion and abandons a multipart upload. A cleanup worker must distinguish abandoned staging data from a committed READY object; deleting by age alone can race a legitimate slow upload.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 9. Case 6: payment system walkthrough
text: 9. Case 6: payment system walkthrough For payments, begin with one intent and the point at which money can move. Persist stable local/provider identity, define local and remote commit boundaries, and treat a timeout after submission as an unknown outcome. Use inquiry, supported repeat-safe retry and reconciliation before issuing another irreversible action. Then integrate inventory and fulfillment. Protect local invariants with appropriate atomic mutations, publish committed intents durably, make consumer local effects repeat-safe and reconcile external effects separately. Validate crash gaps, expiry races, cross-tenant access and peak/failure capacity. The chosen AWS/Spring components must map to these responsibilities rather than substitute for the argument. Durable local intent → Stable provider identity → Known / unknown outcome → Reconcile + publish fact The remote provider is outside the local database transaction. Baseline: scope the caller key, validate fingerprint, persist intent, call the provider with stable identity, and store outcome conditionally. A timeout becomes UNKNOWN when the effect may have happened. Authenticated duplicate/out-of-order webhooks use event identity and state/version guards. Failure: a provider without retry identity or inquiry cannot offer the same single-effect guarantee through arbitrary crashes. State that constraint rather than hiding it behind a distributed lock. Reconciliation uses provider references and settlement records with controlled operator actions. Implementation: Spring/RDS ledger and outbox, SQS reconciliation tasks, provider SDK with explicit retry/timeouts, protected status reads and auditable refund commands. Test every commit/call boundary, repeated refund, restore from an older backup and late success. See the detailed API checkout design .

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 10. Cross-case review and trade-offs
text: 10. Cross-case review and trade-offs A pattern name is not a complete justification. An outbox does not choose reservation duration; a replica does not establish fresh reads for every operation; a circuit breaker does not provide idempotency. For each component, state the requirement it serves, its cost and the boundary left unprotected. Finish with evidence: representative capacity measurements, invariant assertions, failure/recovery walkthroughs, compatibility tests and operating ownership. Expose a constraint that makes a requested guarantee impossible rather than silently weakening it or drawing another service. Design question Evidence expected Where is authority? One named owner/store for each invariant. What can repeat? Stable command/event identity and retention horizon. What can be stale? Operation-specific freshness and cache/replica policy. What happens after a crash? Commit/ack/call boundaries and recoverable state. How does it scale? Measured bottleneck and workload distribution. How do we operate it? SLOs, auditability, runbooks, safe rollout and recovery. Finish each design by changing one assumption: a hot tenant, regional failure, strict revocation or a tenfold burst. Explain which part must change and which requirement drives that change. This tests understanding better than memorizing a diagram.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 11. Interview ladder
text: 11. Interview ladder Foundational What should you clarify first? Core users/operations, scale, invariants and acceptable delays. The product name alone does not define the design. Foundational Why not start with a technology list? It hides the reason for choices. Establish the operation and guarantee, then choose mechanisms that supply them. Intermediate When should you introduce a cache? When measured repeated-read cost and a clear freshness/isolation policy justify it, with a protected miss/failure path. Intermediate How do the six cases share an identity problem? Retries/replays need stable intent/event identity, while each domain defines which repetitions are legitimate new work. Advanced How do you answer a region-failure follow-up? Specify authority, replication/RPO, recovery/RTO, dependency readiness and external-effect reconciliation before claiming multi-region safety. Advanced What makes a design defensible? Every component traces to a requirement, its guarantee has a stated scope, and failure/recovery paths are testable with honest limitations. Intermediate Which failure should you analyze first in an unfamiliar prompt? Locate the authoritative commit or irreversible remote effect, remove the response and ask what the caller knows. Then introduce concurrent legitimate operations and a crash on either side of each commit boundary. Advanced How do you compare two plausible architectures fairly? Use the same requirements, invariants, workload, failure conditions and team constraints. Compare protected boundaries, intermediate states, recovery burden, measured capacity and cost, and record evidence-based revisit triggers.

title: End-to-End Design Practice
heading: 12. References and deliberate practice
text: 12. References and deliberate practice HTTP semantics : redirect and method behavior. S3 presigned URLs : capability and expiry behavior. API Gateway WebSocket : connection-oriented service behavior. AWS idempotent APIs : intent and retry recovery. Practice: take 40 minutes for one case. Spend the first five clarifying, then write a contract, data/invariant model, request paths and two failure timelines. Review against the table above.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: Overview
text: Start with an invariant, compare the mechanisms that can enforce it, and write a decision you can defend through a crash.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 1. Start with one decision, not the whole stack
text: 1. Start with one decision, not the whole stack The checkout service must reserve stock before confirming an order. “Use PostgreSQL and Kafka” is not yet a decision: neither name explains which operation prevents overselling. Write the rule first: for a given SKU, available stock must remain nonnegative and a repeated reservation command must not allocate stock again. Then locate the authority that can enforce the rule under concurrent requests. A local conditional update may be sufficient; a distributed workflow becomes relevant only when ownership crosses a commit boundary. A useful decision record contains context, required guarantees, options, chosen approach, failure behavior, operational cost and revisit triggers. Record what was measured and what remains an assumption. An assumption such as “one database can serve the next year” needs an explicit load-test or utilization trigger, not an indefinitely valid promise.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 2. Separate hard rules from preferences
text: 2. Separate hard rules from preferences Input Example Effect on choice Invariant No negative stock Needs atomic enforcement at the stock authority. Freshness Browse availability may lag five seconds Permits a projection for browsing, not final reservation. Target Illustrative p95 reservation under 150 ms Constrains coordination and critical-path dependencies. Constraint Team operates PostgreSQL and EKS Makes an unfamiliar store an additional cost requiring evidence. Preferences can be traded. An invariant cannot be silently weakened to reach a latency target. If requirements conflict, expose the conflict to product owners through concrete outcomes: “the page may show a seat that another buyer has just claimed” differs from “two buyers receive confirmed ownership.”

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 3. SQL or NoSQL: derive from operations
text: 3. SQL or NoSQL: derive from operations Choose when Candidate Prove before adoption Related writes and local invariants dominate PostgreSQL / RDS Constraints, transaction contention, indexes, pool capacity and restore. Known keyed operations and distributed managed capacity dominate DynamoDB Partition distribution, conditional mutation, transaction limits and exact read path. Aggregate-shaped documents change together MongoDB Document size, update atomicity, index cost and cross-document rules. Text relevance and faceting dominate Search projection Freshness, replay, deletion and source-of-truth separation. Do not compare product categories in the abstract. Express a real operation, expected key distribution and transaction scope. A single hot inventory key remains a coordination point in any store. Splitting that key requires a business allocation protocol, not merely a new database brand.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 4. REST or messaging: start with completion semantics
text: 4. REST or messaging: start with completion semantics Use a synchronous request when the caller needs a bounded immediate answer and the dependency fits the deadline. Use a durable asynchronous handoff when acceptance can be separated from completion. The API must then expose pending, terminal and recovery states. A message bus does not make the caller’s original operation complete. Question Synchronous choice Asynchronous choice Must the caller learn a final result now? Return the result within a bounded deadline. Return acceptance plus a durable operation ID when deferral is allowed. What survives a process crash? Durable local operation state and retry identity. Durable handoff plus deduplication and replay policy. What does coupling cost? Availability and latency of required dependencies. Schema evolution, backlog, eventual completion and recovery ownership. Spring HTTP clients, Kafka clients and SQS SDKs implement communication. Application state machines still own business completion. Retry libraries cannot decide whether another charge is safe.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 5. Transaction, saga, or reservation?
text: 5. Transaction, saga, or reservation? Prefer a local transaction when the relevant facts share one authority and commit boundary. When independent authorities are necessary, describe the intermediate states first. A saga coordinates local commits and recovery; a reservation temporarily allocates a resource while later steps run. A saga may use reservations, and neither makes remote effects part of a local ACID transaction. For booking, reserve a seat until a defined expiry. If payment completes after expiry, a coordinator must apply a declared rule: obtain a new reservation if allowed, otherwise refund or route to manual recovery. A queue, retry annotation or distributed lock cannot decide that business policy.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 6. Worked decision record: protect inventory
text: 6. Worked decision record: protect inventory Context: one inventory authority; requests can repeat; payment is external. Decision: reserve using a positive-quantity conditional SQL update and insert the reservation and outbox in one transaction. Scope a unique operation ID by tenant. Keep payment outside the lock-holding transaction and persist its unknown/terminal states. Rejected: Java read-then-write, because concurrent buyers can both pass; a Redis-only lock, because ownership can expire while work continues and it does not itself make SQL mutations atomic; moving inventory to another store without a measured need, because it adds migration work without removing the invariant. Trade-offs: hot SKUs serialize, reservations need expiry and reconciliation, and payment completion can race cancellation. Evidence: race tests, affected-row checks, expiry/payment reconciliation and a contention benchmark. Revisit: measured hot-key throughput exceeds safe capacity or independent domain ownership becomes necessary.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 7. Decision 1: cache the view, protect the purchase
text: 7. Decision 1: cache the view, protect the purchase The shop’s product description is read frequently, while merchant changes are occasional. Browse responses may lag under a stated policy; checkout must apply current pricing and stock rules. This is the trigger for a cache decision: repeated read cost is measurable, and the product allows some copies to be stale. If the indexed query is already cheap at the projected workload, adding another dependency may not yet be justified. First define the reusable representation: tenant, product, language, currency and any relevant personalization. Record the actual source-read cost and popularity distribution. Then compare options using the same failure conditions. Do not compare a warm-cache benchmark against an unindexed database scan and call the difference an architectural result. Alternative What it provides Failure/cost to own Indexed source only One authority and simpler freshness Repeated source work; bound capacity and query cost. Local Caffeine view No network hop on local hits Independent copies; cold starts and cross-instance freshness. Shared Redis/Valkey view Reusable shared representation Network/serialization dependency; miss/refill races and source fallback. Public HTTP/CDN cache Reuse near public readers Cache-key/privacy rules; personalized representations require a different policy. Selected under these assumptions: use a shared product-description view only where measured savings justify it, and edge-cache public media. Keep personalized discounts separate. Checkout uses authoritative rules rather than trusting the browse copy. Commit source updates with durable invalidation intent if lost invalidation needs recovery. The reader/writer refill race still needs the selected freshness protocol; the outbox does not make cache publication part of the source transaction. Rejected shortcut: put stock in a cache and rely on TTL for correctness. Expiry does not coordinate two purchases. Likewise, catching every cache exception and falling through to SQL can turn cache loss into database overload. Cap fallback/refill, use permitted stale data or reject optional reads, and measure the protected checkout outcome. Evidence gate: compare source work and useful completion latency under warm/cold cache, a hot key, slow old fills, invalidation delay and tenant-key variation. Revisit: freshness needs tighten, personalization changes the key space, hit distribution changes or the miss path cannot meet the failure contract. The decision record should retain those assumptions and measurements, not just the selected product name.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 8. Decision 2: move receipt delivery off the request
text: 8. Decision 2: move receipt delivery off the request Checkout is durable after its local transaction, but email latency holds the customer connection. Product accepts eventual receipt delivery and requires the intent not to vanish after acceptance. That permits separating order acceptance from receipt completion. It does not permit calling an in-memory task queue a durable delivery contract. Alternative Acceptance and recovery Reason to choose/reject Synchronous provider call Caller waits; response can be uncertain Choose only if bounded completion must be part of this contract and recovery is explicit. In-memory async executor Fast handoff within process lifetime Insufficient as the only record of required accepted work. Local outbox plus worker Order and intent commit together; relay may repeat Fits durable deferred work when consumer/provider repetition is handled. Retained event log with independent consumers Replay and separate progress by group Useful when those requirements justify partition, retention and consumer operations. Selected under these assumptions: commit OrderAccepted/receipt intent with the local order state, relay it to the chosen queue and create a repeat-safe local delivery task. Keep notification identity separate from delivery attempts. Choose SQS-style work dispatch when one durable job owner is enough; choose a Kafka-style retained log when independent replay/order requirements and operations justify it. Both require effect-specific recovery. The provider can accept the email while its response disappears. If it supports stable identity or inquiry, use that contract; otherwise state the residual duplicate-delivery risk and the policy for ambiguous attempts. An inbox proves only the protected local task/mutation boundary. It cannot make a human receive exactly one message under every provider failure. Evidence gate: interrupt after order commit, after publish, after local task commit and after provider acceptance. Preserve identity and prove the intent remains recoverable without issuing uncontrolled repeats. Measure accepted-to-delivered age and unresolved attempts, not only queue depth. Revisit: receipt completion becomes mandatory before order confirmation, replay requirements change, the provider contract changes or backlog cannot meet the target.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 9. Decision 3: retain the relational stock authority
text: 9. Decision 3: retain the relational stock authority Two buyers compete for the last unit. The service already owns inventory and reservations in one relational database. The rule is that available stock never becomes negative and one intended reservation is not applied twice. Begin with the atomic decision and workload, not a general claim that one database category scales better. Alternative Invariant boundary Trade-off Conditional SQL mutation plus reservation transaction Stock check/decrement and local reservation commit together Hot rows, transaction duration, deadlocks and pool capacity require measurement. Redis lock around SQL writes Separate temporary ownership and durable state Lease expiry/stale owners and cross-system failure gaps; lock alone is not the invariant. DynamoDB conditional/transactional model Appropriate DynamoDB-owned items under its exact protocol Migration, access model, key skew and transaction/read-path semantics. Partitioned stock allocations Separate bounded ownership portions Changes allocation/rebalancing and product availability behavior; not merely more shards. Selected under these assumptions: validate positive quantity, enforce stable scoped command identity and perform the conditional decrement with reservation/outbox changes in one transaction. Check affected rows, update multi-item operations in a deliberate order and handle bounded whole-transaction retry where required. Keep the payment provider outside lock-holding work and preserve unknown outcome recovery. A Redis lock is rejected as the only correctness mechanism because a paused worker can return after lease expiry, and the lock does not atomically commit the SQL effect. A store migration is rejected without evidence that the current authority cannot meet the workload or ownership need. That does not declare another store inferior; it identifies an unproven benefit and a definite new migration boundary. Evidence gate: concurrent last-item requests, duplicate identities, rollback after reservation failure, deadlock retry, expiry/payment races and representative hot-SKU contention. Revisit: measured sustainable throughput or team/data ownership changes. Any replacement must preserve the same invariant and failure tests, with a controlled write-ownership cutover.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 10. Defend the decision
text: 10. Defend the decision Intermediate Why not choose the fastest database? A benchmark without the actual invariant, key distribution and failure mode can measure an irrelevant operation. Establish required semantics first, then compare sustainable throughput and operational cost. Advanced When is a distributed lock justified? When exclusive ownership is necessary and a defined lease/fencing protocol can prevent obsolete owners from acting. Prefer authoritative conditional mutations when they already enforce the invariant; a lock alone is not durable effect deduplication. Intermediate Why compare the same failure scenario for every alternative? Warm happy-path performance can hide the cost or correctness weakness of one option. Hold workload, invariants, freshness and failure assumptions constant, then compare useful completion, recovery and operating burden. Advanced What should a rejected alternative record contain? The requirement it fails or the cost not justified by current evidence, its remaining merits, and the assumption change that would warrant reconsideration. Avoid permanent product rankings unsupported by the actual operation.

title: Architecture Decision Guides
heading: 11. Read with a question
text: 11. Read with a question AWS architecture decision records : structure a durable decision and its consequences. PostgreSQL isolation : check which anomalies a proposed protocol permits. Saga orchestration : inspect distributed recovery rather than assuming rollback.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: Overview
text: Investigate six fictional incidents: cache storms, duplicate payments, stranded fulfillment, mixed versions, restore gaps and cached authorization.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 1. Use a repeatable investigation method
text: 1. Use a repeatable investigation method Start with customer impact and the invariant at risk. Preserve a time window, affected population and identities before logs rotate. Form at least two plausible explanations; an alarming graph alone is not causation. Compare changes, dependency behavior and business state. Mitigate using the smallest action that protects correctness, then verify recovery through completed business outcomes. Use this sequence in each case: symptom → evidence → competing hypotheses → discriminating check → mitigation → repair → recovery proof. Do not replay work merely because a queue is quiet or an HTTP call timed out. First establish whether the effect already happened.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 2. Case 1: a cache expiry becomes a database incident
text: 2. Case 1: a cache expiry becomes a database incident Symptom: catalog p99 rises after a popular collection expires. Application CPU is moderate; database connections and lease wait spike. Hypotheses: a query regression, database resource loss, or synchronized misses. Correlate expiry/miss rate, active queries, query plans and the deployment timeline. Stable plans plus a sudden concentration of identical reads support the stampede hypothesis. Mitigation: constrain refill and fallback concurrency, serve permitted stale catalog data, and shed lower-priority work. Increasing every pod’s connection pool would add pressure. Repair: per-key request coalescing, TTL jitter where appropriate, bounded refresh and admission control. Local single-flight reduces duplication within one process; fleet-wide behavior still needs analysis. Recovery proof: source query load returns within its budget, oldest waits shrink, cache freshness stays within its contract, and checkout success does not degrade. A recovered hit ratio alone is insufficient. See the cache race explanation .

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 3. Case 2: a customer reports two charges
text: 3. Case 2: a customer reports two charges Symptom: two provider charges map to one intended checkout. Hypotheses: duplicated HTTP attempts, webhook replay, or reconciliation creating a fresh provider operation. Compare tenant, order ID, local operation key, request fingerprint and provider operation IDs across attempts. Trace IDs can differ during a legitimate retry and cannot establish business uniqueness. Discriminating check: did an earlier call time out after provider success, followed by a call with a new key? If so, local uniqueness may be intact while the remote boundary is unprotected. Mitigation: stop unsafe automatic reissue for affected states, reconcile provider records and handle refunds under the established business policy. Do not bulk-mark unknown payments failed. Repair: stable provider identity, durable UNKNOWN state, bounded reconciliation and explicit retention behavior. Recovery proof: every affected local operation maps to its known provider outcome, unresolved cases have owners, and crash-window tests no longer produce a second effect.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 4. Case 3: a healthy broker hides a stalled business flow
text: 4. Case 3: a healthy broker hides a stalled business flow Symptom: paid orders remain unfulfilled while broker delivery is healthy. Hypotheses: publication failed, consumers lost capacity, a poison schema repeats, or remote fulfillment is slow. Compare oldest business-state age, outbox lag, delivery rate, consumer commit rate and quarantine records. Queue depth alone may fall when messages move to a dead-letter queue. Mitigation: isolate the incompatible population, retain event identity and restore a compatible reader. Replaying without a durable consumer guard can create duplicate shipments. Repair: compatibility checks, per-event failure isolation and an explicit replay protocol. Decide whether preserving order for an aggregate requires pausing later events rather than skipping the bad one. Recovery proof: affected paid orders reach the correct terminal fulfillment state, oldest age drains and replay does not duplicate shipment identity. See acknowledgement boundaries .

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 5. Case 4: a successful rollout causes intermittent errors
text: 5. Case 4: a successful rollout causes intermittent errors Version B writes a new status that version A cannot parse. Probes pass because they never read that state. Errors appear only on A pods and only for recently changed orders. Distinguish this from network flakiness by joining version, state and failure class with bounded telemetry dimensions. Disable the incompatible writer feature if that is safe, retain evidence and deploy a tolerant reader. Rolling all pods back to A can spread the failure because new data survives. Prevent recurrence using expand/contract sequencing, mixed-version contract tests and backward-compatible readers before writers. Recovery requires checking the already-written population, not just the next health probe.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 6. Case 5: restore succeeded, payment state is wrong
text: 6. Case 5: restore succeeded, payment state is wrong Scenario: a fictional shop restores its order database to 10:00 after corruption at 10:05. The application starts and ordinary reads succeed. A customer charged at 10:03 now sees pending. An operator suggests replaying all pending payments. The immediate risk is a duplicate financial effect, not a failed database health check. Competing hypotheses: the provider declined, a callback was delayed, the restored ledger predates a successful capture, or the order/provider mapping is wrong. Preserve the restore position and incident time range. Compare stable payment intent, provider operation/reference, retained callbacks/outbox history and the order ledger. A missing local terminal row after restore is not evidence that the provider did not act. Decisive evidence: the original provider operation shows capture at 10:03 while the restored state is from 10:00. Classify the local state as needing reconciliation; do not create a fresh provider key. If the provider cannot establish an outcome through its supported contract, keep the case unresolved and governed rather than inventing success/failure. Mitigation: pause unsafe reissue for the affected population, retain evidence and reconcile under controlled identities. Restore the local truth through a conditional/audited recovery path that cannot conflict with a later refund or an existing terminal transition. Keep unrelated safe journeys available where the incident boundary permits it. Permanent repair: extend the recovery runbook beyond database startup to include external facts, message positions and write ownership. Test a restored ledger containing old pending operations alongside newer provider and shipment outcomes. Record observed RPO/RTO against the required business journey, including reconciliation time. Recovery proof: every affected intent maps to an established provider outcome or an explicitly owned unresolved case; no new charge was issued merely because the restored row was pending. Validate customer status and fulfillment prerequisites, retain an audit trail and rehearse failback. A green endpoint alone cannot establish recovery.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 7. Case 6: a removed permission still grants access
text: 7. Case 6: a removed permission still grants access Scenario: a fictional partner loses access to an account, but a later export/download request succeeds. Credential validation passes. The incident could be stale authorization caching, an already-issued bearer download capability, missing resource checks or a shared response-cache key. These paths require different containment; calling it “JWT is broken” is not a diagnosis. Evidence to preserve: the permission-change time, principal/tenant mapping, operation/resource identity, policy version or cache lifetime, relevant request/response cache metadata and capability issue/expiry times. Exclude bearer tokens and signed URLs from general logs. Compare the exact service path with a fresh authoritative permission lookup under controlled diagnostic access. Discriminating checks: if new capability issuance consults an old cached allow, investigate policy freshness and invalidation. If a link was issued before revocation, inspect its effective lifetime and access contract. If another tenant’s response is reused, inspect all representation/key dimensions. A valid signature or unexpired token does not prove current permission over the resource. Mitigation: stop issuing new unauthorized capabilities, constrain the affected cached decision/response path and apply supported revocation or access controls under the incident policy. An issued bearer capability may remain usable under its contract; state that exposure honestly and use the actual storage/access mechanism to contain it. Do not pretend deleting an application cache necessarily invalidates every copy or signed capability. Permanent repair: define permission freshness per operation, current checks for new exports/download links, safe cache identity and retention, and the model for long-running delegated work. Test valid credentials against another tenant, permission removal during a job, a stale cached allow and a capability issued before revocation. Separate authentication, authorization and representation privacy in both code and tests. Recovery proof: new unauthorized requests cause no side effects or disclosure, affected cached representations are handled under policy, remaining capability exposure is bounded/contained under the supported mechanism, and audit evidence identifies the impacted population. A successful login test or cleared cache counter is insufficient.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 8. Incident interview follow-ups
text: 8. Incident interview follow-ups Intermediate Why not restart everything first? It can destroy evidence, multiply cold-start load and replay work without knowing previous outcomes. Protect the invariant and collect minimal decisive evidence; restart when there is a supported hypothesis that it helps. Advanced How do you prove the mitigation worked? Observe restored customer outcomes, bounded backlog age and correctness of affected records over an explicit interval. Resource graphs alone may recover while business work stays stranded. Intermediate Why not replay every pending payment after a restore? The restored ledger can be older than external completed effects. Match stable provider identities and reconcile before reissuing; local absence or pending state does not establish remote failure. Advanced Why can permission removal fail to revoke an existing download link? A previously issued bearer capability has its own lifetime and access enforcement. Current application authorization can stop new issuance without necessarily invalidating old capabilities. Define and test the actual revocation/expiry contract.

title: Production Failure Case Studies
heading: 9. Primary reading
text: 9. Primary reading Google SRE troubleshooting : hypothesis-driven investigation. SQS dead-letter queues : isolation, retention and redrive considerations. OpenTelemetry signals : understand what each signal can establish.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: Overview
text: Work from daily demand to peak load, simultaneous work, failure headroom, durable bytes and a transparent cost model.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 1. Define the units before calculating
text: 1. Define the units before calculating Suppose a shop serves 2 million active users per day, each making 20 eligible reads. That is 40 million reads/day, or about 463 requests/second averaged over 86,400 seconds. An assumed 8× peak gives roughly 3,704 requests/second. The peak multiplier is an assumption requiring traffic evidence. Reads and writes must be modeled separately; a ten-item batch request is one HTTP request but potentially many database operations. State whether measurements count attempts, successful operations or useful business completions. Retries increase attempts without increasing useful work. Separate cache hits, misses and background refresh from user request volume. Use decimal GB or binary GiB consistently and specify whether replication and indexes are included.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 2. Derive simultaneous work and headroom
text: 2. Derive simultaneous work and headroom Little’s Law relates average work in a stable measured system: L = λ × W. At 3,704 admitted requests/second and 0.120 seconds average response time, average in-flight work is about 445. This is not a p99 prediction, and substituting p99 latency into the formula does not produce p99 concurrency. Burst and tail behavior require measurement or a queueing model. If one replica sustains 350 requests/second at the required latency under the representative mix, twelve replicas supply nominal capacity above the example peak. To remain under 60% of that tested maximum during peak, ceil(3704 / (350 × 0.6)) gives 18 replicas. This only works if shared dependencies sustain that rate. Losing six of eighteen replicas leaves about 88% nominal utilization: acceptable failure capacity must be tested explicitly, not inferred from the normal 60% target.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 3. Estimate durable bytes and write amplification
text: 3. Estimate durable bytes and write amplification At one million new orders/day and 2 KB serialized data/order, the base input is approximately 2 GB/day and 730 GB/year using decimal units. Indexes, row overhead, revisions, retention, replicas, backups and telemetry are additional. Apply explicit measured multipliers rather than calling the base figure “database size.” A replication factor is not a backup strategy. With an illustrative index/overhead multiplier of 1.8, the primary live dataset is about 1.314 TB/year before retention effects. Three live copies would be about 3.942 TB collectively, but billable storage semantics depend on the service. Do not multiply an AWS line item again if replication is already included in that product’s billed unit.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 4. Estimate cache, backlog and partitions
text: 4. Estimate cache, backlog and partitions Calculation Illustrative result Qualification DB reads = incoming reads × miss fraction 3704 × 0.05 ≈ 185 reads/s Assumes every miss causes one read; include stampedes, writes and refresh. Queue drain = backlog / (completion − arrival) 120000 / (900 − 500) = 300 s Only if both rates remain stable and retries do not consume the margin. Memory payload = concurrent work × retained bytes 445 × 64 KB ≈ 28.5 MB Excludes runtime, stacks, buffers, object overhead and idle resources. Connections = replicas × pool maximum 18 × 20 = 360 possible connections Compare with database capacity and operational reserve. Partition count is constrained by sustainable per-partition throughput, ordering and key skew, not simply aggregate volume. A single hot key may remain serialized. Consumer count above available parallel work cannot force additional throughput.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 5. Build a price-independent AWS model
text: 5. Build a price-independent AWS model Use current regional quotes when making a budget. This lesson intentionally uses no asserted current AWS prices. Enumerate units, then attach verified prices: compute instance-hours or vCPU/memory time, database compute/storage/I/O, request charges, transfer, NAT processing, logs, traces, backups and cross-region replication. Include minimum provisioned capacity and operational environments. monthly_cost = compute_hours * compute_unit_price + storage_GB_month * storage_unit_price + billable_requests * request_unit_price + transfer_GB * transfer_unit_price + telemetry + backups + other_fixed_costs Use low/base/high demand and retention scenarios. Compare cost per useful completed order alongside total spend; retries, failed work and excessive logging can make a service more expensive while traffic looks unchanged. Managed-service cost may be higher per unit while reducing operating effort; record that separately rather than inventing a precise labor saving.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 6. Worked review: defend a peak-day plan
text: 6. Worked review: defend a peak-day plan Begin with the 3,704 read/s assumption. Validate the 350 read/s replica figure under realistic cache hit ratio, tenant skew, payload size and dependency behavior. Test with one availability-zone share unavailable. Cap database connections and admissions, pre-scale where startup delay exceeds burst tolerance, and define what work is shed first. Then repeat with 20% cache misses and a dependency slowdown. The database read estimate becomes about 741/s before write/refresh overhead; CPU scaling alone cannot establish this is safe. Publish the measured saturation point, latency distribution, useful completion rate and cost range. Revise the plan when a model assumption changes.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 7. Worked review: change the assumptions, recalculate the load
text: 7. Worked review: change the assumptions, recalculate the load Use an illustrative workload of 1,000 read requests/second. Each cache miss performs two database reads; hits perform none. At a 90% hit ratio, the normal source demand is 1,000 × 0.10 × 2 = 200 database reads/second. The HTTP rate and the database operation rate are not the same quantity. Background refresh, writes, retries and stampedes are excluded from this simplified baseline and must be added for a real service. Change Calculation Meaning Hit ratio falls to 50% 1,000 × 0.50 × 2 = 1,000 DB reads/s Five times the ordinary source demand. Cache is lost 1,000 × 1 × 2 = 2,000 DB reads/s Ten times the ordinary source demand before amplification. Average HTTP duration rises from 0.1 s to 0.8 s Stable averages: 100 → 800 in-flight requests Not a prediction of tail concurrency or a DB pool setting. Eighteen pods, pool max sixteen 18 × 16 = 288 possible connections Fleet demand before surge, jobs and operations. Six additional surge pods 24 × 16 + 40 reserved = 424 Exceeds an illustrative safe connection budget of 400. One candidate is a pool maximum of fifteen at twenty-four total pods: 24 × 15 + 40 = 400. This only satisfies that connection-count budget. It does not prove the database can execute 360 expensive queries concurrently, nor that the workload meets latency during failure. Find a useful execution/concurrency operating point under contention, then use admission to keep demand within it. For cost, compute units for normal, peak and failure/rebuild conditions separately. Cache loss may increase database reads and telemetry while useful throughput falls. Attach current regional unit prices only after deciding which operations are actually billable, and avoid multiplying replicas into a service unit that already includes replication. Report ranges and cost per useful completion with the assumptions beside them. Review question: what invalidates this plan? A different request mix, fan-out, hot key, service-time distribution, cache failure policy, replica loss or rollout limit can do so. Preserve the worksheet and measured saturation evidence so another reviewer can reproduce the argument.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 8. Estimation interview
text: 8. Estimation interview Foundational Why start with daily traffic if it is not the peak? It supplies a reproducible baseline and exposes assumptions. Apply and justify a peak model rather than presenting the average as capacity. Advanced Why is 50% fleet CPU not proof of spare capacity? A database, hot key, connection pool or single-threaded stage may be saturated. Aggregate CPU also hides skew and failure-domain concentration. Identify the limiting resource for the target operation.

title: Capacity & Cost Estimation
heading: 9. Sources for verification
text: 9. Sources for verification AWS Well-Architected : performance, reliability and cost trade-offs. AWS Pricing Calculator : apply current region-specific prices to explicit units. Google SRE overload : measure overload and admission behavior.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: Overview
text: Open the implementation boundary: trace execution, connection acquisition, local commits and resource release in a Spring service.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 1. Follow one checkout request
text: 1. Follow one checkout request A request reaches a controller, validates a DTO, invokes an application service, opens a database transaction, runs statements, commits and serializes a response. HTTP-client calls, executor handoffs and event listeners can insert additional boundaries. Draw where the transaction begins and where each resource is held. Latency accumulates in waits as well as execution. The servlet request thread and a database connection are different resources. A thread may wait for a connection, or hold one while waiting for a remote provider. Increasing the request executor can admit more waiting work without increasing database throughput. Instrument pool acquisition and statement time independently.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 2. Thread pools and connection pools
text: 2. Thread pools and connection pools A bounded executor limits active tasks; a bounded queue limits waiting tasks. Rejection must have an explicit caller-visible or durable recovery policy. An unbounded queue can turn overload into delayed failure and memory pressure. HikariCP pools reusable database connections, but its maximum does not mean the database can execute that many expensive queries efficiently. Budget across the fleet: twenty pods with a pool maximum of twenty can request 400 connections, plus administration, migrations and other services. A larger pool can increase lock contention and query time, keeping connections occupied longer. Determine a useful operating point through workload measurement, not by setting every pool to the server limit.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 3. Spring transaction boundaries
text: 3. Spring transaction boundaries In ordinary proxy-based Spring transaction management, an external call through the proxy applies the transaction advice. Calling another annotated method on this bypasses that proxy boundary. The annotation expresses a policy; it does not make arbitrary code transactional. Use an explicitly proxied application-service boundary or a deliberate programmatic transaction when the control flow requires it. // Teaching fragment: caller invokes this Spring-managed service. @Transactional public Reservation reserve(Command command) { int changed = inventory.reserveIfAvailable( command.sku(), command.positiveQuantity()); if (changed != 1) throw new InsufficientStock(); Reservation saved = reservations.insert(command); outbox.append(saved.toEvent()); return saved; } // Call the payment provider outside this lock-holding transaction. The repositories must participate in the intended transaction manager and data source. Default rollback rules commonly differ for unchecked versus checked exceptions; configure and test the intended policy. Catching a database exception does not necessarily restore a usable transaction. JPA flush can surface a constraint violation later than the method that staged the write.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 4. Virtual threads, reactive code and blocking
text: 4. Virtual threads, reactive code and blocking Virtual threads make many waiting Java tasks cheaper to represent; they do not increase database connections, provider capacity or CPU. Do not use a pool of virtual threads as the concurrency control for a scarce dependency. Use explicit admission or permits around the resource while creating virtual threads according to the supported execution model. Reactive pipelines coordinate nonblocking work and backpressure when the participating components support it. Blocking a small event-loop pool can stall unrelated requests. Wrapping blocking JDBC in a reactive type does not change JDBC into nonblocking I/O. Conversely, a virtual-thread approach may simplify blocking code but still requires cancellation, context and resource limits. Choose for the actual workload and team, not as a universal throughput upgrade.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 5. Memory, GC and context propagation
text: 5. Memory, GC and context propagation A growing heap may reflect retained pending work, cache growth, oversized payloads or a leak. GC activity is evidence to interpret, not the root cause by definition. Compare allocation rate, live set after collection, pauses, queue lengths and payload distribution. Bound collections and request bodies before merely enlarging memory. MDC is commonly thread-bound. Executors, reactive pipelines and message boundaries need supported context capture, restoration and cleanup. ScopedValue can carry scoped in-process values but does not propagate HTTP headers or create distributed spans. Keep security context, trace context and business operation identity distinct and avoid leaking one request’s state into another.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 6. Worked diagnosis: low CPU, slow requests
text: 6. Worked diagnosis: low CPU, slow requests Observe 90% database-pool occupancy, long acquisition waits and moderate query execution time. A code change placed an HTTP provider call inside @Transactional after the first query. Connections are now held across remote waits. Verify the timeline using tracing plus transaction/pool metrics, then move the remote step behind a durable state boundary without losing recovery identity. Bound provider waits, use a persisted payment state and reconcile unknown outcomes. Do not simply move the call earlier if that creates an unrecorded remote effect. Validate resource release on timeout and exception, mixed load across endpoints and total fleet connection usage.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 7. Worked review: the method returned, but did the transaction commit?
text: 7. Worked review: the method returned, but did the transaction commit? A repository save call returns an entity and the caller immediately sends an email. Later the surrounding transaction fails during flush or commit. The in-memory return value was not proof of a durable order. JPA may defer SQL, and a database constraint can surface after the line that staged the change. Trace the actual commit boundary before coupling a nontransactional effect to that return. Place the business mutation and durable notification intent inside the intended local transaction. Publish the intent after commit through a recoverable relay. Verify that the application call crossed the Spring transaction proxy or used the deliberate programmatic mechanism, that repositories share the intended data source/manager, and that exception/rollback policy matches the requirement. Observation Hypothesis Evidence/repair Annotated method invoked through this Proxy advice may be bypassed Inspect call boundary; use an explicit managed application boundary. Constraint appears late Deferred flush/commit exposed the rule Observe actual SQL/transaction outcome; do not send external effects based on staged state. CPU quiet, pool wait high Connections held across slow work Separate acquisition/query/remote wait and shorten lock-holding scope safely. Exception was caught but commit still fails Transaction may be rollback-only/unusable Recover through the correct transaction boundary instead of continuing blindly. Do not mechanically add REQUIRES_NEW or a larger pool. A new independent transaction changes atomicity and can consume another connection; a remote provider still remains outside both commits. First decide which facts must commit together and what evidence is needed if the next step is unknown. Then test success, constraint conflict, rollback and response loss using the actual engine and framework configuration. For runtime diagnosis, compare allocation/live set, queue length, pool wait and useful completion before blaming GC or choosing reactive/virtual-thread execution. Cheaper waiting tasks can still overwhelm finite dependencies. The runtime model should make the boundary easier to enforce and observe, not hide it.

title: Java & Spring Architecture Internals
heading: 8. Runtime interview ladder
text: 8. Runtime interview ladder Foundational Does @Transactional include a remote REST call? It does not enlist an ordinary remote HTTP service in the local database commit. The remote effect can succeed even if the local transaction rolls back. Intermediate Why did self-invocation not start a new transaction? Under normal proxy mode the call did not cross the transaction proxy. Refactor the boundary or use an explicit supported transaction mechanism; do not rely on an annotation that was never intercepted. Advanced Do virtual threads remove backpressure needs? No. They reduce the cost of many waiting tasks, which can actually make it easier to overload finite dependencies. Bound admissions and scarce resources separately.
