title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: Overview
text: Attempt the questions before opening the answers. Progress from definitions to concurrency, crash recovery and an architect-level checkout argument.

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 1. Use the answer ladder
text: 1. Use the answer ladder Begin with a two-sentence definition and one concrete operation. Then extend the answer only as the question demands. A foundational question tests vocabulary; an intermediate question tests implementation under concurrency; a senior question tests crash windows and trade-offs; an architect question tests ownership, constraints and operations together. Score Evidence 0 Names a product or pattern with no mechanism. 1 Defines the concept and a plausible happy path. 2 Explains implementation and the key concurrency/failure case. 3 Defends alternatives, scope, recovery, measurable validation and operational ownership. The rubric assesses the reasoning shown, not years of experience. For each answer below, add a follow-up you would ask as an interviewer. A strong response explicitly distinguishes what is known from what must be clarified.

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 2. Foundational: define before naming libraries
text: 2. Foundational: define before naming libraries Foundational What makes an operation idempotent? Repeated application of the same intended operation has the same intended effect as applying it once. Responses need not be identical. For POST /orders, explain operation identity and atomic duplicate enforcement rather than assuming POST itself provides the guarantee. Follow-up: what happens when the same key carries a different payload? Foundational Authentication versus authorization? Authentication establishes identity under a trust model; authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action on a resource. A valid token does not grant access to every order. Follow-up: where is tenant ownership checked for an export? Foundational Cache versus read replica? Both can serve copies, but an application cache reuses selected answers with explicit key/freshness policy, while a read replica maintains a database copy under its replication protocol. Both can be stale. Follow-up: which path can confirm a newly committed order? Foundational Latency versus throughput? Latency is the time for an operation over a stated boundary; throughput is completed operations per unit time. Higher concurrency can improve throughput until a resource saturates and waiting increases. Follow-up: which measurements distinguish CPU work from pool waiting?

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 3. Intermediate: make the mechanism concrete
text: 3. Intermediate: make the mechanism concrete Intermediate How do you prevent two buyers taking the last item? Use an authoritative conditional mutation such as UPDATE inventory SET available=available-:qty WHERE sku=:sku AND available>=:qty with positive validated quantity. Check affected rows and commit the reservation in the same transaction. Follow-up: how is a repeated reservation request recognized? Intermediate How do you avoid lost updates in a REST API? Expose a version or strong validator with a defined representation scope; require a conditional update and atomically compare the expected version at the storage boundary. Return the documented precondition failure when stale. Follow-up: what does the client do after reading the new state? Intermediate Why can cursor pagination still repeat or omit results? The cursor must encode stable ordering and a unique tie-breaker, but changing sort fields, deletions and dataset evolution still affect traversal. Define whether the contract is a live traversal or a snapshot. Follow-up: how would an export establish a consistent view? Intermediate How would Spring publish an event safely after an order commit? Store order and outbox in the same local transaction, then relay committed rows. A relay can republish after a crash, so consumers need repeat-safe processing. An in-memory after-commit callback alone is not a durable publication ledger. Follow-up: what protects an external fulfillment effect?

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 4. Senior: walk the failure window
text: 4. Senior: walk the failure window Senior The payment provider succeeded but the client timed out. Now what? Treat the outcome as unknown until verified. Keep the provider operation identity, query or retry according to its idempotency contract and persist reconciliation progress. A fresh payment key risks another charge. Follow-up: what if the provider retention window has elapsed? Senior Why did adding replicas increase errors? Test whether a shared bottleneck was amplified: total pool capacity, retries, hot locks or dependency quotas. Compare fleet admissions with useful completions and dependency saturation. Bound global pressure before adding callers. Follow-up: what capacity remains when one zone fails? Senior A message repeatedly fails deserialization. Should it be skipped? Preserve the event and identity, isolate the incompatible population and establish ordering requirements. Skipping can allow later aggregate events to overtake a prerequisite. Repair a compatible reader and replay under a durable deduplication/state protocol. Follow-up: what proves business recovery? Senior How do you roll back a release that wrote new data states? Check whether old code can read and act on those states. Image rollback does not reverse data. Disable unsafe new writes if supported, deploy compatible readers or forward repair, then reconcile affected records. Follow-up: what would have prevented the rollout hazard?

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 5. Architect: a complete checkout prompt
text: 5. Architect: a complete checkout prompt Prompt: design checkout for a multi-tenant shop with a flash sale, external payments and asynchronous fulfillment. Browsing can be stale, overselling is forbidden, and an unknown payment must not cause a second charge. Ask for actual workload, latency, completion and recovery targets before choosing components. Expected reasoning: establish authoritative inventory and payment state; reserve atomically with repeat-safe identity; commit outbox with local facts; invoke the provider with stable identity outside lock-holding transactions; persist unknown outcomes; deduplicate local consumer effects and reconcile remote fulfillment. Isolate tenants, cap admissions, define expiry/late-success policy and measure completion age. Strong follow-ups: Where is the last-item claim serialized? Who wins payment versus reservation expiry? What if the provider has no idempotency or lookup contract? Which read may be stale? What state survives a region loss? A strong answer may conclude a guarantee cannot be met under a stated provider constraint and propose a business or integration change. Architect How would you evaluate two technically plausible designs? Compare invariant coverage, intermediate states, failure recovery, peak/failure capacity, security and team operating cost. Require evidence at the critical boundaries, not only a clean topology diagram. Architect What if the business requires instant completion during every dependency outage? Expose the contradiction: a final authoritative remote result may be unavailable. Offer durable acceptance with pending state, degraded scope or a revised availability guarantee. Do not promise an outcome that the system cannot establish.

title: Architecture Interview Workbook
heading: 6. Evaluate three answers to the same checkout prompt
text: 6. Evaluate three answers to the same checkout prompt Prompt: a Spring API creates an order, reserves the last item and calls a remote payment provider. Clients retry after timeouts. Explain how you prevent overselling and duplicate charges, including a crash after the provider accepts payment. Answer Assessment Missing reasoning “Use Redis, Kafka and retries.” Score 0: product names without a protocol. No authority, commit boundary, stable identity or recovery evidence. “Use a unique request key and @Transactional.” Score 1–2 depending on the mechanism explained. Can protect a suitable local effect, but does not include an ordinary provider call or explain competing legitimate buyers. “Protect local stock/identity atomically, persist remote intent, reuse provider identity and reconcile unknown outcomes.” Score 3 only when qualifications and validation are defended. Must still state provider limitations, expiry races, retention, authorization and evidence. A strong answer begins by asking whether payment acceptance must be synchronous and what the provider supports. It validates positive quantity, scopes command identity and protects the local reservation with a conditional mutation/appropriate transaction protocol. A repeated intention must not reserve again, while two distinct valid intentions still compete on the stock authority. It keeps remote payment outside lock-holding local work, records the original provider identity and treats a lost response as unknown. A durable worker/status path reconciles that intention. If the provider has no adequate identity or inquiry contract, the answer exposes the weaker guarantee and governed unresolved path rather than claiming exactly once. Reservation expiry and late success require a conditional business recovery policy. Follow up with four variations: reuse the same key with a different amount; replay after retention; a worker resumes after ownership expires; restore local data to before a provider completion. The candidate should preserve the right identities and authority under each change. Naming another component without repairing the failure argument does not improve the score. Intermediate What distinguishes an adequate local answer from an architect-level answer? The local mechanism can explain uniqueness and a transaction. The stronger answer defends every independent authority, ambiguous outcome, failure/retention condition, operating owner and measurable validation without promising an impossible guarantee.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: Overview
text: Follow an overlapping-version change from inventory and compatibility through backfill, cutover and the point where rollback needs data reconciliation.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 1. Inventory the change before moving anything
text: 1. Inventory the change before moving anything Begin with consumers, data writers, scheduled jobs, runtime dependencies, message schemas and operational tooling. A Java upgrade changes more than a compiler target; a database migration changes more than a connection string. Capture the current contract and failure behavior so improvements do not silently break existing consumers. Separate reversible routing/configuration changes from irreversible or difficult-to-reverse data changes. Define which source owns each fact at every stage. A rollback plan that says “point back to the old database” is incomplete if new writes exist only in the target.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 2. Expand, migrate, verify, contract
text: 2. Expand, migrate, verify, contract Suppose full_name becomes given_name and family_name. Add nullable new columns first and deploy readers that tolerate incomplete backfill. Define the transformation honestly: many names cannot be split reliably by spaces. Backfill in bounded, restartable batches using stable progress identity and conditional updates so a concurrent edit is not overwritten. During overlap, define which representation is authoritative and how old writers remain compatible. When all readers and writers are upgraded, verify reconciliation and stop the old path. Remove old columns only after the rollback/support window ends. If two representations are stored, their consistency is a protocol to own, not an incidental implementation detail. Do not treat a successful deployment as permission to drop old columns immediately. Old instances, batch jobs, delayed messages and rollback paths may still require them.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 3. Java and Spring upgrade sequence
text: 3. Java and Spring upgrade sequence Inventory application server support, bytecode targets, libraries, reflection, removed APIs, build plugins, agents, TLS providers and test tooling. Choose a supported target combination using the actual vendor support matrix. Upgrading Spring and changing the deployment runtime at once can make failures harder to isolate; stage changes where compatibility allows. Compile and test business paths, integration protocols, serialization, security, database behavior and startup/shutdown. Benchmark representative CPU, allocation, latency and memory with comparable limits. A lower GC pause in a microbenchmark does not prove a safe production migration. Canary the new runtime, retain compatible images and define observable rollback triggers. If an application server does not support the required JDK, evaluate a supported framework/JDK combination, a server upgrade or moving the application to an independently supported runtime. Do not assume putting newer bytecode in a container makes the host application server support it.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 4. Database copy and catch-up
text: 4. Database copy and catch-up An online migration usually needs a consistent baseline plus a position from which subsequent changes can be captured. A bulk copy without a matching change stream can miss or reorder updates during the scan. Preserve deletions, transaction/order semantics required by the target and schema transformations. Measure lag by relevant source positions and business freshness, not merely whether a process is running. Verify counts, keys, sampled/full checksums where meaningful, query results and critical invariants. Define a controlled write-ownership switch using fencing or a brief write pause when necessary. “Zero downtime” must specify what readers and writers can observe and whether bounded retries or deferred acceptance are allowed.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 5. Extract a service with a strangler route
text: 5. Extract a service with a strangler route Choose one cohesive behavior and place an explicit interface around it. Route a limited operation or tenant population to the new implementation while retaining ownership rules. Shadow reads can compare outputs if authorization, side effects and sensitive data are controlled. Shadow writes to real business providers are unsafe without a separate harmless environment. Avoid long-lived uncontrolled dual writes. If local commit and remote publish are required, use a durable handoff and reconciliation protocol. Move data ownership deliberately; leaving every service able to mutate the same tables undermines independent boundaries. Retire old routing and jobs only when no supported path still depends on them.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 6. Worked cutover: new account and new database cluster
text: 6. Worked cutover: new account and new database cluster Assume one authoritative writer and a target cluster in a new account. Establish identity/network/secret access, copy a consistent baseline, capture changes, apply idempotently and compare critical records. Rehearse full recovery before scheduling cutover. Freeze schema changes or handle them through an explicit migration-compatible process. At cutover, stop or fence source writers, record the final change position, wait for target application and invariant checks, then enable the target writer and redirect traffic. If the target is unhealthy before accepting writes, routing back may be straightforward. After target-only writes begin, rollback requires reverse synchronization, a bounded write pause plus merge/reconciliation, or forward repair. Never enable both writers merely to reduce downtime. Gate completion on business paths, queue consumers, scheduled jobs, access control and telemetry in the new account. Record unresolved differences and retain the source according to the recovery plan. Cross-account DNS success does not prove that IAM, KMS, network policies and background jobs all function.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 7. Worked plan: choose a bounded write pause and defend it
text: 7. Worked plan: choose a bounded write pause and defend it Assume the business permits a short, explicitly bounded write pause while reads remain available under a stated freshness contract. The source database has one writer; the target receives a baseline plus change capture. A bounded pause can simplify the final ownership transition compared with independently writable copies. It is a product/operating decision, not an automatically acceptable shortcut. Gate Required evidence If it fails Before scheduling Restore/recovery rehearsal, access/keys, capacity, schema compatibility and reconciliation plan Repair prerequisites; do not make the production cutover the first rehearsal. Baseline plus catch-up Known source position, changes/deletes applied under the supported protocol, critical comparisons Continue catch-up or repair; do not infer completeness from row count alone. Pause/fence source writers Web, jobs, consumers and support writers controlled; final position recorded Do not activate target writes while source authority remains uncontrolled. Target ready Final position applied, invariants/critical journeys verified, routing and identity prepared Resume source only under the still-valid rollback boundary. After target-only writes Business paths, queues/jobs, access control, useful completion and reconciliation observed Use defined reverse catch-up/forward repair; a routing change alone cannot restore missing facts. The key rollback boundary is the first target-only fact the source does not have or cannot interpret. Before that point, reverting controlled routing may be straightforward. After it, the plan must account for reverse synchronization, transformed data, conflict ownership and external effects. Never enable both writers merely to make the service appear available. Bound the pause by evidence and a stop condition, not optimism. If final catch-up or validation exceeds the allowed interval, follow the rehearsed abort/recovery path. Keep critical comparisons restartable and ensure ongoing reads do not produce a misleading promise of current writable state. This plan differs from a release that only changes binaries, but both require mixed-version compatibility. Record exactly which operations were deferred/rejected, which facts moved, and how accepted work survived. Completion means the intended journeys and recovery posture work in the target environment, not merely that a new connection string succeeds.

title: Migration & Modernization
heading: 8. Migration interview
text: 8. Migration interview Intermediate Why is dual write not an atomic migration strategy? Two independent writes can fail separately. Define durable capture, ordering, retries and reconciliation, or constrain the transition so one authority remains clear. Advanced When does rollback become a data problem? As soon as the new path commits facts the old path lacks or cannot interpret. Define that boundary before cutover and prepare reverse catch-up or forward repair with business reconciliation.

text: 1. A practical review cycle Read one lesson, close it and explain the main operation in plain language. Name the invariant, the simplest implementation, its failure window and the chosen mechanism. Then compare your explanation with the answered checkpoints. Record a gap such as “I cannot explain lease expiry” rather than marking a whole subject vaguely incomplete. A suggested cadence is next-day recall, another review later in the week and a later scenario-based review. Adjust it to your recall rather than treating a schedule as proof of learning. The checklist below is browser-local, is not an assessment and does not sync across devices. Reset review marks

title: Revision & Learning Toolkit
heading: 3. A focused glossary of commonly blurred terms
text: 3. A focused glossary of commonly blurred terms Find a term Invariant A condition that must hold after every allowed state transition. A target permits a measured error budget; an invariant defines a forbidden outcome. Atomicity A defined group of changes commits together or does not commit. Specify which resources share that boundary. Isolation Rules governing concurrent transaction observations and permitted anomalies. A transaction annotation alone does not specify every business-safe protocol. Consistency The observations or histories an operation permits. State the model and scope; do not confuse replica freshness with multi-system atomicity. Idempotency Repeating one intended operation preserves its intended effect. Recognizing identity and enforcing it atomically are separate implementation tasks. Deadline The latest acceptable completion time across a defined operation. Individual timeout budgets should account for remaining time. Backpressure A mechanism for signaling or limiting work according to downstream demand/capacity. It requires participating boundaries and does not create capacity. Outbox A durable publication intent committed with local business changes, then relayed. Relaying can repeat and does not include arbitrary remote effects. Inbox A durable consumer-side receipt/identity record used with a local mutation to make repeat processing safe within that boundary. Fencing Rejecting actions from an obsolete owner using authoritative ownership/version evidence. Lease expiry alone does not stop old execution. RPO Recovery point objective: the tolerated data-loss window. Measure it against recoverable business facts, including external effects. RTO Recovery time objective: the tolerated duration to restore a defined usable service, including dependencies and reconciliation. SLI A precisely defined measurement of service behavior, with eligible events and good/bad criteria. SLO A target for an SLI over a stated window. Acceptance and eventual business completion can require separate indicators. Projection A derived representation maintained from authoritative facts. Its ordering, freshness, deletion and replay policies must be explicit. Cardinality The number of distinct values/combinations in a dataset or telemetry dimension. Unbounded metric labels can create unbounded series. Optimistic concurrency A mutation commits only if an expected version or condition still holds. Handle conflicts explicitly rather than overwriting newer state. Compensation A business recovery action after a committed step. It may not perfectly undo the original effect and can itself fail.

title: Revision & Learning Toolkit
heading: 4. Recall the distinction
text: 4. Recall the distinction Pair Key distinction Test yourself Timeout / failed effect Waiting ended / business action did not happen Can the provider have charged already? Cache / authority Reusable copy / fact used to enforce a rule May stale data authorize a purchase? Rate / concurrency Arrivals per time / work currently active What changes when service time increases? Trace ID / operation key Observability identity / repeat-safe business identity Which one prevents a second mutation? Replica / backup Operational copy / recovery representation What happens after a bad delete propagates? Rollback / compensation Revert uncommitted local changes / business recovery after commit Can the customer already have seen the effect?

title: Revision & Learning Toolkit
heading: 5. Self-check: the disappearing response
text: 5. Self-check: the disappearing response A customer creates an order. The database commits, the connection drops, and the customer retries. Explain the possible states without assuming the first request failed. Identify the durable operation identity, payload mismatch policy, concurrent duplicate guard and response reconstruction mechanism. Intermediate What should the answer contain? A stable scoped key, a fingerprint or equivalent mismatch rule, atomic enforcement with the local order effect, and a documented response for completed/in-progress/conflicting requests. A lookup can recover an already committed result. If payment is external, analyze that provider boundary separately. Advanced Change the scenario: the retry arrives after retention expires. The deduplication guarantee may no longer apply. Business uniqueness and provider reconciliation can still matter. Define retention relative to real retry/replay windows and document what happens outside it rather than implying infinite protection.

title: Revision & Learning Toolkit
heading: 6. Recall the boundary: five short scenario checks
text: 6. Recall the boundary: five short scenario checks Attempt each answer before expanding it. Explain the authority, the observation, the uncertainty and the recovery identity in plain language. If you cannot, return to the linked core lesson and try again later with a changed scenario. A checklist mark should reflect an explanation you can give, not only a page you opened. Foundational A cache hit is fast. What has that proved? Only that the cache returned a reusable value according to its current path. It has not proved freshness, tenant isolation or a valid stock/permission decision. Check representation identity and the freshness contract. Intermediate The consumer committed and then crashed before acknowledgement. What happens? Redelivery may occur. A durable consumer-scoped receipt committed with the local effect can recognize the repeat. A remote effect still needs its own identity and recovery contract. Intermediate The same RPS suddenly requires more memory. What changed? Service time or retained work may have increased. In stable averages, more time at the same admitted rate means more work present. Inspect waits, payloads and queues before treating it as a CPU-only scaling problem. Advanced The backup restored, but a customer was charged afterward. What is authoritative? Identify the local restore point and the original provider operation. Reconcile the provider fact and local state before another irreversible action. A restored pending row is not evidence of remote failure. Advanced A token is valid but the user no longer owns the order. What decides access? Current resource authorization under the chosen freshness/delegation policy. Token validity and broad scopes do not by themselves establish ownership; already-issued capabilities can have a separate revocation/lifetime contract. For a second round, change one assumption: remove the provider lookup, add a cache layer, replay an old event or require a tighter revocation bound. Explain which mechanism must change and which guarantee is now impossible without a different contract. This tests transfer of understanding rather than memorization of the original answer.

title: Revision & Learning Toolkit
heading: 7. Explain it without notes
text: 7. Explain it without notes Choose a weak concept and answer: What does it mean? Why is it needed? Which failure exposes it? Where is it enforced? What remains unprotected? What test would disprove the design? Use the interview rubric to assess the answer.
